full_text:
Rookie linebackers Kendal Daniels (pictured) and Harold Perkins are bringing an injection of youth to the Falcons defense. Dale Zanine / Imagn Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — Rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels has been a quick study, according to his Atlanta Falcons coaches and teammates. For instance, on Monday, Daniels found himself on a collision course with Bijan Robinson during a practice drill.
“I was running the alley. He was in the alley,” Daniels said. “But I’m smart enough not to hit Bijan.”
Instead, the two fell back into the comfort of trash talk that dates back to their days as opponents in the Big 12. (Daniels played at Oklahoma and Oklahoma State; Robinson at Texas.)
“It’s fun,” Daniels said. “Me and Bijan talk to each other every day. That’s my big brother now. It’s very fun.”
Much to his chagrin, fellow rookie linebacker Harold Perkins missed the exchange. He would have jumped in. On Daniels’ side, of course. They have been hip to hip since April, when Atlanta drafted Daniels in the fourth round and Perkins two rounds later.
They are dorm roommates at training camp, and following Monday’s practice, Perkins jumped into the media group asking Daniels questions and threw in a few of his own. Daniels has even credited Perkins with helping him catch up on the practice field after a calf injury sidelined him during spring practices.
“KD, that’s my dog,” Perkins said. “I help him, but he helps me out, too. Don’t let him gas me up like that.”
Harold Perkins Jr. crashing Kendal Daniels presser. Asked some good Qs 🤣 pic.twitter.com/YLXU7nzl2I
— Tori McElhaney (@tori_mcelhaney) August 10, 2026
Now, Daniels and Perkins are spending a lot of practice time next to each other with the first-team defense. Those positions may not last into the season. Veterans Divine Deablo and Christian Harris are expected to start Friday’s preseason opener against the Broncos at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, but just the presence of both rookies with the first team in practice is a testament to their progress.
“Kendal and Perk are way ahead of what I was expecting from rookies,” Deablo said. “Obviously they have to keep it up, but I’m excited. They don’t mess up a lot. They are on their P’s and Q’s, for sure.”
The Falcons will play their starters for “one series, (maybe) 10 plays” Friday night, coach Kevin Stefanski said this week, so Daniels and Perkins should get plenty of time on the field.
“I think anytime you have an opportunity as a young player to get reps with the 1s, it’s a great test,” Stefanski said. “It’s a testament to their studying, paying attention in these meetings. It’s a testament to their coaches.”
At the moment, Daniels and Perkins view their relationship as a partnership.
“It’s not a competition against each other. We’re competing with each other,” Daniels said. “We’re competing against who we are going against. That’s how we’ve been looking at it.”
That dynamic could change as the Sept. 13 regular-season opener approaches. While Deablo is established in one of the two starting inside linebacker spots, Harris — who joined the team on a one-year, $2.75 million deal this offseason — could be supplanted by one of the rookies at some point.
“Our relationship has been good since day one,” Perkins said. “Nothing about us was competition. We came in together, and we’ve been working to help get each other better.”
The 6-foot-5, 245-pound Daniels started his college career as a safety, but he has taken to his new position in Atlanta. Daniels will wear the green dot when he’s on the field, meaning his helmet is equipped with the radio that receives the play calls from defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich. Daniels is then responsible for relaying those calls to the entire defense. Deablo will have the green dot when he’s on the field.
“Nothing is easy playing middle linebacker,” Daniels said. “Having to say the call is probably the hardest thing when you are tired. Everybody is depending on you. If you’re dead tired and you can’t get the call out, nobody performs well.”
Daniels’ college coaches signaled the play calls in from the sideline throughout his career, so making the calls is a new experience for him. He practiced it throughout the spring in empty meeting rooms.
“It’s a long call,” he said. “It’s saying it the second time that’s hard when you’re tired.”
Daniels didn’t practice in the spring because Atlanta’s training staff was trying to help him manage a calf injury that has bothered him since college.
“I don’t know what I would call it, tendinitis maybe,” he said. “It wasn’t like something that happened in one practice. It happened over time. I dealt with it all last season, so it’s something we wanted to get figured out.”
He has learned to manage it with a long preparatory routine before every practice.
“Back in college, I didn’t really have time to warm my body up. Now I can take that time,” he said. “I don’t think my body will ever get to 100 percent like I was in high school.”
While Daniels is separating himself with his understanding of the defense, Perkins has stood out for his pass-rush acumen.
“He’s got some natural feel for it,” inside linebackers coach Barrett Ruud said. “You can tell he’s trained himself to do that as well. A lot of linebackers aren’t very comfortable in the pass-rush game and having a couple of go-to moves. He’s put the time in where he already has a couple of those.”
Perkins started his career at LSU as an edge rusher and had 13 sacks in his first two seasons, including 7.5 as a freshman.
“It’s just something that God gave me,” he said. “I’m just natural with it. I can’t explain it. It’s just something I can do.”
He can do it so well that Atlanta’s coaches might be tempted to ask him to play some outside linebacker this year to help make up for the loss of Jalon Walker. A position change feels like the only thing that could break up him and Daniels at this point.
“I am just taking it day by day, trying to build trust with my teammates and coaches,” Perkins said. “I’m not going out there saying, ‘I’m repping with the 1s, or I’m repping with the 2s.’ My mindset is to go out there and kill, whoever I am with.”

full_text:
Rookie Josh Cuevas is among those who make up a fresh tight end room behind veteran Mark Andrews. Stephanie Scarbrough / Associated Press
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Baltimore Ravens rookie tight end Josh Cuevas says it partly in jest, but there’s also a curiosity behind the question that he regularly poses to veteran teammate Durham Smythe. And there’s maybe some desperation mixed in, too.
“I ask him every day, like, ‘Hey, man, does it get easier?’” Cuevas said earlier this week.
Smythe played with the Chicago Bears last year in an offense similar to the one Declan Doyle is installing in Baltimore. He’s also a nine-year veteran who knows the ins and outs of preparing for an NFL season and embracing a specific role.
On that front, Cuevas and fellow first-year tight end Matt Hibner have a lot to learn, and the daily lessons have threatened to overwhelm both players.
“It really is like drinking from a firehose for the first— it’s actually still a little bit like that,” Hibner said. “I think that’s part of the challenge that our offense is trying to establish. Declan talks about it like, ‘Yeah, it’s hard. We want to stress you guys, but also we want to make it complex for us so that it’s complex for defenses.’ That is kind of the whole point.”
The Ravens’ preseason opener against the Philadelphia Eagles Saturday at M&T Bank Stadium represents a milepost for new head coach Jesse Minter’s team, and its young players in particular.
The last three weeks have answered some of the pressing questions that accompanied the start of Ravens training camp. Quarterback Lamar Jackson, who won’t play Saturday — or maybe at all this preseason — is in a good place . He looks healthy and excited about the direction of the team and the offense. Defensive end Nnamdi Madubuike is taking it slow, but he remains on track to return from a career-threatening neck injury. Outside linebacker Trey Hendrickson is fitting in just fine.
When you talk about the lingering questions — and perhaps some of the team’s preseason concerns — the play of the Ravens’ tight ends rises to the surface, particularly because they are expected to be relied on heavily in this new-look offense.
Mark Andrews, the veteran leader of the group, has struggled to find space and hold on to the ball when he does, which is notable as the soon-to-be 31-year-old is coming off one of the most challenging seasons of his career. Hibner and Cuevas, fourth- and fifth-round picks, respectively, have mixed promising reps with plays that show just how far they still have to progress with the regular season looming. Smythe’s confidence and worth as a blocker are evident, but he’s neither a field stretcher nor a big-play threat.
It remains to be seen whether the Ravens possess a viable complementary pass-catching tight end to Andrews or a reliable blocking complement to Smythe. At least in terms of the former, there have been few big plays and far too many drops or bobbles in camp practices.
“I would say nothing is set,” Doyle said Wednesday. “We are still a month away from that first snap against Indianapolis. Over time, roles play themselves out as we continue the installs and introduce different concepts and things and ask guys to be in different spots. Today, you’re watching us do short-yardage, and we’re figuring out who those guys are that we can trust in situations like that. They’re very technical. They’re very specific to defensive structures and jobs that you’re doing. We’re going to ask everyone to do it, take their swing at it, and then we’ll figure it out and reshape from there.
“The tight end position — because they really have a role in pass-game protection and the run game — those are a lot of jobs to have to evaluate. I certainly have a vision of utilizing that position, and at the same point in time, who is doing which role kind of sorts itself out over time.”
Doyle and the Ravens would prefer that their offense remains a mystery for as long as possible, giving them a potential advantage early in the season. However, Doyle’s history alone suggests that tight ends will be heavily involved. He is a former tight ends coach.
As the non-play-calling offensive coordinator in Chicago last year, Doyle was part of an attack that used 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends and two wide receivers) 36 percent of the time, the third-most in the NFL, per Sharp Football Analysis. The Bears also used three-tight-end sets just over 8 percent of the time, the fifth highest in the NFL.
Of course, the Bears also had a tight end room that included Colston Loveland, the 10th overall pick in the 2025 draft; Cole Kmet, a 2020 second-round pick who had 17 touchdowns from 2022 to 2024; and Smythe, another established veteran.
The Ravens, meanwhile, are still trying to figure out what they have beyond Andrews and Smythe. Hibner, who played at SMU, was the 10th tight end taken in the draft, and Cuevas, who went to Alabama, was the 16th. They and Smythe are essentially being asked to replace the departed Isaiah Likely, Charlie Kolar and Patrick Ricard, who joined Andrews in forming one of the NFL’s best tight end rooms in recent seasons.
“They play fast. They know what to do. They are smart kids. They are wired the right way. They work hard at it. They prepare for practice the right way,” said Ravens tight ends coach Zack Grossi. “I thought that has allowed them to kind of show some of their natural skill sets early on because they are not playing slow. I’m pleased with the way those guys have approached things so far, (but) we have a long way to go.”
Asked specifically about what he hopes to see Saturday, Grossi said, “I don’t really think about what I’m hoping to see. We are just trying to be process-driven. What do we have to do that day to get better? What do we have to do for that practice? What’s next? Whatever the next thing is, we give it all of our attention.”
The coaches concede that they are throwing a lot at the rookie tight ends. No. 1, they have to learn a new offense. Then, they have to understand their blocking responsibilities and be able to hold up physically. They have to be able to execute in the passing game, as well. If Hibner and Cuevas are active on game days, they will almost certainly be playing on special teams, so they need to be quick studies in that phase, too.
It’s a lot to ask and probably explains why it can take rookie tight ends some time to settle in.
“They’re giving us a lot of stuff really quickly, and going from that college offense to NFL offense, it can get pretty overwhelming,” Cuevas said. “Knowing you have somebody there to kind of confide in and be like, ‘You know what, what do we have on this play? Are you sure we have this and that?’ — and then we will go back into the notes that we have taken and really get that cleared up. Having that other person in there along the way, along the journey — it has been awesome.”
Hibner and Cuevas are competing against each other, too. Andrews and Smythe will play a lot, and there’s probably room for one of the two rookies to earn a game day role. It seems unlikely that there would be snaps available for both rookie tight ends on game days, unless Hibner and Cuevas both morph into core special-teamers.
So essentially, the Ravens really only need contributions from one of the rookies, which is probably why they’ve taken a patient stance and haven’t brought in another veteran. Arguably, the best free-agent fit came off the board earlier this week when Darren Waller, a former Raven, signed with the Carolina Panthers . That leaves a list of available tight ends that includes Jonnu Smith, Will Dissly, Zach Ertz and John FitzPatrick.
For now, though, it’s Hibner and Cuevas who will get every opportunity to earn their spot. A strong performance Saturday night would be a significant step.
“There is definitely a level up,” Hibner said. “Every play is probably a little bit higher in intensity. There is a lot more athleticism on the field as a whole, but…

title: Bills 53-man roster projection: Who makes the cut as preseason begins? As Saturday’s preseason opener against the Panthers approaches, we look at the Bills’ roster locks and players on the bubble. Joe Buscaglia
summary:

The Buffalo Bills are just a day away from beginning their preseason journey under new head coach Joe Brady. The Bills will play in their first official game at the new Highmark Stadium against the Carolina Panthers at 1 p.m. Saturday.
It’s a game in which many of their healthy starters are expected to play. Along with it, plenty of roster competitions will get their biggest chances to make an impression
full_text:
Buffalo Bills DT Deone Walker leads a revamped defense into 2026. Joe Hrycych / Getty Images
The Buffalo Bills are just a day away from beginning their preseason journey under new head coach Joe Brady. The Bills will play in their first official game at the new Highmark Stadium against the Carolina Panthers at 1 p.m. Saturday.
It’s a game in which many of their healthy starters are expected to play. Along with it, plenty of roster competitions will get their biggest chances to make an impression on Brady and general manager Brandon Beane.
So, with the Bills entering the next phase of the summer before the 2026 regular season, where do things currently stand on the roster after 11 camp practices?
Here’s a brand new Bills pre-preseason 53-man roster projection.
The backup quarterback competition has left a bit to be desired. At first, it appeared Kyle Allen, the clear favorite to be the backup going into the summer, breathed some life into it, making it somewhat of an open competition. However, Shane Buechele has struggled, too, with a multi-interception performance on Thursday in limited team drills. It’s not an ideal backup situation, but Kyle Allen is the better option of the two — but expect Buechele to be back on the practice squad.
James Cook, Ray Davis, Ty Johnson
The only variable about this group right now is the injury to third-down running back Ty Johnson. He was a part of the cluster dealing with a “lower body injury” and Brady declined to give a timetable. As long as he is healthy enough to begin the season, Cook, Davis and Johnson will be the three running backs yet again in 2026.
Cut: Frank Gore Jr., Ian Wheeler
DJ Moore, Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, Joshua Palmer, Skyler Bell, Mecole Hardman
We’ve made it to our first change from the pre-camp 53-man roster projection . Last time around, I had Hardman on the outside looking in, thinking that the Bills could try to get the rookie, Bell, to be their punt returner. During the open practices, Bell was rarely involved in punt return reps. On top of that, everyone else besides Hardman was either a roster long shot or struggled in those punt return reps, and now Bell is injured. So, even though Hardman may only be a onesie position as a punt returner, they might have to keep him and try to work him into a handful of offensive snaps to make it worth it.
PUP: Tyrell Shavers Cut: Trent Sherfield, Stephen Gosnell, Dante Pettis, Ja’Mori Maclin, Mac Dalena, Max Tomczak, Quentin Skinner
Dalton Kincaid, Dawson Knox, Jackson Hawes, Jackson Acker (FB)
I tried to get Keleki Latu on the 53-man roster, I really did. Latu has had an outstanding camp and has been getting increased high-leverage opportunities. But there are just too many positions elsewhere that needed a spot to make one for Latu. His best path would be if the Bills cut both fullbacks, but that doesn’t seem likely at this point. However, if the Bills get creative elsewhere, Latu is my number-one potential surprise to keep at final cuts. As for fullback, I have the Bills going with Acker, as he’s young, cost-controlled for the next three years and a restricted free agent after that. Even if Ben VanSumeren has the experience, I think they could probably get him back to the practice squad as Acker insurance.
Cut: Keleki Latu, Ben VanSumeren (FB), Shane Zylstra
Dion Dawkins, Alec Anderson, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence, Spencer Brown, Austin Corbett, Jude Bowry, Tylan Grable, Lloyd Cushenberry III
If you asked what this would look like a little over a week ago, I would have leaned toward Cushenberry being on the outside looking in and with Van Pran-Granger making it. However, since that point, McGovern went down with an injury, and in the two practices after on Monday and Tuesday, Cushenberry was getting the lion’s share of first-team time with Josh Allen. Along that same timeline, Van Pran-Granger has struggled a bit. However, since he plays center, there is still a chance they could get a late-round pick for him ahead of final cuts.
Lundt has struggled this summer, and was moved inside to guard quite a bit during their time at St. John Fisher University, so perhaps they could get him to clear waivers. One wildcard to keep an eye on, though, is the Thursday injury to Grable. Grable walked off with the team’s head athletic trainer and didn’t return to the session. He’s had a strong camp, but if this is a long-term injury, it could change the math a bit. For now, until we know more, this group is my best guess.
Traded before final cuts: Sedrick Van Pran-Granger Cut: Chase Lundt, Nick Broeker, Ar’maj Reed-Adams, Da’Metrius Weatherspoon, Bruno Fina
Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, T.J. Sanders, Landon Jackson, DeWayne Carter, Zane Durant
Once the pads went on, we’ve seen several of the team’s reserve defensive line draft investments step up their game. That group includes Sanders, Jackson and Carter, with Carter’s development being the most substantial. It took a bit longer for Carter this summer than others, but he’s playing at a high level recently, and that could potentially make veteran Phidarian Mathis expendable. Even if they don’t keep Mathis on the 53-man roster, expect him to be a priority practice-squad addition to provide needed depth. The rookie, Durant, has flashed some good reps during camp and should be a roster lock.
Cut: Phidarian Mathis, Zion Logue, Tommy Akingbesote, Travis Clayton
Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Parker, Michael Hoecht, Javon Solomon
With Hoecht ahead of schedule in his recovery, something has to give with the edge rusher group. As long as Hoecht avoids beginning the year on Injured Reserve, and that’s the way it’s trending since he’s practiced every single day since camp began, it could cause a decision point for a veteran with guaranteed money. Mike Danna, an early May signing, has over $1 million guaranteed on his one-year deal, but he’s faded into the background of the outside linebacker group. With investments in Hoecht and Parker a roster lock, and Solomon as one of their best special teams assets, I’ve got Danna on the outside of this projection.
Cut: Mike Danna, Andre Jones Jr., Cade Denhoff
Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Keonta Jenkins, Joe Andreessen
With Bernard, Williams and Elarms-Orr all locks, from there, it’s about whether they keep four or five inside linebackers and, if it’s only four, which of Jenkins or Andreessen they select. In this projection, I’ve got them keeping both, but there’s a major caveat here. The Bills are a bit thin at cornerback in this projection from a numbers standpoint, and if they had to trim a spot to bring in a veteran corner, I think Jenkins, Andreessen or Hardman would be the likeliest candidates. Jenkins, to me, has been one of the biggest risers of the summer. During open practices, he routinely ran with the second-team defense, he has a good special teams background and he’s fitting well into the new defense. As of now, I feel more confident in Jenkins making the team than Andreessen, but there’s still a long way to go.
Cut: Jimmy Ciarlo, Theron Gaines, Otis Reese IV
Dee Alford, Jordan Hancock
Alford has been one of the best players during training camp, period. The way he’s come in and embodied what the redefined nickel position in defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme wants has been outstanding. If he plays the way he has all summer during the regular season, Alford could be an impact defender for the Bills in 2026. His understudy, Hancock, has really come on strong over the last week or so and is playing with a lot of confidence. I’d even leave the light on for Hancock to work in at safety if they need him to. While this isn’t anything we’ve seen during camp, Hancock is playing so well that I could see him getting worked in as a dime backer during the regular season in certain packages. He’s been that good lately.

title: What I think after the Panthers add a tight end and their starting RB is banged up The addition of Darren Waller — pending his physical — could be a wake-up call to Carolina's tight ends. Joseph Person
summary: What I think after the Panthers add a tight end and their starting RB is banged up The addition of Darren Waller — pending his physical — could be a wake-up call to Carolina's tight ends. Joseph Person
full_text:
Last season, Darren Waller gave the Panthers fits in a game when he played for the Dolphins. Now, Carolina is hoping the tight end gives the position a lift. Bob Donnan / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — A group of Carolina Panthers fans stood behind the temporary barrier outside the practice fields Thursday morning, several holding items to be autographed.
At least one of them was waiting for Darren Waller. He asked a reporter when the newly acquired tight end would be leaving practice. Waller had not yet gone through his physical or signed his contract at that point, so he wouldn’t be coming by — a league source said Waller plans to sign Monday pending his physical.
It’s hard to fault the guy’s enthusiasm. Panthers fans have been waiting for an impact tight end to arrive since Greg Olsen was released in 2020 before the start of the Matt Rhule era.
The post-Olsen years have been a fallow period for Panthers tight ends, spanning the tenures of three head coaches and a dozen or so tight ends. With the exception of veteran Hayden Hurst in 2023, the Panthers have tried to fill the Olsen void via middle- to late-round draft picks like Ian Thomas, Tommy Tremble, Ja’Tavion Sanders and Mitchell Evans.
That strategy hasn’t produced much.
The Panthers’ 319 receptions by tight ends are the fewest in the NFL since the start of the 2020 season, according to TruMedia’s Jason Starrett. Every other team had more than 400 catches by tight ends over the same span. The New York Jets had the second-fewest receptions with 411.
Carolina’s tight ends have accounted for less than 15 percent of the team’s targets since 2020, the smallest share in the NFL. The league average was 21 percent between 2020-25.
So taking a low-cost, dart throw on a street free agent who was among the league’s best receiving tight ends for a two-year stretch isn’t the worst idea, even if Waller has been hurt or retired for much of the past two years and will turn 34 in September.
Dave Canales mistakenly added two years on to Waller’s age Thursday. But the Panthers coach knew Waller’s height to a fraction, mentioning it twice in an eight-minute session with reporters.
“With Darren, he brings 6 foot, 6 1/2 and he still can run,” Canales said. “He could be 36 (sic) in September. But if you put on the film from last year, he’s playing at a high level.”
Canales has seen the Week 5 film a few times. What he saw was Waller — in his second game post-retirement — catching all five of his targets for 78 yards and a touchdown for the Miami Dolphins in the Panthers’ 27-24 win at Bank of America Stadium.
“Just watching him over the years — he had a fantastic game here when they came last season and made some big plays against us,” Canales said.
Waller was a wide receiver at Georgia Tech and could help fill the role the Panthers envisioned for wideout Chris Brazzell before the rookie went down with a season-ending knee injury.
“I’m excited about adding that (size-speed) part,” Canales said. “Chris Brazzell was here for that reason as well — to stretch the field, be that big target.”
Panthers safety Tre’von Moehrig, who played with Waller for two seasons in Las Vegas, said Waller has a unique skill set that makes him a tough matchup for defensive backs.
“It’s different. On tape you can see it,” he said. “Obviously, he’s very tall. He has a great wingspan. He’s fast. He’s strong. He has all the intangibles to make it hard on the defense. So I’m glad he’s gonna be coming over here.”
A handful of other things I think as the Panthers prepare to head to Buffalo for their second preseason game …
1. I think the other tight ends have been put on notice. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Maybe it was a coincidence. Maybe it was a product of the Panthers doing a lot of red zone work. But the tight ends seemed to have an extra pep in their steps Thursday, when Tremble, Evans and Sanders each made plays.
That’s what Canales, Dan Morgan and Brandt Tilis had in mind by bringing Waller in on a one-year contract. “Just on brand with Dan and I,” Canales said. “Just looking for ways to challenge our roster, challenge our rooms, bring different types of talents into the rooms to really challenge the group and see what we have there.”
2. I think Darrell Bevell will have some sway in any discussions involving the offense. Bevell was the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive coordinator for seven seasons when Canales was on the offensive staff. Bevell was in Miami last year when a fourth of Waller’s 24 receptions went for touchdowns. “Darrell was around him and had great things to say about him as a pro, the way he prepares, the way he works,” Canales said.
The Panthers had former head coaches Jim Caldwell and Dom Capers in senior advisory roles for Canales’ first two seasons. This year he has two former Seahawks colleagues to lean on: Bevell and Carl “Tater” Smith, the father of special teams coordinator Tracy Smith. Offensive coordinator Brad Idzik will call the offense, while Bevell will provide an extra set of eyes — “great eyes,” according to Canales.
“A lot of the concepts that you see, a lot of our plans and different situational things go way back to what Darrell taught me and what we were able to create over the years in Seattle.”
3. I think Canales needs to walk a fine line with Jonathon Brooks, especially in light of Chuba Hubbard’s hamstring injury. The Panthers — especially the safeties — haven’t been treating Brooks with kid gloves in his return from his second ACL surgery. And there’s a benefit to getting Brooks game reps the next two weeks at Buffalo and Jacksonville.
But with Hubbard week to week with a hamstring issue, Canales doesn’t need to over-expose Brooks to a potential injury with too many preseason carries. And he won’t. Starters are only expected to play a couple of series Saturday. And with Trevor Etienne also slated for first-team reps, Brooks can break a sweat, get a few touches and call it a day.
4. I think the clock is ticking on the 2024 draft class, Morgan’s first as general manager. Xavier Legette is having a good camp, but has already been passed by Jalen Coker on the depth chart and was in danger of losing ground to Brazzell before the rookie’s LCL injury. Brooks has looked explosive, especially as a pass catcher, but enters the season as one of the team’s biggest unknowns.
Sanders led the Panthers’ tight ends in receptions the past two seasons, but could be on the roster bubble if Waller stays healthy. Linebacker Trevin Wallace is competing with Claudin Cherelus for the spot alongside Devin Lloyd after starting 20 games in his first two seasons. Chau Smith-Wade looks to have the edge at nickel, but might not be on the field much if Will Lee keeps playing well and Jaycee Horn spends a lot of time in the slot.
Seventh-round pick Michael Barrett, the Michigan linebacker who was traded to Seattle for Mike Jackson two summers ago, is responsible for the biggest return on investment.
5. I think Morgan has surrounded Bryce Young with some exciting playmakers , but the key to the offense’s success could be the play of offensive tackles Rasheed Walker and Monroe Freeling.

full_text:
Jack Endries has a reputation as a receiving tight end, and he flashed that skill nicely in his debut — along with a powerful spike to christen his first NFL score. Lauren Bacho / Associated Press
CINCINNATI — The Cincinnati Bengals won their preseason opener against the Detroit Lions, 16-14, for anyone who cares about the final score. They didn’t play particularly well.
The starters on offense and defense enjoyed two drives, with the first-team offense managing only one 54-yard Evan McPherson field goal and two hits on quarterback Joe Burrow.
Burrow was not especially pleased after the game.
“Places we could be better,” Burrow said succinctly, summing up his night. “All you can do is evaluate the reps that you get and grow and learn from it.”
Nobody is concerned about Burrow or his crew of stars on offense, though, no matter how imperfect the 2026 debut looked.
Thursday’s game was largely about staying healthy, which they did, and seeing players step up in depth competitions. In that respect, there were risers and fallers on both sides of the ball.
Here’s a look at four players who helped their cases, three who hurt their cases and one question bubbling to the surface about a prominent offensive starter.
The Bengals laid out a battle at the back of the deep defensive line room before camp started. Jonathan Allen would join BJ Hill in a rotation to fill the starting role, but the final spot at three-technique would come down to Jenkins, a second-round pick entering his third season, and rookie seventh-rounder Robinson.
Each helped themselves Thursday, making the Bengals’ good problem even harder. Jenkins consistently found himself in the backfield, racking up five tackles, one for loss, and ended a Lions drive with a sack. He even offered a Macarena celebration.
He badly needed a debut like this coming off a disappointing 2025.
As for Robinson, the 2025 American Conference Defensive Player of the Year had the most impressive rep of any Bengals defensive lineman all night. He split a double team, getting held by both players in the process, with the Lions backed up in their own end. He still ended up hitting the quarterback while drawing the holding flag that backed Detroit up even more.
“It’s motivating and good to get that momentum going into the rest of this preseason,” Robinson said.
The seventh-round pick out of Texas endured a rough stretch of practices this past week, which included a fumble and falling on an open pass from Joe Flacco.
When the lights came on Thursday, however, he made every play that came his way. That included the Bengals’ lone touchdown. It wasn’t the most challenging of plays, but Endries smoothly slipped out near the goal line and hauled in the 4-yard pass from Flacco.
“I’m happy about it,” Endries said. “Step in the right direction. Now it’s just on to Saturday practice. Keep stacking days and building confidence.”
Later, he snagged a third-down reception and made two Lions defenders miss on his way to a 17-yard gain.
Endries will need to prove he can hang at the point of attack. His reputation is as a receiving tight end, and he flashed that skill nicely in his debut — along with a powerful spike to christen his first NFL score.
“You can’t spike in college,” he said. “I wanted to spike the ball. I’ve never done it before. On the sideline I did it one time just to get ready.”
The battle for the punt and kick return job has an early leader. Williams, who joined in the middle of last season on waivers from the Pittsburgh Steelers, brought juice to the return game after starter Charlie Jones went out with an injury. Rookie Dohnte Meyers is also in the mix and enjoyed an excellent night at receiver, adding an 11-yard punt return.
On Thursday, Williams showed elite burst through an open hole on a kickoff return just before halftime and ripped off a 48-yard return that set the Bengals up in Lions territory. Williams doesn’t bring as much to the table as Jones and Meyers as a receiver, but those are the types of plays that will land him a spot on the active roster.
The Bengals are keeping a close eye on the fourth safety spot in a battle between PJ Jules and Anthony. Both endured rough moments, including an ugly pass interference on third-and-long by Jules, but Anthony’s stood out.
The fourth-year safety twice missed tackles as runners broke through to the second level, including an ugly attempt around the collar on a run that got called back due to a hold elsewhere on the play.
The last safety spot will be relied upon as a critical special teams contributor. Yet, on a punt return, Anthony buzzed down the outside and whiffed on the returner, allowing them to spring free for extra yardage. For a player in a position battle, this wasn’t the impression he needed to make.
In this offense, running backs must be trusted to catch the ball out of the backfield. There’s no situation where that can be in doubt. Not once, but twice Thursday, the second-year running back dropped passes.
The first was a late throw into the flat from Flacco that came in low as it rained, but Brooks still could have hauled it in. The second was more egregious. The Bengals ran a slant for Brooks that cleared space in front of him to take off. Flacco’s throw hit Brooks right between the numbers and fell incomplete.
Brooks didn’t see much playing time last year, logging only 47 offensive snaps, so this is an important preseason for him to solidify his role as the third running back behind Chase Brown and Samaje Perine. Those two drops were a rough start.
The Bengals are searching for a fourth tackle they can trust to fill the spot behind Amarius Mims, Orlando Brown and Cody Ford. Coker is one of the primary candidates. Yet he endured multiple rough moments against the Lions.
He allowed a strip sack around the left edge by Ahmed Hassanein that killed a promising drive. He also committed a false start.
Nobody was expecting Coker to be a lockdown tackle, but as a whole, this wasn’t his best night.
The Bengals extended Brown this offseason, adding two years and $32 million to his contract that was set to expire after this year. He’s held down the left tackle spot since signing from the Kansas City Chiefs in free agency in 2023. Brown was a captain and key cog in the continuity the Bengals are thrilled to boast with all five starters back for the first time in Burrow’s career.
Yet, we’ve seen rough moments for Brown getting beat around the edge during training camp by backups Cashius Howell and Cedric Johnson, among others. Those moments planted a seed, but the benefit of the doubt is undeniably given to the 30-year-old four-time Pro Bowler.
On the second drive Thursday, that seed sprouted above the soil. Eric O’Neill, an undrafted free agent out of Rutgers, sprinted around the edge and beat Brown handily on third down, hitting Burrow square in the back as he looked to throw. It was the biggest hit of the night on the star quarterback, even greater than the sack that killed the first drive.
“It’s never fun. That’s not what we wanted to happen,” Taylor said of Burrow taking two hits. “But, again, we’ll continue to improve.”
It’s not that Brown isn’t allowed to get beat on a rep. Or that anybody should be overreacting to preseason football. But this wasn’t Myles Garrett or Trey Hendrickson. This was a 23-year-old kid who transferred from James Madison to Rutgers and only managed 2.5 sacks last year for the Scarlet Knights. He can’t be beating the starting left tackle clean around the edge on third-and-4.
This isn’t saying the Bengals need to bench Brown or reconsider available free agents, but periodic struggles in camp and this ugly rep against O’Neill leading to Burrow’s hit broaches the question: What is going on with the Bengals’ left tackle?

full_text:
Second-round receiver Denzel Boston has been one of the standout players for the Browns in training camp. Ken Blaze / Imagn Images
The Cleveland Browns open the preseason Saturday in Chicago with coach Todd Monken planning to play all of his healthy starters. But the regulars won’t play long, and the defense currently has multiple first- and second-team players dealing with injuries.
With a new head coach, new special teams coach and an organizational plan to eventually have one of the league’s youngest rosters, Saturday’s game is about much more than just Monken evaluating quarterbacks Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders in a game-like setting.
Across the roster, there are plenty of jobs to be won. If you’re planning on keeping score at home, here are eight names to know for the guys in the orange helmets Saturday.
For many fans, Saturday will be their first glimpse at the rookie who’s arguably been the standout offensive player of the spring and summer . Boston has earned a full-time role and will play mostly as the outside X receiver.
Another drafted rookie who catches the eye because of his size, Barber moved back to his primary college position of left tackle last week. Barber is definitely making the roster and is in the mix to be Cleveland’s top swing tackle, but he had played almost exclusively right tackle this spring and summer before the last few days. He might eventually get a look at right guard, too, but the real evaluation will begin this weekend with Barber’s first reps against outside competition.
McMillon made the team as an undrafted rookie last year and played in every game on special teams. He’s clearly a more confident player in his second season, but the safety group is more crowded, and the fight for roles is an interesting one. Rookie second-rounder Emmanuel McNeil-Warren is ascending quickly, and veteran Daniel Thomas is a physical player who should excel on special teams. McMillon needs a strong preseason to ensure he’ll be back in the mix.
Larvadain enters the weekend sixth in the Browns’ wide receiver line. The team will definitely keep five on the initial 53-man roster and could keep six, so Larvadain needs to impress over the next two weeks as a wide receiver and return specialist. Sanders and Larvadain have chemistry dating back to last summer, so look for Larvadain to get chances once Sanders enters the game in the third quarter. For now, Larvadain is definitely behind rising second-year wide receiver Isaiah Bond but probably slightly ahead of Luke Floriea.
Ulofoshio was signed to Cleveland’s practice squad during the 2025 season and has played in five NFL games, mostly on special teams. He’s made a few notable plays in training camp and will have a chance to make the roster via special teams during the preseason. The Browns are thin at linebacker and currently dealing with injuries at multiple defensive spots across the depth chart, so every young defensive player who suits up Saturday is going to get a legitimate shot at making an impression — either by their primary position or in kick coverage.
Early in camp, it didn’t appear that Wypler was in the plans. Veteran Elgton Jenkins has guaranteed money and a starting spot on the new line, while fifth-round rookie Parker Brailsford was drafted in part because Wypler is only signed through 2026. But Brailsford is out due to an undisclosed injury to his snapping hand, and Jenkins has missed several practice days for injury management. Wypler is clearly next in line and will try to prove to the new coaching staff that he can produce if called upon.
Coats didn’t play high school football, and after three college stops he caught on with the Browns during the team’s rookie minicamp in May. He’s shown up around the ball on multiple occasions in training camp, and the Browns’ scramble for healthy bodies at cornerback has left them with four undrafted rookies due to suit up Saturday. Of that group, Coats is probably first in line. On Saturday, he gets a chance to perform for his current team and others who may eventually be looking.
The Browns probably are going to stick with Corey Bojorquez as their punter for one more season. But there are three punters in camp, and Pahl is interesting enough that there’s a real competition taking place. Pahl averaged 46.5 yards per punt in his final college season last fall.

The preseason opener for the Detroit Lions looked like, well, the preseason opener.
That’s probably the best way to summarize a 16-14 loss to the Bengals . There were crushing holding penalties, dropped passes and plays that were there but just weren’t executed. There were also strong individual efforts, signs of growth for young players
full_text:
Jacob Saylors led the Lions in rushing yards (55) and tied for the team lead with 28 receiving yards Thursday against the Bengals. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images
The preseason opener for the Detroit Lions looked like, well, the preseason opener.
That’s probably the best way to summarize a 16-14 loss to the Bengals . There were crushing holding penalties, dropped passes and plays that were there but just weren’t executed. There were also strong individual efforts, signs of growth for young players and an understanding that what’s being taught in practice is translating to games.
“It’s the first one, we’ll learn from this, the guys will get better,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said.
The Lions will face the Washington Commanders at home on Aug. 22 in their next preseason contest. Until then, let’s take a look at some risers and fallers from the opener.
As if folks needed another reason to hop on the Hassanein bandwagon, the 2025 sixth-round pick provided a couple more in the preseason opener. One of our players to watch entering Thursday, Hassanein didn’t disappoint. He filled up the box score, recording four tackles, a pair of sacks (including one versus Joe Burrow) and a forced fumble. For a player who’s worked hard to prove to this coaching staff he belongs in the rotation, a night like this goes a long way. Hard to think of a player who helped his stock more than Hassanein.
You knew it was going to be a heavy dose of Saylors, considering Detroit’s top three running backs weren’t playing. We know what he brings to the table on special teams, but when given a hefty workload, Saylors proved to be the best back on the field for either team. Saylors led the Lions in rushing and receiving yards, finishing his night with 11 touches for 83 yards. He was an ankle tackle away from a rushing touchdown, but it doesn’t make his night any less impressive. If the Lions carry four running backs into the season, it’ll be hard for another back to supplant Saylors.
“He was probably our most potent player on offense,” Campbell said.
Miller has had the difficult task of blocking Aidan Hutchinson in training camp. It’s gone about as well as you’d expect from a rookie tackle facing an All-Pro. However, the Lions are adamant that those reps against Hutchinson will only make Miller better. They wanted to see growth in the preseason opener. Have to think they liked what they saw.
You didn’t really notice Miller on Thursday, which sounds like a knock, but it’s a compliment. There weren’t any alarming losses, and while some of his wins were quiet, they were still wins. When Miller was beat off the edge, he recovered quickly and stayed in the play to redirect his defender. You really saw his athleticism in the screen game, getting upfield in a hurry on a negated screen to Tom Kennedy. That’s where Miller can be a weapon, even as he learns on the job. Not a perfect night, but a solid debut for Miller. He looked the part.
“I didn’t feel like my eyes were ever on he or Larry, and that’s a positive,” Campbell said. “That’s a pretty good sign. Like, man, we’re handling our business. I didn’t feel like we had any issues on the perimeter with those two guys in there. I thought he did a good job.”
Gill-Howard quietly had an excellent night. He used a swim move in the first half to blow by a Bengals guard and force an errant, off-target throw by Josh Johnson for a pressure and a near sack. In the fourth quarter, he used his speed to corral Johnson on a third-down scramble attempt — preventing a first down and holding the Bengals to a field goal. On the evening, Gill-Howard recorded two QB hits and that first-down-preventing tackle. The Lions are looking for help at three-technique, and with Mekhi Wingo going down during the game, Gill-Howard has a real chance to pass him with efforts like this.
A bit of a disappointing night for TeSlaa. His first target of the evening went through his hands, bounced off his facemask into the air and was intercepted by the Bengals. On a later target, TeSlaa couldn’t come down with a fourth-down catch on a slant through contact. He didn’t do much to help his quarterback. Maybe the focus wasn’t there, or perhaps the conditions (it was raining in the first half) added to an off night. Either way, we’ve seen better from TeSlaa.
While TeSlaa has gotten off to a slow start in training camp, catching the football hasn’t been a problem. TeSlaa has plenty of tape highlighting his hands and ability to make contested catches. It’s worth believing in his track record and the tools that made him a player worth trading up for a year ago. That said, TeSlaa’s lack of separation has been a topic of discussion. If that aspect of his game is still a work in progress, he needs to catch the passes he’s capable of catching. He didn’t do that Thursday.
It was a rough outing for Frazier, whose three first-half holding penalties stalled the offense on several occasions. One of them negated a 20-yard completion to Kennedy, and another wiped out a 7-yard run by Kye Robichaux. It felt like every time a flag was thrown, you expected to hear the official say, “Holding, No. 71.” In the fourth quarter, after moving to left tackle, Frazier allowed a sack after getting beat cleanly by Isaiah Foskey.
Frazier finds himself in contention for the starting left guard job, though it was clear to those who’ve watched practice that Frazier was below the likes of Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs and Ben Bartch on the depth chart entering Thursday night. The Lions are trying to get a hard look at Frazier — playing him at both guard and tackle in the opener — but despite that versatility, it’s hard to say he helped his case. His youth is still evident at this stage of his career. He needs more time.
The one thing that couldn’t happen to Rakestraw on Thursday happened. In the second quarter, Rakestraw lowered his shoulder for a tackle attempt and remained on the ground well after the play, clearly in pain. The broadcast showed Rakestraw getting his arms looked at on the sideline. He later headed inside to the locker room. His night was over.
However, Campbell provided some good news after the game.
“It’s not major,” Campbell said of Rakestraw. “We just think he got a little contusion in the arm. … I think he’ll be all right.”
A positive update, but seeing Rakestraw leave yet another game with an injury doesn’t make for a productive night. As a rookie, Rakestraw landed on IR twice and appeared in only eight games. He missed the entire 2025 season after a shoulder injury suffered in camp required season-ending surgery. The hope was that Rakestraw could compete for the starting cornerback job opposite D.J. Reed, and the 2024 second-round pick said he added muscle in an effort to stay on the field. However, Rakestraw has been inconsistent in practice and suffered an injury in a game he needed to flash. A rough night for Rakestraw.

The Green Bay Packers lost 28-9 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night.

full_text:
Rookie Trey Smack was the player of the game for the Packers after entering Thursday 20-of-28 on field goals in camp. Charles LeClaire / Imagn Images
The Green Bay Packers lost 28-9 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night.
That result doesn’t matter, especially since the Steelers scored 21 of those points in the second half against many guys who won’t be on Green Bay’s active roster in two weeks, and plenty of key players on both sides of the ball either barely played or didn’t play at all. What does matter, however, is we sit just one month away from the Packers’ season opener Sept. 13 in Minnesota.
With one exhibition game in the rearview, here is our first of three 53-man roster projections this preseason with an observation from Thursday’s game and a list of guys who didn’t suit up at each position group.
Quarterback (2): Jordan Love, Tyrod Taylor
Released: Kyle McCord, Kyron Drones
Kyle McCord has some moxie. The Packers haven’t kept three quarterbacks on the initial 53-man roster since 2020, when they kept Aaron Rodgers, Jordan Love and Tim Boyle because Love wasn’t ready to be the backup but couldn’t be subjected to waivers, so they probably won’t keep three this year. If anything, McCord showed why he’s ahead of Kyron Drones in the battle for what might be one practice-squad spot, and not just because he was first up in Thursday’s game.
McCord’s most impressive sequence came in a four-play series that spanned about 30 seconds in the first half’s final minute. He completed four consecutive passes, covering 35 yards, with a timeout after the third before spiking the ball with one second left. Rookie kicker Trey Smack then hit a 58-yard field goal as time expired.
“Great poise,” coach Matt LaFleur said of McCord, who was a sixth-round pick by the Eagles in 2025 and signed with the Packers in January. “To operate in that two-minute drive the way he did, I don’t believe he’s had that live yet in that situation. We’re in a down-down clock situation. He rifled the inside slant, and to have the urgency to get up and spike the ball … I thought that was just incredible execution.
“I thought the other thing that he did a really nice job (of) was just hanging in the pocket. Obviously took a hit, delivered the ball to, I think it was Isaiah Neyor on that one, so I thought he did a lot of good things.”
Running back (3): Josh Jacobs, MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks
Released: Pierre Strong Jr., Jaden Nixon, Damien Martinez
MarShawn Lloyd came out of Thursday’s game healthy after touching the ball five times. That’s the only worthwhile takeaway here. Can he make it another month staying on the field? We shall see.
“It felt really good, honestly, just getting hit,” Lloyd said. “I knew about the defense the Steelers had, so it was good to go against a team like that in your first hit in like two years. It’s cool. I enjoyed every bit of it.”
Who didn’t suit up: Jacobs, Brooks
Wide receiver (6): Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden, Skyy Moore, Savion Williams, Bo Melton
Released: Isaiah Neyor, J. Michael Sturdivant, Will Sheppard, Kaden Prather, Kisean Johnson, Chris Hilton Jr.
Neyor and J. Michael Sturdivant are giving general manager Brian Gutekunst plenty to think about this summer. They consistently make plays and did so again Thursday, most notably when Sturdivant made an outstretched grab near the sideline for 14 yards on third-and-6.
Neyor led the team with four catches for 34 yards. Skyy Moore is all but on the team, if we’re to believe what Gutekunst said last week, and Savion Williams isn’t getting cut since he’s last year’s third-round pick. Bo Melton is a coach and locker room favorite who can take the top off a defense, so his release would come as a surprise, too. Will Gutekunst keep seven receivers, or will he try to get both guys through to the practice squad?
Tight end (3): Tucker Kraft, Josh Whyle, Drake Dabney
Released: Messiah Swinson, McCallan Castles, Thomas Yassmin
There wasn’t much to write home about with the tight ends. All we know is the Packers had better hope Tucker Kraft is healthy and his regular self come Week 1 because this position group is in rough shape elsewhere.
Who didn’t suit up: Kraft, Musgrave
Offensive line (10): Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Jager Burton, Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk, Anthony Belton, Zach Bako-Bewele, John Williams, Donovan Jennings, Darian Kinnard
Released: Dalton Cooper, Dillon Wade, Dylan Barrett, Josh Gesky, Travis Glover, Brant Banks
The Packers surrendered five sacks, but Love didn’t take any of them. That’s all that matters. Aaron Banks and Zach Bako-Bewele didn’t play, and they’ll surely be in the starting lineup come Week 1. Burton continues to get valuable reps as the first-team left guard, a spot he’s earned in recent practices, so could he push for regular-season playing time at some point?
Who didn’t suit up: Banks, Bako-Bewele
Interior defensive line (6): Devonte Wyatt, Karl Brooks, Warren Brinson, Javon Hargrave, Chris McClellan, Nazir Stackhouse
Released: Anthony Campbell, Jonathan Ford, Jaden Crumedy
Warren Brinson has been one of the standouts in camp, and he flashed more Thursday, drawing a hold on first-and-goal, pressuring the quarterback (he did whiff on the sack) and stuffing a draw play for a loss of 1 yard.
Who didn’t suit up: Wyatt, Hargrave, Riley
Edge (5): Lukas Van Ness, Brenton Cox Jr., Barryn Sorrell, Collin Oliver, Dani Dennis-Sutton
Released: Arron Mosby, Nyjalik Kelly
Lukas Van Ness had a sack and a run stop early, Brenton Cox Jr. had a powerful sack, and Collin Oliver looked explosive at times. Maybe, just maybe, this group will be able to tread water without Micah Parsons for five games if that’s how long he’s out.
“I think we’re looking at a real vanilla style of our defense right now, but we made it a point of emphasis to put our effort on tape and our physicality on tape, and we came out fast,” Van Ness said. “A little taste of what’s to come.”
Who didn’t suit up: Parsons, Dennis-Sutton
Linebacker (5): Edgerrin Cooper, Zaire Franklin, Isaiah McDuffie, Ty’Ron Hopper, Nick Niemann
Released: Kristian Welch, TJ Quinn
Zaire Franklin has drawn rave reviews this spring and summer from his teammates and coaches. His first impression in an actual game for his new team? Destroying a running back on a blitz to set up a sack for Van Ness. That’ll do. New defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon knows Franklin from their days in Indianapolis together, and he’s trusting him to relay the plays, and make plays, for his defense.
Cornerback (6): Keisean Nixon, Brandon Cisse, Carrington Valentine, Benjamin St-Juste, Kamal Hadden, Domani Jackson
Released: Jaylin Simpson, MJ Devonshire Jr., Shemar Bartholomew
It wasn’t the prettiest night for this group. The Steelers picked on MJ Devonshire Jr. in the second half, especially. Keisean Nixon wasn’t great in his cameo, notably missing a tackle along with safety Kitan Oladapo on the perimeter that led to an explosive gain. Cisse made a nice touchdown-saving tackle in space, though, and that’s a marked difference from Carrington Valentine’s perimeter tackling woes last season.
Who didn’t suit up: Valentine, Hadden, Jackson
Safety (4): Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams, Javon Bullard, Kitan Oladapo
Released: Mark Perry, Murvin Kenion III, Tra Fluellen, Trey Dean III
Mark Perry and Murvin Kenion III made consecutive great plays on third and fourth down to save touchdowns early in the second quarter, but it’s hard to compliment anyone in the secondary too much when the Steelers completed 27 of 33 passes for 332 yards and two touchdowns.
Who didn’t suit up: Bullard
The rookie was the player of the game for the Packers after entering Thursday 20-of-28 on field goals in camp, officially hitting field goals from 37, 58 and 38 yards with another make from 58 yards that was nullified by a Steelers penalty. None of his kicks looked particularly close to missing, either. Special teams coordinator Cam Achord said he puts more stock in stadium and game…

full_text:
Colts quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr. started Thursday night's game slow but bounced back in a big way late in the first half. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
Shane Steichen buried his head in his hands. The frustration was obvious for the Indianapolis Colts coach. Anthony Richardson Sr. had just made a good play in Thursday’s 13-13 preseason tie against the New England Patriots, as he broke free for a 10-yard scramble in the second quarter. But at the end of the run, Richardson lost a fumble .
It was the kind of play that could’ve buried Richardson, a player already behind the eight ball as he challenges Riley Leonard for the Colts’ backup QB spot. Richardson, however, bounced back.
Here are three players, including Richardson, who saw their stock rise and three who saw their stock fall in the Colts’ first preseason game.
In the absence of starting QB Daniel Jones, who is fully cleared from his torn right Achilles tendon but won’t play in the preseason, Richardson started the first half Thursday. It was the first time he had been QB1 in roughly a year, and early on, Richardson looked in over his head. His first pass was a severe underthrow to wide-open tight end Will Mallory. Four plays later, he was intercepted by Patriots cornerback Kindle Vildor, though that turnover was more on Colts receiver Coleman Owen, who allowed the slightly high pass to slip between his hands and into the lap of Vildor.
Then came the fumble, Richardson’s second turnover, and this time around, there was no one else to blame. He should’ve slid or covered up the ball, but he didn’t, and it appeared he was on the brink of unraveling.
Until he turned into a completely different player.
Richardson went on to lead two scoring drives to finish the first half, highlighted by a touchdown march in which he went 4-of-4 passing for 59 yards. He also had two runs for 8 yards, punctuated by a 1-yard TD plunge.
All told, Richardson finished 11-of-14 passing for 145 yards and one interception, plus six carries for 53 yards and one touchdown and one lost fumble. His performance was a lot more good than bad, which had been the opposite throughout most of training camp, and at least kept Leonard (more on him later) from running away with the backup QB job. Richardson’s solid showing could also ignite some outside interest in the 24-year-old, who still hasn’t rescinded his trade request .
Let’s start with the obvious: The play on which McGowan fumbled early in the second quarter should’ve been ruled a touchdown. The replay on the TV broadcast appeared to show that McGowan stretched the ball over the goal line for a 1-yard score well before it was slapped out of his hand. It was shocking that the officials didn’t review the play, and it would feel disingenuous to pin that turnover on McGowan.
Patriots recover the fumble at the goal line!
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/eLsEqnUWrS
— NFL (@NFL) August 14, 2026
Nevertheless, the rookie seventh-round running back delivered a promising debut. McGowan totaled just 17 yards on five carries, but his first run, a 9-yarder, displayed the physical running style that has quickly endeared him to his teammates and coaches. McGowan also had a 26-yard kickoff return that offered a glimpse of what he can do on special teams as he continues to make a strong case to serve as the top backup behind Jonathan Taylor.
Boettcher started his NFL preseason debut and provided one of the biggest hits of the night late in the first quarter. The former Oregon star, who led the Big Ten with 136 tackles last season, hammered Patriots running back Lan Larison in the backfield for a 4-yard loss. Boettcher ended the night with just three tackles, though his motor was impossible to miss.
The Colts have rotated linebackers a lot in training camp, but with rookie second-round pick CJ Allen still sidelined due to a hamstring injury, Boettcher, a fourth-rounder, is putting himself in position to at least be considered as a potential Week 1 starter.
TE Will Mallory : Mallory totaled six catches for 80 yards, continuing a training camp trend. His knack for making downfield receptions begets the question: Can the Colts afford to keep a fourth tight end on their 53-man roster behind Tyler Warren, Mo Alie-Cox and Drew Ogletree?
DE Caden Curry: The rookie sixth-round pick recorded five tackles (tied for the team lead), two tackles for loss, three QBs pressures and two passes defensed. Yes, Curry’s arm length was a major concern during the pre-draft process, but stat lines like this are a reminder that measurables don’t mean everything.
K Spencer Shrader : He was 2-for-2 on field goal attempts, including a 61-yarder late in the fourth quarter. Shrader has been outdueled in training camp by Blake Grupe, who missed his lone field goal attempt, also a 61-yarder, wide right at the end of the second quarter.
Leonard started the second half and never found a rhythm. On his first drive, the 2025 sixth-round pick threw an interception that was caused, in part, by the Colts’ leaky backup offensive line (which Richardson also played behind). Facing pressure on first-and-10 from Indy’s 31-yard line, Leonard tried to find receiver Eli Pancol over the middle but severely underthrew the ball, and Patriots safety John Saunders Jr. easily picked it off.
Leonard finished 10-of-21 passing for 89 yards and one interception. He also had two carries for 12 yards as the Colts failed to score a TD in the second half. Thursday’s poor showing probably wasn’t enough to completely derail Leonard’s chances of winning the job as Jones’ backup, since he has performed better than Richardson throughout most of training camp — though the gap between the QBs appears to have shrunk after the preseason opener.
The Colts didn’t play their starting cornerbacks, Charvarius Ward Sr. and Sauce Gardner, as several first-stringers on both sides of the ball sat out. Blackmon, who started 11 games last year mostly because of injuries to Ward and Gardner, picked up two pass interference penalties on the Patriots’ first drive. The fourth-year pro also had a rough showing in Tuesday’s joint practice.
Edwards became one of the Colts’ underdog success stories last year, as he went from being an undrafted rookie to a player who started five games. Edwards, however, was repeatedly picked on in coverage Thursday, including when Patriots receiver Kyle Williams beat him for a 12-yard TD reception in the second quarter. Edwards’ outing didn’t inspire a lot of confidence in his ability to step up if the Colts’ secondary gets banged up. (Keep in mind, Ward is sidelined indefinitely due to a back injury.)
LG Josh Sills: The backup left guard was inconsistent, as Leonard and Richardson were frequently under duress as Sills continuously got beat in the trenches.
DE Jaylahn Tuimoloau: The 2025 second-round pick registered just one tackle. He’ll need to be a lot more active to climb the depth chart, which for now likely has Arden Key ahead of him as the second starting edge rusher opposite of Laiatu Latu.
WR Nick Westbrook-Ikhine: The veteran wideout made just one catch for 19 yards. Granted, he was targeted only once, in the first quarter by Richardson. Still, after a quiet showing in Tuesday’s joint practice, it would have behooved Westbrook-Ikhine to have more of an impact Thursday if he plans on clinching the third starting receiver job behind Alec Pierce and Josh Downs.

full_text:
Indianapolis Colts special teams coordinator Brian Mason has spent four years with the franchise. Alex Slitz / Getty Images
Indianapolis Colts special teams coordinator Brian Mason suffered a knee injury on the last play of Thursday’s preseason opener against the New England Patriots, coach Shane Steichen announced after the 13-13 tie at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass.
“He got rolled up right on the sideline on that last play,” Steichen said. “So, we’ll see.”
Mason is flying back to Indianapolis with the team Thursday night, according to a team source not authorized to speak publicly , with further evaluation slated for Friday and the coming days.
Mason was standing on the sideline in the final seconds of the game when Colts quarterback Riley Leonard attempted a Hail Mary that fell incomplete but would have given Indy the walk-off win. But as Mason was watching the play unfold, the TV broadcast showed a Colts player and a Patriots player shoving each other on the field before they spilled over to the Indianapolis sideline and knocked down Mason . The coach immediately appeared to scream out in pain and rolled around on the ground as Indianapolis’ medical staff gathered around him.
Mason is entering his fourth season as the Colts’ special teams coordinator. The Zionsville, Ind., native also served as Notre Dame’s special teams coordinator in 2022.

title: Vikings players who have the most to gain — and lose — Saturday at Giants Alec Lewis
summary: Vikings players who have the most to gain — and lose — Saturday at Giants Alec Lewis
full_text:
J.J. McCarthy, shown here against Green Bay last season, may be forced to make some quick decisions in the preseason opener. Stephen Maturen / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — The Vikings’ starting quarterback announcement shifts the attention to the rest of the roster, appropriate considering the team is approaching its first preseason game.
On Friday, the Vikings will fly to Newark, N.J., ahead of a Saturday matchup with the New York Giants. Head coach Kevin O’Connell said earlier this week that most starters would play. This declaration adds intrigue.
Which players have the most to gain — and lose — Saturday? Here is a comprehensive breakdown of 11 of them:
Defenses rarely dip into their complex schemes during the preseason. This makes it hard to evaluate quarterbacks, but you can still take clues from the smoothness of the operation and consistency with decision-making. McCarthy has a nice opportunity here. In front of cameras and a stadium stocked with fans, he will receive space to show growth.
Accuracy remains the foremost priority. From there, Vikings staff will monitor his speed in getting through progressions. Playing behind some of the backup offensive linemen may force him to make quick decisions. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing for someone who has played only 10 meaningful games since he left Michigan.
If you are searching for a sneaky young player to find his way to the back end of the 53-man roster, Thomas fits. Multiple NFL teams sought his services this spring in undrafted free agency. He starred as a strong safety at James Madison. As a senior, he captained a team that won the program’s first Sun Belt Conference title and made the College Football Playoff.
Thomas has taken snaps with the backups in training camp. He has also spent a noticeable amount of time with special teams. Make plays Saturday, and he will further stamp his case to add another promising youngster to a deep group of safeties.
All the quarterback attention delayed focus on the team’s two highly drafted interior defenders, Caleb Banks and Orange. Both are integral to the Vikings’ defense remaining menacing. It’s not that former defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Allen performed well in 2025. Nor is it the case that Minnesota cannot rely on interior defenders Jalen Redmond and Levi Drake Rodriguez.
This becomes more a ceiling conversation than anything else. The quicker Banks and Orange progress under the tutelage of respected defensive line coach Ryan Nielsen, the more chaos the Vikings’ defense can create. Orange has shown flashes in the first two weeks of camp. Preseason production would further validate his potential as a rookie.
Any time the Vikings infuse the roster with a versatile defender, it’s worth eyeing. Adams already switched numbers from 54 to 32, allowing him to line up at safety and all over the field. In practice, he’s blitzed effectively. Other times, he began far from the line of scrimmage as a deep safety and floated to the football.
Where he plays is as interesting as how he plays. The 2017 No. 6 draft pick hasn’t started more than 10 games in a season since 2021. He is now almost four years removed from a torn left quad. It will be fascinating to see if he still has the spark in live games.
Special teams tend to take a back seat, but the unit matters. In 2025, the kicking and punting groups kept the team in games. Replacing former punter Ryan Wright won’t require elite-level ability, but he performed better than Hekker last season. Fewer than 30 percent of Hekker’s punts landed inside the 20-yard-line, which ranked in the bottom 10 of qualified punters.
The Vikings signed Ray Guy Award winner Brett Thorson in undrafted free agency. Saturday is a platform for them to prove their talent and their reliability as holders for kicker Will Reichard.
In organized team activities, veteran Vikings running back Aaron Jones raved about Claiborne’s skill set. You cannot miss the juice. He glides. He also goes from deciphering to blurring through holes in a flash. The questions never hinged on his talent. More than anything, for the sixth-round rookie to find the field in 2026, Claiborne needed to learn the playbook and display consistency with work habits and ball security.
He has impressed in spurts throughout training camp. Preseason games mean more eyes on the overall operation. As long as Claiborne positions himself in the correct spots, he may become one of Saturday’s key storylines.
Few Vikings coaches have proven their ability to develop players more than Keenan McCardell. The team’s receivers coach earned the trust of superstar receiver Justin Jefferson. McCardell built a connection with third-year wideout Jordan Addison. Already, the team’s 2025 third-rounder, Tai Felton, is following a similar arc as former Vikings receiver Jalen Nailor.
The back end of the room warrants some discussion, too. Undrafted signings from recent years such as Jeshaun Jones and Myles Price have made plays in recent practices. Fleming, another undrafted signing in 2025 from Tulane, may be the most explosive and dynamic as a route runner.
Former Arizona Cardinals coaches reiterated the role interior pass protection plays for quarterback Kyler Murray. The Vikings used 17 combinations of offensive linemen for at least 10 snaps throughout the 2025 season. That allowed Huber, a 2025 signee from Cincinnati and Wisconsin, to get regular-season snaps against the Cleveland Browns in London. Huber held his own versus defensive tackle talent such as Maliek Collins. This fall, he’s competing to keep his backup position with other versatile depth like Henry Byrd.
Huber and many of the offensive line backups are likely to play an extended period Saturday. That’ll provide the team with critical film to evaluate.
Why not lob in a bit of a wild card here? Among the rookies, none has flown under the radar more than Tiernan. The third-round pick, drafted following an exceptional career at Northwestern, has mostly mixed in with the backup offensive line group at right tackle. The 2025 season underscored the importance of reliable tackle depth — especially for an offense committed to pushing the ball vertically through deep-drop passing concepts.
The Giants’ stable of edge rushers may not play significant snaps. But Abdul Carter, Brian Burns and Kayvon Thibodeaux would give a nice glimpse at Tiernan’s status.
O’Connell arrived in 2022, and since then, the team has valued its tight end depth. For years, Johnny Mundt occupied the No. 3 tight end job and gave the team comfort. His departure led Minnesota to take Bartholomew with a sixth-round pick in 2025. A serious back injury ended his rookie season before it began, but he returned to 2026 training camp with a level of motivation that has been evident.
Almost every day, Bartholomew snatches a pass down the seam. The biggest question, especially regarding how far he can push current Vikings backup tight end Ben Yurosek, is whether he can displace defenders in the run game. Saturday is the first real test.
Observing Ingram-Dawkins, 23, coincides with the earlier point regarding Banks and Orange. The longer it takes for the two rookie interior defenders to find their footing, the more responsibility will fall on players like Rodriguez and Ingram-Dawkins.
The Vikings selected the former Georgia Bulldogs defensive tackle with one of their five picks in 2025 for a purpose. They projected major upside. In fact, one AFC evaluator suggested Ingram-Dawkins could’ve returned to Georgia and proved himself to be an early-round selection. Ingram-Dawkins played only 250 snaps last season, but he has slimmed down ahead of 2026. Saturday stands as his chance to inspire optimism in the defensive tackle depth.

full_text:
Second-year wide receiver Kyle Williams scored the lone Patriots touchdown of the game on a 12-yard pass from Tommy DeVito. Jaiden Tripi / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — With most of the New England Patriots’ starters sidelined for the preseason opener, there weren’t a ton of standout plays in their 13-13 tie Thursday against the Indianapolis Colts. But the team got what you’d generally hope for out of a preseason game.
They mostly stayed healthy. Some young players had some nice moments. And now they can turn the page to a pair of joint practices with the Philadelphia Eagles next week before their second preseason game next Saturday. If the Patriots starters — like Drake Maye — play in any of the three exhibition games, it’ll be that one.
But before transitioning to next week, let’s look at whose stock rose and whose fell on Thursday night at Gillette Stadium.
After a slow start to training camp, Williams came down with the Patriots’ lone touchdown on a play that showed why coaches are still excited about his potential — even if he has been relegated to playing mostly with the backups in practice.
From the 12-yard line, Williams got off the line of scrimmage with ease, showing his ability to release quickly. Coach Mike Vrabel has mentioned that the Patriots will have a distinct role for Williams, and maybe that’s in the red zone where fine-tuned breaks at the top of a route, an area where Williams has struggled, aren’t as necessary.
Later in the game, Williams caught a downfield hitch and broke a tackle for a 25-yard gain. Quarterback Tommy DeVito looked to him on a go route on the very next play, but Williams didn’t cut back inside for the ball, which appeared to frustrate Vrabel on the sideline. Still, it was a positive night overall for Williams.
The race for the Patriots’ final cornerback jobs is an important one with Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis dealing with injuries. The Colts got the better of the New England corners in Tuesday’s joint practice , but the Patriots responded well on Thursday.
Vildor showed great instincts in the first quarter, leaving his wide receiver to drive downhill as quarterback Anthony Richardson locked onto a target in the flat. The pass bounced off the hands of Coleman Owen, and Vildor was there to nab the interception.
Vildor increased his chances of being the team’s No. 5 cornerback.
The Patriots were dealt a blow before the game when they announced that running back Terrell Jennings had suffered a season-ending injury. Jennings was the favorite to win the No. 3 running back job while also playing on special teams.
Now, that job will likely come down to Miller, a rookie seventh-round pick, or Lan Larison, an undrafted free agent in 2025 who missed last season due to injury.
Miller was the more productive back Thursday night. He turned 14 carries into 55 yards, while Larison had just 1 rushing yard on seven carries, though he did add 38 receiving yards on six catches.
Miller ran a 4.42 40-yard dash before the draft and would bring speed to the run game while being an option to return kicks.
The Patriots could use depth on the interior of the defensive line behind Milton Williams and Christian Barmore, and Gregory could fit that billing. He has size (319 pounds) that the Pats otherwise lack on defense.
Gregory made a nice move in the third quarter to put pressure on Colts quarterback Riley Leonard and forced an underthrown ball that led to a John Saunders interception.
With Harold Landry still out due to injury, the Patriots need their backup edge rushers to step up. Against the Colts, Swinson did.
He looked capable against the run, notching an impressive stuff of Roydell Williams, and in the pass rush, getting into the backfield with Gregory to help force a bad throw. He also batted down a pass to get the Patriots defense off the field.
The veteran played more snaps than any other Patriots receiver a year ago, a sign of how highly coaches think of him. That’s part of why it seems safe to say he’ll again have a role in this offense.
But while Williams helped his stock, Hollins had a pass go through his hands on a second-and-8 slant and caught only two of his four targets for 24 yards.
It was a surprise this offseason that the Patriots didn’t do more to improve their depth on the interior offensive line, especially considering the injury history of new left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker.
They put a lot of faith in the versatility of Ben Brown, who is capable of being the backup at both guard and center.
The Pats were dealt a tough blow Thursday when Brown suffered an injury that forced his removal from the game. Without Brown, undrafted rookie Jacob Rizy is the team’s lone backup center. The only other with experience there would be Andrew Rupcich, who also left the game due to injury.
So, it won’t be a surprise if the Patriots seek more depth there in the coming days.
The Patriots asked a lot of Borregales on Thursday, teeing him up for field goal attempts of 40, 49, 52, 56 and 57 yards.
Borregales went just 2-of-5, missing from 49, 56 and 57 yards. The latter two are somewhat understandable. But his miss from 49 yards with 13 seconds left in the game was one he’d surely like back.
It wasn’t a perfect start to the preseason for Borregales after he had no competition for the job this summer.
