title: Falcons Name QB Plan vs. Broncos: 5 Key Observations from Final Practice
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons have gone through free agency, the NFL Draft, rookie minicamp, OTAs, mandatory minicamp, and training camp, and they finally get to open the 2026 season against the Denver Broncos on Friday for preseason game one.
The quarterback battle between Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. was settled by default for the matchup against the Broncos. Penix hasn't been fully cleared for contact, and head coach Kevin Stefanski named Tagovailoa the starter for Friday night's game.
Stefanski also said he plans to play the starters at least one series , and maybe more depending on the player, a drastic change over recent years when Arthur Smith treated the preseason with disdain and Raheem Morris tried to avoid them altogether.
The Falcons were in a short session on Wednesday, in their last full practice before Friday (Thursday is a walk-through). Here are some of the key things we saw and learned, other than the starting quarterback.
Cooper Rush will be the next man up after Tagovailoa's game is finished. Undrafted free agent rookie Jack Strand will finish the game. Rush joined the team on the first day of training camp, and Strand had gotten a lot of action with Penix and Tagovailoa limited, but has seen that scaled back in recent days with Rush taking more snaps with the No. 2 offense.
Second-year edge rusher is the only serious injury of the preseason, but there have been several players missing from action this week. Safety Jessie Bates, edge rusher Bralen Trice, linebacker Divine Deablo, defensive tackle Da'Shawn Hand, and cornerback Avieon Terrell have all been held out of action. It would be a surprise to see any of them on Friday.
Offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor was on the field Wednesday, and Zach Harrison has been a full participant this week. Taylor likely won't play on Friday, but we may see some snaps from Harrison.
With Deablo out, rookie linebackers Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. have seen extensive time working with what we would call the first-team defense. Safety Sydney Brown was acquired in a trade before the draft and should see plenty of time along with veteran DeMarcco Hellams.
Jake Matthews had a veteran rest day on Wednesday, and Michael Jerrell saw all of his reps at left tackle. Jerrell had been part of a rotation at right tackle that has also included rookie Ethan Onianwa and Brandon Walton. All three players should see extensive action against the Broncos.
Nickel has been the other position that's seen a lot of rotation, including Terrell. With Terrell out and Brown seeing more time at safety, it's a chance for A.J. Woods and Darnay Holmes to hoover up the bulk of the reps.
They were helped by a stiff wind at their backs, but punters Jake Bailey and Matthew Hayball were routinely hitting 60+ yard punts inside the 10-yard line. Bailey will be the team's punter this year, and when they moved to midfield, Bailey still showed good placement on his short punts.
Rookie Zachariah Branch should get his first chance to return punts and kicks against a live defense this week. He's looked electric as a wide receiver, but the team has been going through the motions in kick returns and coverage.
No, not that one, and probably not the other one you're thinking of either. Safety Jammie Robinson was back on the field for the first time. He had a nice interception on a tipped pass from Tua Tagovailoa. The quarterback extended the play, then extended it some more in what likely would have been a tackle-or-throw-away situation in a real game, before throwing into traffic that included Kyle Pitts and Drake London.
Robinson came down with the ball and will hope to push for a spot on the 53-man roster.
The Falcons will have a walk-through at Flowery Branch on Thursday before taking on the Broncos on Friday night at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. Long-time Falcons tormentor Sean Payton brings a strong Broncos squad to Atlanta, and he has typically played a lot of starters in the preseason as well.
The Falcons had 44 of 90 players on one-year, or the last year, of their contracts, and competition should be fierce despite the generally blase nature of preseason games.

title: Kevin Stefanski Explains Why Falcons Starters Will Play in Preseason vs. Broncos
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – Kevin Stefanski officially announced that Tua Tagovailoa and several starters will be active for the Atlanta Falcons ’ Friday night preseason game with the Denver Broncos. The plan is written “in pencil,” but it will be the first time that the starters have seen action in several years.
Under Stefanski, the Falcons are taking a very different approach, and the preseason playing time of starters is just the most recent of these changes. The head coach has also instituted live tackling periods to build calluses for the players ahead of a rough regular season.
“It’s callus, but don’t blister,” he explained about his methodology during the summer. “The mindset being, we’re not just going to work for the sake of doing work, or beat guys up for the sake of beating guys up. It’s all with a plan in mind to get the guys ready for a 17-game season, and then more if you earn it. In order to do that, you need to be physically ready for that challenge, and you need to be mentally ready for that challenge.”
Atlanta enters the season with several unresolved position battles and a quarterback competition still underway, so this evaluation period is at a premium. They have several prominent players, namely Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and others who may still not play, but also plenty of other question marks.
“Preseason football will resemble the closest [thing we have] to regular season football,” Stefanski said. “Schematically, it’s not exactly the same thing, but the fundamentals and techniques don’t change. I think there’s value in getting game reps with your fundamentals and techniques in mind.”
Aside from the quarterback, they need answers at right tackle, linebacker, wide receiver, and nickel corner. Stefanski did not specify who would play at these spots, but several players are competing for playing time and will see sufficient action.
“We will vary playing time by players,” he said. “So, there are some guys who may get more. Some guys who may get less, but we are just trying to get our guys ready for the season based on what we think they need in these games.”
The Falcons will prepare for this matchup, but it will not be a “full game plan.” Stefanski said they will look back at previous preseason games the Broncos have played, just to get a feel for coverages and fronts.
“I don't believe in showing a lot in the preseason and doing all sorts of exotic things and whatnot,” Stefanski said. Later explaining “It’s really about us, and for it to be about us, we have to keep it simple and let those guys just play.”
As of Wednesday, the expectation is that Tagovailoa and the starters will get a series, or about 10 plays, whichever comes first. Stefanski later clarified that this does not mean that Tagovailoa will be the starter come Week 1, saying the team “will cross that bridge when we get to it.”
After that drive, backup quarterback Cooper Rush will rotate in under center, followed by rookie undrafted free agent Jack Strand. Incumbent starter Michael Penix Jr., who has yet to be cleared for team drills, will not be available on Friday. Stefanski said he remains encouraged by Penix's progress, though the quarterback has yet to receive medical clearance for team drills.
Penix will travel with the team ahead of their second preseason game with the Indianapolis Colts, but he will again be limited to individual drills and 7-on-7 action.

title: Kevin Stefanski Names Starting QB for Falcons' Preseason Clash with Broncos
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - With two days remaining before the Atlanta Falcons open up their preseason against the Denver Broncos on Friday evening at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, the only thing we really knew going in was that Michael Penix Jr. would not be playing .
Penix has yet to be cleared for 11v11 at training camp, while Tua Tagovailoa, Cooper Rush, and Jack Strand took turns running team sessions. Penix has competed in everything else at training camp, dating back to OTAs in June, but the Falcons and his medical team are taking extra precautions with his surgically repaired knee.
Tagovailoa missed the first week of training camp as well with back tightness. He was cleared as a full participant this week and has looked sharp running the offense. Head coach Kevin Stefanski confirmed Tagovailoa will start against the Denver Broncos.
"The plan for play time it's in pencil, and we need to get through this practice to then get it into pen, but feel good about it," Stefanski said on Wednesday afternoon. "We'll play our starters a series, maybe 10 plays to see how that feels, and then we'll roll our guys through. We'll also vary playing time by player. Some guys may get more; some guys may get less.
"Tua will start in this game. I won't go up and down the roster player by player, but just understand that we'll vary."
Stefanski was quick to point out that Tagovailoa being named the starter doesn't mean he's named a starter for Week 1 against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
"I know the semantics (of what he said). I'm not there yet," Stefanski said. "We're not there to name a starter for Week 1. We'll cross that bridge."
Strand was signed as an undrafted free agent by the Falcons out of Minnesota State-Moorhead. With both potential starting quarterbacks limited or out in the first week of training camp, he took advantage of his opportunity . He's a big quarterback at 6'5 and 240+ pounds and has a quick, 3/4 release and a strong arm.
He stands to get a lot of action during the Falcons' three preseason games as he attempts to make the initial 53-man roster as a third quarterback. The Falcons took just two quarterbacks last year, Penix and Kirk Cousins.
Cooper Rush joined the Falcons on the first day of training camp. Trevor Siemian was signed as a free agent in the spring, but he was waived before ever suiting up for Atlanta. Rush got the call the day before camp, signed, and was on the field the next morning. He has looked like a steady presence the Falcons needed at camp to help run the 90-man practices and get everyone reps.
Rush has 16 starts in his career, including eight in 2024 with the Dallas Cowboys. He has a 9-7 record as a starter in an eight-year NFL career.
Stefanski confirmed Rush would be the second quarterback in behind Tagovailoa, followed by Rush to finish the game against the Broncos.
Stefanski noted last week that he believed in starters playing in the preseason and pegged game one against the Broncos and game three against the Dolphins as the games starters will see action. The Falcons travel to Indianapolis next week for joint practices with the Colts before they face each other in game two. Stefanski said the presumed starters will get the bulk of the reps in joint practices, giving reserves a much bigger chance to shine in the second game.

title: Falcons Rookie Linebacker Getting Surprise Reps with 1st Team
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - Harold Perkins Jr. is making an early impression on the Atlanta Falcons defense.
The rookie linebacker out of LSU has already earned significant reps with the starting defense throughout training camp.
But the sixth-round NFL Draft pick isn’t surprised. It’s what he expected.
“I feel regular. I do this every day,” Perkins told reporters after practice on Monday, Aug 10. “This ain’t nothing new.”
Perkins is primarily playing the inside linebacker spot in Atlanta’s starting rotation. It’s one of many positions he played for the LSU Tigers, where he starred as an edge rusher, inside linebacker, and safety.
His versatility made him a potential draft steal for the Falcons.
“I think anytime that you have an opportunity as a young player to get reps with the ones or move up from the threes or the twos, it’s a great test for our guys,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said.
“I think ‘Perk’ has continued to get better every day,” the head coach added. “Certainly, I’ve shared that with ‘Perk,’ just making sure he stacks these days. He’s being very diligent about what he has to do on our defense and on special teams.”
Perkins has ascended as an echoing voice and a helping hand for the Falcons’ defense.
He’s part of a youth movement that also features former Oklahoma Sooner and fellow rookie Kendal Daniels earning valuable time in the first defense as a mike linebacker. Daniels wears the green dot for the second-team defense, meaning he handles defensive play-call communications.
Perkins and Daniels are training camp roommates, and also lived together during rookie minicamp earlier this summer.
“Great person,” Daniels said of Perkins. “Keeps me going. Tells me the plays when I mess up. He helps me out a lot. Great player.”
Though taking linebacker responsibilities, Perkins could also get increased playing time as an edge rusher during the 2026 season. The Falcons will be without their rising star Jalon Walker, after the second-year edge tore his left ACL at training camp .
“It’s just football,” Perkins said, “My mindset is just to go out there and kill.”
Perkins will make his NFL preseason debut on Friday, Aug. 14, against the Denver Broncos.
That will be the first in-game evaluation of his impact in defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich’s system.
“The mentality of our defense, we want to be the alphas,” Perkins said. “We want to come out and stamp things from the go.”

title: Falcons' Zachariah Branch Is Turning Heads at Training Camp
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons believe they have something in Zachariah Branch, and the early returns from training camp have done nothing to dampen those expectations for the rookie.
The Falcons saw a player too talented to pass up, with the Georgia product dropping to them in the third round (12th wide receiver taken) despite finishing with 811 receiving yards and an SEC-leading 81 receptions during his lone season in Athens. Despite his output and outstanding measurables (4.35-second 40-yard dash and 20 reps of 225 pounds on the bench press), there were concerns about his diminutive frame and lack of a route tree coming out of college.
Ian Cunningham was happy to take the chance on him, and whether it has come on the practice field or in front of the media, the rookie has done nothing but impress since. After many initially thought he would be relegated to a kick return/gadget role as a rookie, Branch has quickly raised the bar for what could come from his first professional season.
“Zachariah, we continue to give a little bit more to each day,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said. “It goes back to really all these guys just trying to find roles for them as they earn them and trying to find different things that they can do that can help our offense or our defense. In this case with Zachariah, it's what routes do we feel like he can run really well, and then what personnel groupings do we want to get him in there.
“He's earning that because he practices very hard, [and] is showing up in these drills. When you go to team drills and it's 11-on-11, he continues to show up.”
Branch is finding a role, ironically being utilized in one of the things that helped him drop to the Falcons back in April. The offense has spent much of the early weeks of camp working on its screen game, heavily utilizing both Branch and All-Pro running back Bijan Robinson.
This usage plays nicely into what the rookie does best, and that role will help him adjust to life in the NFL this season, even if he sees more for himself. Branch’s new teammates are learning firsthand how he can change a play once the ball touches his hands.
“He's very explosive – down the field, in the short game, catching the ball and transitioning into a runner,” Michael Penix Jr. explained about what makes Branch such a dangerous player. “With the ball in his hands, he’s definitely special. That's somebody we want to get the ball to a lot this year, so he's definitely been looking good.”
“That dude can be anywhere,” Tua Tagovailoa added during the first week of training camp. “You find him, he’s open. That dude, he’s fast. He can get away from guys. Great separation, great hands and great elusiveness when the ball’s in his hands.”
Branch has made an impression, but the early success comes as no surprise to Cash Jones. The other Georgia rookie on the Falcons’ roster this summer spent only one year with Branch, and his early impact was expected.
Jones knew from “day one” that Branch was different, both on and off the field. The two met briefly, but he quickly learned that the former five-star wideout was much more than just a speedster.
“He’s a freak athlete, and he can be running at full speed and stop on a dot. He has great hands. He’s a super smart kid,” Jones said. “I’m super excited to see what happens this year for him.”
Finding small improvements and carving out a role is paramount in the do-or-die NFL, whether that comes on offense or special teams. To this point, Branch has accomplished that and then some.
The next test comes Friday night, when Branch will make his preseason debut at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. For a rookie who has spent the first week of camp expanding expectations, it will be his first chance to show that the hype can translate to game action.

title: Falcons Add More OL Depth, Sign Former Eagles, Alabama OL
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons got some good injury news on Monday morning when they cleared offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor for practice and removed him from the PUP List. Taylor wasn't seen at practice yet on Tuesday morning, and the Falcons are still looking far and wide to address their offensive line depth.
On Tuesday afternoon, they put a claim on former Alabama Crimson Tide offensive lineman Jaeden Roberts, who was previously with the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted free agent. Roberts was placed on waivers by the Eagles, and he didn't last long before the Falcons claimed him.
Roberts was a combine invite in February. He didn't participate in any of the agility drills, but he measured a massive 6'5 1/4" and 333 pounds and did 25 reps on the bench press with 33 3/8" arms.
He was a three-year starter at Alabama and was a preseason All-American heading into 2025. He played in 10 games last season after starting 12 in 2024. He was on the Outland Trophy watch list in both 2024 and 2025, but regressed some last season with Alabama.
Roberts will compete with Kyle Hinton, Kam Dewberry, and Layden Robinson for a reserve guard spot. The Falcons took nine offensive linemen on their 53-man roster last season, and if they take nine again this year, it's likely to be Jake Matthews, Matthew Bergeron, Ryan Neuzil, Chris Lindstrom, Jawaan Taylor, Wanya Morris, Michael Jerrell, Hinton, and either Corey Levin or James Brockermeyer as the backup center.
Roberts has an uphill battle to climb to make the 53-man roster, but he could be a practice squad candidate after cuts on August 30th, when the roster must move from 90 players to 53.
The Falcons take on the Denver Broncos on Friday night in their first preseason action of 2026 under new head coach Kevin Stefanski. Roberts isn't likely to see much, if any, action with just a maximum of two days of preparation before Friday night's contest.
However, Stefanski has said he prefers starters to play in preseason games to get ready for the season. He has pegged Friday night's game against the Broncos and the preseason game three against the Miami Dolphins on August 28th as starter games. Game two next week against the Indianapolis Colts will not include many, if any, starters, as the team uses its joint practices to get first-team reps.
Roberts is just the latest player to join the Falcons this week. They've also added edge rusher Cameron Sample , running back Trey Sermon , and tight end Nick Muse as they work their way through the dog days of August to get ready for their Week 1 clash with the Pittsburgh Steelers on September 13th.

title: Will Tua Tagovailoa Play In Preseason Opener? Potential Falcons QB1 Weighs In
full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa is days away from his first opportunity to showcase himself with the keys to the Atlanta Falcons offense.
However, it remains unclear if the quarterback will play in Friday, Aug. 14’s preseason opener against the Buffalo Bills at Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
“Whatever is asked of me, whatever’s asked of the guys,” Tagovailoa told reporters after practice on Tuesday, Aug. 11. “I think that’s what we’re going to go with, whatever Stefanski has.”
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski has said in training camp that he plans to play starters in the first preseason game against the Bills and the finale against the Miami Dolphins on Aug. 28. Starters will likely rest during game two at the Indianapolis Colts on Aug. 22, with most of their reps coming in the joint practices.
Stefanski may have an answer on Wednesday, Aug. 12, on whether Tagovailoa plays in Friday’s preseason game.
“I’ll let you guys know I think, Wednesday when we talk what the plan is for the preseason games,” the head coach said. “I want to obviously sit down with the coaches and Ian and Matt, and talk through the plan, and finalize that, share it with the players, and then I’ll share it with you guys.”
Preseason could be key for Tagovailoa getting ahead in his ongoing quarterback battle with Michael Penix Jr. The former Miami Dolphin and seventh-year NFL veteran has picked up the majority of the 11-on-11 reps. Conversely, Penix takes most of the 7-on-7 plays due to not being cleared for 11-on-11 while he recovers from a left ACL tear.
There’s currently no timetable for Atlanta to name a starting quarterback.
“Preseason plays a big role for your team collectively,” Tagovailoa said. “You don’t have the coaches out there. You’ve got to go out there, make the calls, whether it’s right or wrong, you’ve got to live with them. And from there, you come in the next day, watch film, talk about it, and go from there.”
Tagovailoa has been impressive in the days leading up to the NFL preseason, following a back tightness flare-up that forced him to miss the first day of training camp .
His field vision and ability to exploit defensive breakdowns have turned heads.
“He’s getting better every day,” said Falcons quarterbacks coach Alex Van Pelt. “I think he’s getting more comfortable with the system, the play calls, and the protection adjustments. It’s tough always coming into a new system. So, picking that up, missing the first part of camp, set him back just a little bit. But the last three or four days, he’s really come on.”

title: Ravens Get Encouraging Injury Updates on Top Cornerbacks From Jesse Minter
full_text:
Usually, when a team with Super Bowl aspirations and plus-1200 odds to make it to the ultimate title tilt, according to FanDuel's sportsbook, has two of it's best players at a premium position, leave practice early with undisclosed injuries on back-to-back, it's cause for major concern.
Thankfully for the Baltimore Ravens and their passionate fan base, that isn't the case for them as it pertains to the health status of the starting cornerback duo of Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey, according to head coach Jesse Minter .
“Got good reports on both of them.” Head Coach Jesse Minter with status updates on Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey pic.twitter.com/ZVrsbB0WIm
"I would say both are trending very well to potentially be back early next week," Minter said Thursday. "Both just dealing with a couple of small things. Got good reports on both of them. Expect both of those guys back."
Wiggins went down about an hour into Tuesday's practice with what looked like a potentially major injury after he wasn't able to put any weight on his left knee and needed to be carted off the field.
"Especially in this role, but even as a position coach or a coordinator or whatever, one of the worst feelings is seeing something like that where a guy goes down and, obviously, you don't know what it is at the moment," Minter said. "But again, [I'm] happy that it's hopefully a good report and I expect Nate to be back out there fairly soon."
Fortunately, the MRI Wiggins underwent later that same day didn't reveal any structural damage, per reports, which was about as great an outcome as anyone could've hoped for, given how grim and somber the initial reaction to the injury scare was in the immediate aftermath.
Humphrey left Wednesday's practice alongside some of the Ravens' medical staff and did not return, sparking even more concern that the team's depth at the position would be getting tested with the regular season still about a month out.
"I got a lot of confidence in the corner room," Minter said. "T.J. Tampa has done a lot of great things; Keyon Martin has done a lot of good stuff, Chandler [Rivers] has done a lot of good stuff and we got some young guys battling for trust and spots so I feel really good about the secondary overall."
The Ravens' top two cornerbacks weren't the only players that Minter fielded questions about and provided or revealed details about. Among the most important, because of how central he is to their success on defense, was the progress of star defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike's gradual ramp-up from injury.
"There's just some timeline things there that we're working with, and I think [he's] another guy that's progressing really well," Minter said. "Over the next week or two, I think you'll start to see him really mix into the action."
The two-time Pro Bowler suffered a neck injury in Week 2 of last season that not only cut his 2025 campaign short but also required surgery to address it and was rumored to threaten to end his career at one point. He opened training camp on the Physically Unable to Perform list but passed his physical and was removed from it before the Ravens took the field for their first practice. While he's been participating in individual drills, he has yet to take part in full-team 11-on-11 sessions.
Although the Ravens dodged a major bullet with their starting corners, the same couldn't be said for a  veteran player who was fighting for a roster spot as veteran quarterback Skylar Thompson became the first to land on season-ending injured reserve.
"[He was] dealing with a little bit more than maybe we thought; that was the result of that," Minter said.
Another starter who was absent from Thursday's practice but is expected to be back soon is left guard John Simpson, who Minter said is just "working through something small."
"Don't expect it to be anything that hinders his availability for the long-term," Minter added.

title: Ravens Rookie Head Coach Jesse Minter Likely To Skew Conservative On 4th Down
full_text:
The Ravens went from a new-school, aggressive program on fourth-down to one stuck in the past under John Harbaugh.
A decade ago, he was a bit of a rebel with a sympathetic ear to the advanced analytics crowd and earned a reputation for considering fourth down in some non-traditional ways, when needing more yardage that you might expect and going for it on areas of the field that wouldn’t be the norm. That changed in a big way during his final, underwhelming years in Baltimore, and the new boss is much more of an open book.
Jesse Minter is a rookie head coach, who was a very young assistant under Harbaugh here and then spent the rest of his career with Harbaugh’s brother, Jim, as conservative as they come (at Michigan and then the Chargers). And Minter’s closest NFL head coaching buddy, and the guy who his defense and mindset is most patterned after – Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald (another former Ravens assistant) – is even more of a staunch punt proponent than either Harbaugh brother (and he too coached under both).
In case you were wondering, the offensive coordinator is even younger and far less experienced than Minter, with Declan Doyle just turning 30 and spending the bulk of his career on the staff of Sean Payton, who is decidedly TEAM PUNT also. Minter said after Thursday’s practice that his philosophies on fourth down will evolve and every case will be different – Doyle, by no means the deciding voice, sounded similar on the topic – and it’s one of many new horizons for this latest chapter of Ravens football.
“Both sides of the ball will inform those decisions on how the game is going and how we’re playing,” Minter explained after the final practice of the week Thursday. “If we’re smoking on defense and we can pan pin them back inside the 5, sometimes that’s a real weapon. If we’re rolling on defense and we’ve got (running back) Derrick (Henry) rolling downhill, obviously some of those you can go - you can put the ball in the best quarterback in the world’s hands and see what happens. So there’s a lot of scenarios, and with a young punter, sometimes, let’s see what he can do. So all those things go into that.”
I don’t know about you, but this doesn’t sound like a guy who is gonzo to really empower his two-time MVP and go for it as much as anyone in NFL. I’d be quite surprised if that’s how this played out, even if Henry and Lamar are firing away. Minter didn’t want to make it about the fact that he’s a defensive-minded coach, but he is, you cannot escape that, and you can’t escape his past, either.
The Ravens defense has better personnel and a proven playcaller running it and more continuity and Minter’s scheme is very similar to what Macdonald just ran here a few years ago. The offense is entirely foreign to everyone, and Doyle has never done this job before in any real capacity let alone call plays. The defense must lead the way early, Minter is going to skew conservative and it just might stay that way.
And if he does, it’s “not because I’m a defensive coach,” Minter said in what sounded a little like a warning. But rather based on “how the offense and defense are playing in those exact moments.”
We’re all products of our mentors and environments and NFL coaches are especially so. It’s literally what gets them hired in many cases. Here’s what Minter’s mentors (and Doyle’s) tend to do in these situations:
John Harbaugh went for it on fourth down just 25 times with the Ravens last season; the league average was 28. Over the past three years, Harbaugh went for it just 54 times, third fewest in the NFL. From 2019-2022, Harbaugh went for it 90 times, 12th most in the NFL.
Jim Harbaugh went for it just 37 times during his two years back in the NFL (with Minter his defensive coordinator), tied for second fewest in the NFL. And, as you might have surmised ( or if you read our preview of this back in the spring ) only Macdonald went for it less (31 times) trusting his defense immensely even with eventual Super Bowl MVP Sam Darnold as his QB last season.
And as for Doyle, Payton, since returning to the NFL in Denver three years ago, has gone for it just 42 times, the 10th fewest times in the NFL in that span. He’s an aggressive play caller and his on-side kick decision to open the second half of a Super Bowl is one of the ballsiest and most effective coaching moves in the history of the game, but that hasn’t extended as much to fourth down.
Preseason is a bit of a dress rehearsal for the new staff’s process in making these decisions, but without key players taking part and with the results not mattering, it’s hardly a substitute for the real thing. It is a steady topic of discussion for Minter and his top assistants, including defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver and game-management coordinator Charlie Gelman.
“We have spent quite a bit of time meeting, with Jesse, myself, Charlie, Weave — going through some of these situations,” Doyle said this week, “talking about our decision-making. That changes week to week with the kicker, with the weather, with the defense, the offense, whatever.
“I am a part of that, in that I am calling the game and on second down I need to know whether I have a couple downs here or just one. That's the biggest part of it. I am reacting in a lot of ways because it's the head coach's decision.”
Especially early on, don’t be surprised if those decisions lean a particular way. Even with a rookie punter.

title: The Ravens Must Consider These 4 Back-Up QB Upgrades
full_text:
Consider me highly skeptical of the Ravens quarterback room outside of Lamar Jackson.
Of course, losing Jackson is going to mar any season – we just saw it in 2025 – but I don’t believe Snoop Huntley is a top-fight QB2, the Ravens are making a big mistake not pushing him in any way about competition for that role this summer, losing veteran Skylar Thompson to Injured Reserve is a very big deal, and signing Austin Reed out of the UFL does nothing for me.
This is a team in Super Bowl or bust mode, every roster spot should matter and the fact Reed spent a little time in the Bears camp when rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle was there is no substitute for having someone in this building who has been immersed in the Sean Payton (Broncos head coach) or Ben Johnson (Bears head coach) systems, since that’s what Doyle is pulling from having never actually done any of this before.
Going into the first preseason game with a roster loaded with uber-young pass catchers with almost no NFL experience having to spend most of the night trying to catch balls from un-drafted rookie out of UCONN (Joe Fagnano) could prove to be a waste. Once Huntley departs the game Saturday night, look out.
And I have serious reservations about Huntley as a QB in general - a year ago at this time no one wanted him, including the Ravens, until the lowly Browns wanted him for a minute … until they didn’t anymore, either, and cut him for the second straight summer . Especially picking up an entirely new system while Jackson needs maximum practice reps to do the same thing feels riskier than it should be in this QB room.
This is a Sean Payton production , folks, let’s not kid ourselves and Johnson is using a lot of the concepts and schematics that Payton established decades ago. Quarterbacks from that family tree make sense – but with a much deeper pool of time immersed in it than Reed serving as a camp arm in one camp.
So let’s hope that just because Huntley has been ordained QB2 for the summer (they overvalued him like they did tight end Mark Andrews ) that doesn’t mean the Ravens won’t reconsider. Let’s hope their pro-personnel department  – in quite a slump themselves in recent years finding back-end gems and Tuesday try-out guys who help or positive waiver claims – is scouting these QBs in the preseason and general manager Eric DeCosta is willing to pounce, if nothing else to boost the QB3 slot.
Bagent is more of a runaround guy than a great thrower, but man, if you had him in this offense in the role Taysom Hill filled for Payton (and Doyle) all those years in New Orleans that's worth something. The Bears are in no hurry to give him away and several NFL execs told me over the offseason that Chicago made it clear to other teams sniffing around that they valued him. But they also signed Case Keenum to a deal that carries a max value of $8M, and either one would be a major upgrade here at the No 3 spot, and, I believe No. 2.
Bagent is tough, the locker room loves him and every coach he’s been around loves him, including Johnson, who is very challenging to play for and who inherited him in Chicago. Bagent went 2-2 in a terrible situation in 2023 as a terribly raw rookie with a terrible head coach before Johnson eventually took over; yeah he threw six picks in four games but that team was a disaster. He’s been coached up quite well the last two years and they signed him to an extension last summer for a reason ($4M this year and $4M next year), but the Ravens are loaded on defense and the Bears need help there and a trade might make sense.
Keenum is a pro’s pro, he’s been in every system and seen everything and could stabilize your offense for 2-4 weeks in a pinch. Anything more than that at this stage of his career is a stretch, but ditto with Huntley.
Like Bagent, this kid got thrown to the wolves way too soon during a toxic time in Colts history with the owner off the rails and Jeff Saturday plucked out of the midday ESPN rotation from his basement in Atlanta and handed a head coaching gig in the middle of the 2022 season.
Ehlinger lacks ideal NFL traits and isn’t going to wow you with his frame or arm. But he has athleticism and he’s been around Payton for a while now in Denver and we know Payton thinks very highly of his No. 2 QB in Jarrett Stidham, who just started the AFC title game, and he isn’t one to always carry three QBS. Bo Nix is coming off another offseason surgery, so maybe he holds on to three for a while, but if Ehlinger is on a practice squad, and Snoop looks shaky in the preseason, they should act.
If we are down to someone like Reed as the No. 3, then we’re not talking about a true developmental kid with real upside (if the Ravens believed that was the case he would have been here much sooner and playing a ton Saturday ahead of Fagnano). In that case, give me the guy who has seen everything and done everything in this system and been a unicorn “Joker” of sorts (Payton speaks about him at length on “The Daily Flock Show” explaining how his/Doyle’s offense projects to Baltimore).
Hill understands these concepts as well as any coach could. He could do some things in short-yardage and goal line that were big problems here last year . He works cheap. On game day, his skillset and strengths and physicality would actually provide alternatives to Jackson in extreme situations that Huntley never could.

title: Snoop Huntley Is Cemented As Ravens QB2. That Could Be Quite Problematic
full_text:
The Ravens have a back-up quarterback problem.
I’m less than convinced that Snoop Huntley is the solution. And now more than ever, he’s the unquestioned back-up to two-time MVP Lamar Jackson. It’s the antithesis of a “camp battle” or “competition” – it’s an outright anointing a year after the Ravens themselves wanted nothing to do with their former un-drafted free agent signing.
Losing more-than-capable third-string quarterback Skylar Thompson to Injured Reserve before the first pre-season game is a bigger deal than you might think . The Ravens know they have nothing behind Huntley now  - no QB that they’d ever want to see in an NFL game. While they have time to address that with other teams cutting QBs before Week 1, there is no way they can feel great now heading into the exhibition opener.
Jackson isn’t going to play in the preseason though I wonder if that’s the best course of action with this offense completely new and with 30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle having never called a play in his life. And much of the starting offensive line won’t play, and rookie head coach Jesse Minter is going to have to be very careful with Huntley behind that group, after perhaps sinking more money into him ($3.5M fully guaranteed) than they probably had to.
I don’t love the fact there is no one in that QB room who has spent significant time and operated at a functional level in a Sean Payton or Ben Johnson offense before (that’s what Doyle is working from, especially Payton whom he spent almost his entire professional career working under ). Having that resource for Jackson couldn’t hurt.
Huntley has essentially been in one offense his entire career (it’s quite clear previous coordinator Todd Monken was running a derivative of Greg Roman’s offense here and that transition was spoon-fed), and he’s well behind Jackson mentally and physically and Jackson will always get the most meaningful practice reps and that will continue throughout the season as long as he’s healthy.
Which is why having a back-up who has already mastered it made sense here; and the Ravens did the exact opposite.
“They’ve got one of the worst QB rooms in the league outside of Lamar,” one longtime NFL executive who keeps close tabs on the Ravens told me. “I don’t know what they were thinking.”
This offense is “brand new” as Jackson and top receiver Zay Flowers have made very clear using identical language. The verbiage and concepts and most everything else is a total reboot. Quarterback coach Israel Woolfork spoke Thursday of how they are flipping the footwork for what QBs here were used to and noting the import of “timing, progressions, different route styles.” Huntley is not a tactician and this staff is going to be meticulous about details.
I have pause about this construct, and for as well as Huntley operated at times last year, there are many and significant reasons why the Browns preferred people like Dylan Gabriel to him a year ago. Huntley didn’t reveal much during his meeting with the media after Thursday’s practice, though he did enjoy being signed so early in this offseason (“Just being able to learn the playbook from day one,” Huntley noted). As for what’s new …
“Some unique ways we get into our plays,” Huntley said. “It’s a great playbook. I can’t wait until we keep digging away at it.”
A year ago at this time I thought Cooper Rush would be a sage signing and big upgrade over Huntley. And he was such a disaster (general manager Eric DeCosta had an epic-fail 2025 offseason, including no contract extension for Jackson) that Huntley got more run than Rush beginning just a few months later.
Every year is different and I don’t love Huntley as the unrivaled No. 2 given everything else around him. There is some mythologizing that goes on with him, because he is easy to root for and a great story and getting this much out of him given where he came from is awesome. But past is past and he’s not as twitchy as he used to be. He’s now in his age 28 season, and in 16 career starts (30 appearances) he has 13 TD passes, 10 picks, averages a puny 5.6 air yards per attempt with a rating of 82.3 . Sorry, I’m not handing anything to that guy.
It’s one thing to think he can be adequate getting very little practice work if it’s within a system and coaches and concepts he’s been immersed in before (all the rookie pieces in this offense adds another layer of difficulty, too). This ain’t that. It’s not close to that.
And if he ends up playing even more sparingly in the preseason due to some of these other injuries and the state of the offensive line (that second unit hasn’t impressed anyone), it’s going to even more of a stretch for him if heaven forbid they need him for anything in the regular season. A pro personnel department that’s been in quite a funk of its own (how many waiver claims and Tuesday tryout guys have impacted this roster lately?) best be closely evaluating some other options on other rosters with ties to Payton/Johnson.
Having a back-up who it’s worth taking Jackson off the field for in some piledriver situations (Tush Push kinda stuff/short-yardage) wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world and Payton explained in detail on “The Daily Flock Show” why he did that at times, sitting Hall of Famer Drew Brees in place of powerful Taysom Hill.
That dynamic interests me more than what DeCosta did - running it back with Lamar and Snoop despite everything being new. Having Thompson around as a potential safety net if Huntley didn’t make adjustments, at least, did interest me. Someone with a similar career to Huntley, but with like five years spent in this coaching family tree?
That should have been the objective all along. And that still might be what ends up happening. DeCosta gave Rush $4M guaranteed a year ago, and he was on his way out by October.

title: Ravens Cornerback T.J. Tampa Is Ready To Step Up for Baltimore Whenever Called Upon
full_text:
Before the Baltimore Ravens ' cornerback depth got tested after Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey , their top two players at the position, left practice early on back-to-back days, third-year pro T.J. Tampa Jr. proved himself as one of the stars of training camp thus far.
The 2024 fourth-round pick has been sticky in coverage, consistently making plays on the ball and even forcing a fumble by ripping the ball away from his draftmate, running back Rasheen Ali, in an 11-on-11 session.
. @Tamp1A 😤 pic.twitter.com/mY9cfta6Xq
"He has found the ball," defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver said. "He has made plays on the ball, which ultimately, that is what you are looking for at cornerback. And, he goes out and competes every day. He is one of those guys where if he does make a mistake, he very rarely makes the same mistake twice. That is all you are asking for with any football player."
Tampa was already trending toward carving out at least a rotational role on defense before Wiggins' major injury scare. With no timetable for the former first-rounder's return despite not suffering any structural damage to his left knee, Tampa might very well get called upon to play an even bigger role than originally expected, and if so, he feels confident in his ability to rise to the occasion.
"I've really just wanted to show [that] I am reliable," Tampa Jr. said. "I am here to put the work in, [and] I am here to show up when my time is needed."
The Ravens were likely going to involve their top four or five cornerbacks regardless of injury because that is what new head coach and defensive play-caller Jesse Minter did during his two-year stint as the defensive coordinator for the Los Angeles Chargers from 2024-25. Tampa feels like he is picking up and acclimating to this variation of the same scheme he's been in since entering the league and the plays he's been making in practice are proof of concept.
"It is very validating.," Tampa said. "[I'm] just listening to the coaches, coming in with the new scheme and listening to them and they're helping me make plays, so that's always good."
Through his first two seasons, when Tampa has appeared in games, it's primarily been to play on special teams, where a lot of depth defenders in this franchise have started out before seizing the opportunity for more meaningful snaps on defense down the road. He still projects to be a staple in the third phase of the game for the Ravens but is also doing his best to ensure that there is no drop-off in the play the team gets from the corner position when checks in on defense.
"I know I have a big role on special teams and that's what it is, but I am focused on defense and just making that one of the main things. [I'm] just showing up there and not letting there be a decline when the 'twos' come in."
Like the vast majority of players who make it to the league, Tampa has always had the physical tools and athleticism to make plays and contribute at this level, but putting it all together can take time.
"Coming in as a rookie, everything is new," Tampa said. "You're trying to be comfortable, you're trying to learn people [and] you're trying to learn plays, and just having all that in the back of my mind [now], already knowing the plays, [it is] just helping me play a little bit faster."
After seeing the field for just 18 snaps on defense in seven games as a rookie, Tampa appeared in all 17 games last year and played 147 defensive snaps, the bulk of which came in the first half of the season, including his first career start before the bye. He finished the season with 29 total tackles, two pass breakups, and his first career interception.
T.J. TAMPA's FIRST CAREER PICK!!!!!!!!!!! @Tamp1A Back in action Thursday NBC at 8:20! pic.twitter.com/AzZef50LUz
Even though he never saw the field for more than eight snaps on defense after Week 6, the reps he did receive prior to and after that point were invaluable.
"It helps a lot. Experience is everything," Tampa said. "Just getting those reps, getting the higher rep counts has helped me [be] more comfortable and see stuff happen."
If Wiggins winds up being sidelined at the onset of the regular season as he recovers from his injury, Tampa could be called upon early and often and prove to be the steal many draft pundits proclaimed he would be after he fell to Day 3 three years ago.
"He has all the skill sets to be whatever he wants to be," Weaver said. "It is just a matter of going out there and being consistently good, and not occasionally great, and we have seen that from him."

title: The More Declan Doyle Talks About His Influences The More We Learn About Ravens New Offense
full_text:
The more Declan Doyle talks about the offense he is concocting for the first time and his goals and objectives and influences, the clearer it becomes how much it will change from years past in Baltimore.
It’s confirmation of trends and alterations we reported at length on through the spring, and there have been no surprises if you’ve been reading along. And when we discussed what Doyle is trying to accomplish with his primary mentor, Broncos coach Sean Payton, and the architect of the most ripped-off offense in the modern NFL, Rams coach Sean McVay, on “The Daily Flock Show” they helped us determine how the final few pieces fit. and what it means for Lamar Jackson.
Doyle will try to hold back a lot of what he wants to accomplish from the preseason games – which begin Saturday against the Eagles – wanting to save as many surprises as possible for the games that count. And now he will have to operate without veteran third-string quarterback Skylar Thompson, a significant wrinkle that will impact evaluations of critical young players . And it will undoubtedly result in an even more watered down and rote version of what was previously in store.
But now weeks into training camp, we’ve heard Doyle himself talk about the importance of altering tempo and cadence, taking early-down, play-action deep shots and attacking defenses downfield in short yardage . The overwhelming reality that this offense will be under center like never before in Jackson’s tenure isn’t a secret at this point. And Doyle has strongly alluded to the use of Jokers  - hybrid players fulfilling multiple positions at once – without using the word Payton engrained into his football psyche .
For all the talk of throwing the ball, Doyle’s work under Payton (New Orleans and Denver ) and Ben Johnson (Chicago) means he is going to run the ball a ton and do it old school with I formations and blocking tight ends and hybrid fullbacks (Jokers) and Doyle isn’t even shying away from another 300-carry season from 32-year-old back Derrick Henry .
“Sean McVay, [Kyle] Shanahan, Sean Payton, Ben [Johnson] — these are guys that I have watched for a long time,” Doyle said after Wednesday’s practice. “You watch the sequencing, and this is my eighth year in the NFL. Really, since the beginning, you start to watch those guys and how they craft a game plan, how they attack a defense.
“Those are things you're trying to emulate when you're building a plan as an assistant, and certainly something that we're trying to do as an offensive staff as well."
He isn’t hiding who he is stealing from, and that’s the case for everyone. McVay broke down for us what he took from Bill Walsh on the show, and Payton told us he isn’t too big to steal from McVay. It’s not about what he is picking and choosing at this point, it’s about how quickly the players adapt to it, and whether they can avoid pre-snap foibles and procedural mishaps.
Doyle is going to have to learn to adapt in-game and determine when it’s time to chuck a game plan and whether an opponent is too prepared for what he had cooked up. It came as no surprise Wednesday, and was a nod to the reality of his novice status, when Doyle said he will lean heavily into his pre-game script of playcalls.
“I would say that in general, we try to script as much as we can so that our guys have a really good feeling of what we're going to do,” Doyle said. “I read a book by Bill Walsh a long time ago, and he basically talked about how the more decisions you make in the air conditioning, [the better,] because guys have a good feel for what you're going to call.
“You've made the decision based on data and facts, rather than being out there and it kind of feels a certain way and you may lead yourself astray from where you should go.”
What’s most important in the second half of camp is that the offensive line can fall into place, and Doyle builds a deep enough reservoir of potential playmakers he can thrust into as many different situations as possible. The fact that so few players and coaches have strong ties to the coaching family tree he is closest aligned with remains surprising, and the personnel on his side of the ball simply have far more warts and questions than on head coach Jesse Minter’s side of the ball.
For all of the excitement and hype and talk of Doyle being a genius, anyone who thinks this offense is coming out of the gates looking like a juggernaut is probably fooling themselves. He can borrow quite a bit from his mentors, but there is no substitute for doing it yourself.

title: Ravens Rookie Coordinator Declan Doyle Putting No Limits On Derrick Henry's Role
full_text:
Derrick Henry, unicorn that he is, has never carried the ball 300 times or more three straight years in his career as he heads into his age 32 season. Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, 30, who has never called a play before in his life, is not shying away from dialing it up roughly that much for him in 2026.
Doyle isn’t offering any direct projections, and as a total novice he isn’t sure exactly how any of this is going to play out. Heck, he doesn’t even know yet if he’s going to station himself on the sidelines or in the pressbox on game day. But he made it abundantly clear after Wednesday’s practice that he has no intentions to back off of Henry or nurse him through anything. Let’s face it, if you are doing a job as an offensive coordinator for the first time and you can hand the ball off to a guy who has averaged 5.5 yards per carry in his Ravens career, that’s a pretty tempting default.
Given an opportunity to strike a cautionary tone about Henry – surely aware of 55 years of age 32 running back data that would speak to this being when careers collapse – Doyle did anything but that. Sounds like he is fully vested in finding out if Henry can remain the ferocious bell cow he’s always been, and he in no way intimated that his normal Baltimore workload is out of the question.
“He is a special talent,” Doyle said on Henry. “There are not many guys in the league who can do what he does. The vision for him in the offense is an immense role. Obviously, I don't want to put a number on the amount of [carries], because obviously, as you look at every single week, every week is different. You want to be able to deploy things in different ways, and at the same point in time, he's going to have a pretty large workload.”
Alright then! Strap it up!
Well, if it is to be another 300 carry season, Henry would become just the third age 32 back to hit that total, joining Walter Payton (321 in 1985) and Otis Anderson (325 in 1989). To call that a different era in NFL timelines is a massive understatement. Only four backs in history have surpassed 250 carries in their age 32 season (Frank Gore and Emmitt Smith as the others).
In the only previous instance when Henry has carried 300 times or more in consecutive seasons, he suffered a Jones fracture in his foot midway through the following season (2021), missing nine games but returning for the playoffs. Henry remains in tremendous shape, beyond chiseled and beyond driven, still chasing a Lombardi Trophy. He made it clear when he met the media early in training camp that retirement is nowhere near his mind, but we all know Father Time’s record by now.
Eventually, he gets everyone.
“I don’t try to enter another season thinking about retirement or having that on my mind,” Henry explained. “That’s not even in my mindset.”
As to how much he can handle at this stage of his career , Henry offered: “I ain’t really trying to get into the expectation thing,” Alrighty then. Henry has his game face on. Our buddy Ross Tucker, former offensive lineman and CBS game analyst, FWIW, said on "The Daily Flock Show" that Henry might be impervious to Father Time. "I wouldn't put anything past that guy."
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter didn’t put any blinders on precisely how much Henry could see the ball either, but at least seemed to acknowledge the 32-year elephant in the room when probed about a pitch count or some plan for how to help Henry best get through the season.
“I do think - like all the players – we’re going to have to be really smart to get him through the long season,” Minter said. “I don’t look at that as he’s slowing down, from that standpoint. But that’s our job.”
The numbers paint a fairly bleak portrait of what happens to these older legs as the collective weight of 3000 carries mounts . It’s where even the greatest of the greats truly hit the wall. Few maintain their workloads and the ones who have, become plowhorses with far diminished explosiveness.
It’s quite tell that the best age 32 back in NFL history – Ricky Williams – had roughly 1000 fewer carries than Henry at this stage of his career (including playoffs) given his multiple suspensions and time spent away from the game and on the larger fields of the Canadian Football League.
Age 32 RB Seasons Since 1970
RBs to Amass 250 carries: 5
Avg Y/C With 200+ Rushes: 3.8
RBs With 200+ Rushes To Average 4.5/Carry: 2 (Ricky Williams 4.7, DeAngelo Williams 4.5)
Age 31 RB Seasons Since 1970
Avg Y/C With 200+ Rushes: 4.3
RBs With 200+ Carries To Avg 4.5/Carry: 8
Age 30 RB Seasons Since 1970
RBs To Amass 250+ Carries: 18
Avg. Y/C With 200+ Rushes: 4.2
RBs With 200+ Carries To Avg 4.5/carry: 11
Doyle seems undaunted by any of this. He knows a good thing when he sees it, and, for once, his nativity and inexperience may have come to fore a bit on Wednesday when he opined about this topic. This offensive line still might not be particularly good, Henry’s yards before contact dropped from 2.41 in 2024 to 1.60 last season. His yards per carry facing an 8-man box dropped from 6.3 to 3.8, but Lamar Jackson barely running the football and fewer option looks might have had plenty to do with that.
Doyle clearly also knows that Henry was good for 1600 yards again last season and averaged a robust 6.0 yards per attempt on first down. And this team will be running under center more than the Ravens ever have during the Lamar Jackson era , and Henry did more of that than any RB in the NFL during his time in Tennessee. Doyle's time spent on the staffs of Sean Payton and Ben Johnson ensure as much.
“I was telling the offensive staff how cool it is when you call a run play, first-time play caller, and Derrick Henry is the running back,” Doyle noted. “And you're like, 'The odds of this working are a lot higher.'”
So maybe it will be 300 carries for three years in a row. If Henry can hold up yet again.

title: 3 Ravens Veterans Trending Toward the Roster Bubble (And Who is Replacing Them)
full_text:
At multiple positions on both sides of the ball, the Baltimore Ravens are showing a commitment to developing their young talent that has either been drafted or signed as undrafted free agents in recent years during this year's training camp.
This will result in several of the more experienced players at those positions on the fringe of the roster not making the final cut, barring injury.
Here are three of those veteran players on the bubble, and who, at their respective positions, are likely going to prevent them from earning a spot on the team come September, when the regular season rolls around.
Even with no current timeline for the top cornerback Nate Wiggins after he avoided a major injury in Tuesday's practice that saw him get carted off the field, the eighth-year veteran still faces an uphill battle to make the team. According to several accounts from practice, he's been having a solid-to-strong training camp thus far, but he's in a tight battle with a host of youngsters who were recently drafted or made the team as undrafted free agents for one of the final spots on the roster at the position.
Oruwariye plays on the outside, where his main competition for a role as a quality or possibly even a rotational depth piece is third-year pro T.J. Tampa, who has been one of the stars of training camp, and second-year pros Bihlal Kone and Robert Longerbeam, both of whom missed their entire rookie seasons with lower-leg injuries and have been looking better and better as camp as gone on.
The Ravens brought in the 12th-year veteran as experienced tackle depth to fill out the roster and compete for the swing-tackle spot after Hakeem Adeniji was placed on the reserve/retired list a week after being signed by the team.
While there's a chance he could be a prime candidate to be brought back on the practice squad as emergency depth at the premium position, all signs are pointing to second-year pro Carson Vinson being the frontrunner to win the job, if he hasn't secured it already.
The 2025 fifth-rounder has been the first man up to protect Lamar Jackson's blindside whenever two-time Pro Bowl veteran starter Ronnie Stanley has been absent from the practice field dating back to Organized Team Activities.
The Ravens reunited with their former fourth-round pick from the 2016 NFL Draft at the onset of training camp to provide depth at both receiver and on special teams, essentially to serve in the Tylan Wallace role.
Unlike his predecessor, who was pretty much penciled into a roster spot each of the last two years under former head coach John Harbaugh, who placed a high value on core special teams players, Moore faces long odds of making the final cut on this team because their depth chart at his position is all but set in stone with second-year pro LaJohntay Wester primed to secure the sixth and likely final spot, given their needs at other positions to carry a fourth running back and tight end.
He could very well extend his second stint in Baltimore on the practice squad, but it'd take an injury or two at a couple of different positions, including his, for him to be on the initial or final 53.

title: Ravens No. 3 QB Skylar Thompson Going On IR Is A Bigger Problem Than You Think
full_text:
The Ravens placed veteran third-string quarterback Skylar Thompson on Injured Reserve Wednesday, likely ending his season and delivering a significant blow to their summer plans. Thompson has an NFL resume, he has performed gamely in a postseason start and offered the team a high level of competency to execute their offense in the preseason.
They signed journeyman Austin Reed to take his roster spot, and they had better get on the phone immediately to try to upgrade that position on the depth chart. If nothing else, the Ravens will be very active scooping up a veteran QB when final roster cuts are made. Two-time MVP Lamar Jackson is not expected to play at all in the preseason and we’ll see how much they want to put No. 2 Snoop Huntley behind a second-string offensive line that has looked compromised in camp.
The Ravens are short on proven playmakers on offense by any standard, their tight end room looks particularly suspect , with Mark Andrews nearing the end no matter what the Ravens opt to pay him. Zay Flowers, nursing a minor injury, is the only consistent playmaker in his prime in the entire passing game. They are counting on four rookies offering them something this season – receivers Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijan Sarratt and tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas – and the preseason games are vital to establishing baselines on their ability.
You risk putting those young players, who don’t really understand the game yet, in harms way if forced to rely on highly inaccurate and skittish quarterbacks with virtually no pro experience themselves playing significant stretches of these preseason games. The Ravens spent considerable time e valuating quarterbacks in the last two drafts only to use those picks on other positions – we implored them to draft Georgia Tech UDFA Haynes King in the late round, who starred in the Hall of Fame Game FWIW) – and the lack of a true No 3 or developmental prospect with real potential is a double whammy of sorts.
Thompson is highly functional and could put youngsters in positions to succeed and showcase what they can do in the exhibition games. He also, in my opinion, was in a similar tier to Huntley in terms of ability (I espoused a true competition between them), and provided real depth at the most important position in pro sports. The team did not disclose the nature of Thompson’s injury and earlier this week head coach Jesse Minter expressed hope he could come back and play in Saturday's preseason opener.
The Ravens enter practice Wednesday with undrafted rookie free agent Joe Fagnano (UCONN) as their third quarterback – sorry, that’s a problem folks – and they will try to get Reed up to speed ASAP when he arrives. Reed recently completed a season in the UFL and played at tiny Southern Illinois and Western Kentucky in college and is not close to in the same caliber of standing as Thompson.
Reed spent the 2024 preseason in Chicago – prior to Ravens coordinator Declan Doyle’s arrival there – so there aren’t really any obvious ties in that regard. Longtime back up QB/hybrid Wildcat Joker Taysom Hill remains an unsigned free agent; he is at the end of his career but worked with Doyle on Sean Payton’s staff in New Orleans.
Payton probably isn’t in a hurry to part with No 3 QB Sam Ehlinger,  who also has regular season starting experience, with starter Bo Nix coming off season-ending surgery. But Payton also might not carry three QBs and Ehlinger understands Doyle’s verbiage and concepts from his time in Denver.
The Bears signed Case Keenum to add depth to their QB room and, according to league sources, rebuffed overtures about young back-up Tyson Bagent in the past – who has legit NFL starting experience and impressed the Bears coaching staff last season as i hear it. Especially if anything happens to Huntley, even minor, in these preseason games, the Ravens might need to start probing Chicago for help.
Landing a QB who has been in this coaching family tree should have been an offseason priority, given how new all of this is, a nd had better be on their minds now with the season fast approaching.

title: One Major Starter Won’t Play for Ravens in Preseason Opener Saturday
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens are beginning the preseason against the Philadelphia Eagles at home on Saturday.
Fans that are expecting to see their favorite players suit up may be highly disappointed. Ravens head coach Jesse Minter spoke to the media on Tuesday and discussed the team’s potential absences come gameday.
"I would say some established players [will] not [be] playing in this first game,” Minter said on Tuesday, per the team’s transcript . “[It's a] good opportunity for a lot of the guys. It's an individual basis, I would say, based on maybe some of the experience and how many snaps they've played and things like that. I do think there's value [playing during the preseason]. We will have three joint practices, which I view in high regard for the work that we'll be able to get there in a more controlled environment for specific positions especially. So, it's a little bit of an individual basis, for sure."
Quarterback Lamar Jackson hasn’t suited up for a preseason game since 2021. Jackson played one game, completing 3-of-4 passes for 29 yards and was sacked twice for a passer rating of 94.8. He’s only played eight preseason games in his career between the 2018-2019 seasons and 2021. Jackson was beginning to grasp a new offensive system under Greg Roman in 2019 and hasn’t had a change in offensive coordinators until this season.
"Yes, Lamar [Jackson] is not going to play,” Minter said with a laugh.
Baltimore’s two-time MVP-winning quarterback wasn’t the only starter to not participate in preseason games last year. Derrick Henry, Mark Andrews , Zay Flowers, Ronnie Stanley and Roger Rosengarten didn’t play in the 2025 preseason.
Returning defensive starters Marlon Humphrey, Kyle Hamilton, Chidobe Awuzie, Travis Jones, Roquan Smith, Nnamdi Madubuike and Nate Wiggins each did not play in the 2025 preseason. Madubuike, who suffered a season-ending neck injury last season and Wiggins, who suffered a knee injury in Tuesday’s practice , will most likely be long shots to play.
There have been major contributors that played in last year’s preseason. Malaki Starks, Mike Green, Trenton Simpson and Teddye Buchanan (knee) played last year. However, Buchanan’s knee injury suffered an ACL tear and LCL sprain against the Cincinnati Bengals in punt coverage on Dec. 14 last season. Buchanan is currently on the physically unable to perform list and is making good progress, according to Minter.
"I would say that [Teddye Buchanan] falls into that — the next week or two, I think he'll be making some real progress,” Minter said. “We'll start to look out there at times and have all the guys that may be available on September 13. This dude has been incredible in how he's attacked coming off the injury that he's come off of. And again, it's our job to make sure that when we put him into the football environment that he's ready and he doesn't have any setbacks off of that."
With a new coaching staff and new systems in place, players could play who haven’t gotten live repetitions in their respective coaches’ schemes.

title: Biggest Decision Bills' Coach Joe Brady Must Make This Week, And He's Already Made It
full_text:
It's the first time he faces the decision as Buffalo Bills ' head coach.
When the Bills open their three-game preseason schedule at home on August 15, Joe Brady must determine which players will see live action and which ones will watch from the sideline.
In recent summers under former head coach Sean McDermott, the Bills veteran and presumed first teamers saw little, if any, exhibition game action.
"I don't think any one year is the same or there's a lot of there's a lot of the factors that go into it," said Brady prior to Thursday's practice in Orchard Park.
This year, however, Brady appears ready to shift gears.
"Right now, everybody that's healthy is going to be playing out there on Saturday," said Brady.
"Everybody" includes five-time NFL MVP finalist Josh Allen. We wrote about the quarterback's preseason game status shortly after Brady addressed reporters on Thursday.
While there's always an injury risk, Bills' players will likely benefit from learning the gameday flow at the brand-new Highmark Stadium .
From entering the venue to finding the locker room to timing the walk out onto the field, there are plenty of unfamiliar elements due to the stadium change.
"I think we get an opportunity to go into the stadium and I want [to see] the guys, how do we respond from the Red & Blue practice? Us going through it and getting that pregame routine and going out there," said Brady.
There's the competition factor for Brady, too.
"I want to see guys get hit. I want to see guys tackle. I want to see the finishing of the play and the how and all," said Brady. "There's so many variables with it. We obviously have a new everything, and so, it's our first opportunity for us to come together and show an example of what the Buffalo Bills are about. I think that that's important."
For first-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, who is administering an overhaul on that side of the ball, the preseason opener will help in the areas of both acclimation and evaluation.
"I think the plan is for guys to play. Get a taste of the scheme, live, let's go finish," said Leonhard. "As far as I'm concerned, guys are gonna go play, to be determined a little bit on how much. It's gonna be exciting for guys to get out there and just kind of let it rip."
After not taking a single snap last preseason , Allen claims to be fine with starting at Highmark Stadium on Saturday.
"I'd love to play," said Allen. "To get out there, get a good feeling and a good sense of the game and get a good sense of the guys around me, I feel like that's important to do."
Prior to 2025, Allen usually made at least one exhibition appearance per summer, and that's when the Bills weren't breaking in a new stadium with a first-year head coach.
"New environment, new routine, just understanding, again, we want to make this as real game-like as possible because it is a real game. To have those reps before first game, when we have it here in Thursday night, just understanding the process behind everything and not being surprised by anything," said Allen.
The Bills and Panthers are set for a 1 p.m. kickoff on August 15.

title: Josh Allen Anoints Buffalo Bills' Best Offensive Addition Not Named DJ Moore
full_text:
It appears as if the Buffalo Bills have found a No. 1 wide receiver for quarterback Josh Allen, but DJ Moore's arrival isn't the only offseason addition that excites the franchise field general.
After being promoted from the offensive coordinator role, Bills' first-year head coach Joe Brady made the smart decision to fill his old spot by hiring an experienced, well-respected lieutenant .
The 36-year-old Brady tabbed 54-year-old Pete Carmichael as Buffalo's offensive coordinator, whose NFL coaching career dates back to 2000.
While Brady plans to retain play-calling duties as he's done for the past 2.5 seasons, another set of hands, and eyes, is needed especially when it comes to strategy, preparation and game-planning. It's set up similarity to the situation that Carmichael lived for 15 seasons as New Orleans Saints' offensive coordinator.
Just last week, the football world was reminded of the success that the Saints had with Carmichael in that role as quarterback Drew Brees officially entered the Hall of Fame in Canton. New Orleans won Super Bowl XLIV in what was Carmichael's first season as offensive coordinator.
Naturally, Carmichael, with Brady urging him to do so, attended the August 8 enshrinement ceremony for Brees, and Allen found that to be more than appropriate.
"To be around him, obviously, he was just at Drew Brees's Hall of Fame acceptance, and I know that was a big moment for him," said Allen. "He played a part in that, too. To have somebody, who's been around greatness like that, is awesome in the room."
During Thursday's post-practice press conference , Allen fielded a question about whether he prefers the offensive coordinator to be on the field or in the booth on gamedays.
While answering, the 30-year-old quarterback turned the conversation into praise for Carmichael.
"I just want to say, too, Pete Carmichael is freaking awesome. I love the guy," said Allen. "He's been great for our room. The energy that he brings each and everyday, the wisdom that he brings, it's been awesome."
The Josh Allen-DJ Moore connection has been percolating since OTAs , and it's been flashing consistently throughout training camp thus far.
"OTAs, it was just pretty seamless the way that we communicated. the way that he spoke to me, body language wise on the field. Then, in camp, just continuing to building on that. Understanding him as a person, I do believe that pays dividends on the field," said Allen two days before the August 15 preseason opener .
The former first-round wide receiver, who has four 1,150-yard seasons, adds what's been a missing dimension to the Bills' offense.
"He obviously brings a ton of value in the pass game. He has the ability to do quite a bit of different things for us," said Carmichael. "Right now, he's bringing an element of speed and some big plays out there for us."
It's pretty clear that Allen, in addition to loving his new offensive coordinator, can hardly contain his excitement for Moore's arrival.
"He's a fantastic, fantastic teammate. He loves the game. He's attentive to detail. He just does everything the right way. It makes it such an easy job for me to throw it to him," said Allen.
