title: Kyler Murray Quickly Off to Great Start as Vikings' Official Starter
full_text:
On Tuesday, the Minnesota Vikings named Kyler Murray the starting quarterback for the 2026 NFL season. After beating out third-year passer J.J. McCarthy in training camp, Murray is in line to be on the field against the Green Bay Packers in Week 1.
Time will tell if Kyler Murray can help lead the Vikings to be competitive in a daunting NFC North division, but based on how he is handling the news of becoming the starter, all signs indicate that head coach Kevin O'Connell chose wisely.
The former Cardinals No. 1 overall pick should give the purple and gold the best chance to win this season while allowing McCarthy more time to grow and develop as a passer. And that should be a win-win situation for the team.
Murray spoke to the media after practice on Tuesday. His message about becoming the starting quarterback of the Minnesota Vikings couldn't have been clearer .
"It feels good. Obviously, any competitor, you play this game, you want a chance to lead the guys on Sunday and have an opportunity to go win. And whatever that calls for me to do on Sundays, Mondays, Thursdays — whatever it is, I take this job with great pride. There's been a lot of great quarterback play here in the past, and I just hope to continue to carry on that tradition."
Murray said all the right things to the media, but he also did all the right things at practice. His incredibly accurate day throwing the football. He distributed the ball well to the Vikings receivers, including Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Tai Felton and others.
Declaring a starter at quarterback so they can familiarize themselves with the first-team offense is important, especially considering Murray signed with Minnesota as a free agent this offseason and is looking for an opportunity to rejuvenate his career.
Trusting Murray with an offense that was inconsistent last season and ineffective at times is a big responsibility. The Vikings relied heavily on a strong defense led by defensive coordinator Brian Flores to keep them in games, but if the offense can put points on the board, the sky could be the limit for the team this year.
Minnesota will have another tough decision to make after the 2026 NFL season, but at least for now, the team appears to be in good hands with Kyler Murray as the starting quarterback.

title: Brian Flores Sends Clear Message About Caleb Banks' Early Role With Vikings
full_text:
When the Minnesota Vikings drafted Caleb Banks, they knew that his ramp-up to the 2026 NFL season was going to take some time. As we approach the first game of the preseason, we may have to adjust expectations for how often he is going to be on the field as a rookie.
Banks missed most of the 2025 college season at Florida due to injury and then reaggravated a foot injury at the NFL Combine. He was not able to physically participate in OTAs or minicamp. His participation in training camp has not been limited, but he has only taken a handful of full-speed reps each day.
On Wednesday, defensive coordinator Brian Flores was asked about the progress of Banks and fellow rookie defensive tackle Domonique Orange. He indicated that he is always going to take it slow with young players.
“I’m a patient guy with rookies,” Flores said. “I think we’ve got to give them time to really get their feet in the ground ... literally on the field and figuratively just as far as understanding the pro game, the routines, the habits that they’ve got to build to really reach their optimum potential. So I think [Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange] are doing a really good job, but there’s a lot of meat left on the bone.”
Flores’ track record matches his words. In 2024, first-round draft pick Dallas Turner only played 302 snaps as he developed behind Jonathan Greenard and Andrew Van Ginkel. Other players who are currently in the mix for starting jobs, like Levi Drake Rodriguez , Ty Ingram-Dawkins and Jay Ward were also not used much in their first seasons as Vikings.
Banks was talked about as a project type player coming out of college because he did not have huge production or experience at the college level. But the Vikings cut two veteran defensive tackles in the offseason, which seemed to indicate that they were going to lean on Banks’ size and raw tools right away to fill the void. That might not end up being the case from the jump.
“I know that it just takes time for most guys to get comfortable in the NFL game,” Flores said. “It’s probably 99% of players that need to develop, improve, get better, and the 1% are the guys who are All-Pro as a rookie. But oftentimes, every rookie player is putting those expectations on themselves and maybe hearing it from other people, but they’re not going to get it from me.”
If there might be a slower curve for Banks being ready to play, that wouldn’t be unusual for rookie defensive tackles. Last year, only three DTs played more than 500 snaps and one of them was fifth-overall pick Mason Graham of the Cleveland Browns.
It sounded from Flores’ comments that he will be weighing the performance of the rookie DTs in the preseason heavily into his assessment of how much they can contribute right away.
“It’s hard to play D-line in the National Football League,” Flores said. “We’ll really see more of what this is in game. But based off of what we’ve seen, they’re moving in the right direction.”
If Banks and Orange aren’t impact players from the jump, that means that defensive tackles Ty Ingram-Dawkins and Levi Drake Rodriguez will take on a heavy workload. They have been the starters on the D-line alongside underrated standout DT Jalen Redmond.
Flores said that Ingram-Dawkins and Rodriguez have improved in their confidence coming into this year’s camp.
“They’re much more comfortable,” Flores said. “They’re much more comfortable in their techniques and fundamentals. They know their strengths.”
Last year Rodriguez played a total of 461 snaps and had 11 QB pressures and 2.0 sacks while playing the majority of those reps as a run defender. Ingram-Dawkins played 250 snaps with 174 of those coming against the run.
If Banks and Orange aren’t ready to contribute with heavy workloads right away, those numbers and roles are likely to grow.
“We’re constantly talking about and then trying to put them schematically in those positions where they do the things they do well,” Flores said.

title: 3 Biggest Takeaways from Viking’s Training Camp 8/12: Offense Taking Shape After QB Announcement
full_text:
EAGAN, MN — The energy at Vikings practice has felt different the last two days. Gone is the hectic tracking of first-team rep splits and completions. Gone is the uncertainty amongst media and fans. Gone is the difficulty for wideouts trying to gain valuable experience with two different passers. Instead, we have what finally looks and feels like an NFL offense with purpose and direction. An offense that now knows who its quarterback will be and how to prepare for the Green Bay Packers on September 13.
With only one open practice remaining before the Vikings head east to face the Giants this Saturday, the offensive starters had what will likely be the heaviest workload they’ll see this week. The good news is that they continued to make the most of it.
Here are my three biggest takeaways from a humid afternoon in pads.
The Vikings enter a season with a castoff quarterback and expectations of mediocrity, only to shock the world and make a deep playoff run. Sound familiar? Those of us who have followed this team for decades know this script all too well. Now, I’m certainly not promising a soul-crushing NFC Championship performance from the 2026 Vikings, but Kyler Murray’s performance since being named the team’s starter may be cause for a healthy level of optimism.
Murray continues to operate the offense with impressive conviction, especially considering he was splitting first-team reps with J.J. McCarthy until Tuesday. He looks like a QB who’s been operating this offense for years, even though he’s brand new.
He has found a rhythm with his weapons, leading to chunk plays downfield. He connected with Tai Felton for about 25 yards and tossed a quick slant to Jordan Addison, who sprinted upfield for a big gain. The implementation of that route alone should be a sign to Vikings fans that KOC is adding new tools to his play-design arsenal to help Murray succeed.
Most importantly, he continues to build rapport with star receiver Justin Jefferson. The two connected on another big play on Wednesday as Murray hit Jefferson deep over the middle. After experiencing a career-low year for yards and touchdowns in 2025, Jefferson seems determined to get on the same page with Murray quickly.
Kyler Murray finding Justin Jefferson deep at practice. (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/9oj5qjecW3
Quarterback conversation aside, Jordan Mason has been the star of the Vikings offense this week. While he carries the label of an up-the-middle power back, Mason is showing what he’s capable of when he’s able to turn loose on the outside.
The 27-year-old back has had multiple breakaway runs in just the last two days, showcasing a level of speed we’ve rarely seen from his runs up the gut. It seems clear that Mason is a beneficiary of Frank Smith’s newly implemented outside zone scheme.
I can’t wait for the #Vikings run game in 2026. (Via Vikings IG) https://t.co/tEj7fuX2sL pic.twitter.com/AbS22M5CJt
Mason is listed as a co-starter with Aaron Jones on the Vikings' unofficial depth chart released Wednesday, but if he runs like this in season, he’ll have a strong case to hold the RB1 title entirely to himself.
If you were wondering how J.J. McCarthy has performed in practice since officially being officially made QB2, the answer is largely the same as before.
McCarthy still struggles to process the field at the speed needed from a dependable NFL starter, and, to be honest, sometimes struggles to match the processing speed of an NFL backup. McCarthy had multiple plays Wednesday where the result carried no weight, since he would have already been knocked to the turf in a real game. The question now is: where do McCarthy and the Vikings go from here?
Would he even want to be the team’s backup, or would he try to find greener pastures elsewhere?
From what McCarthy told reporters after practice, he wants to see things through in Minnesota.
"This is the place I want to be." J.J. McCarthy on his future with the Vikings. pic.twitter.com/fj4NLl7Tli
McCarthy’s preseason play will go a long way toward deciding the immediate future for the 23-year-old former national champ. A strong performance Saturday could provide renewed confidence in his potential long-term development in Minnesota. It could also open pathways to a QB-needy team if McCarthy or the Vikings decide it's best to part ways.
What’s clear, though, is a bad performance could spell continued trouble for McCarthy, who desperately needs to recapture the hope he gave Vikings fans in his 2024 preseason premiere against the Raiders.

title: 3 Burning Questions Vikings Must Answer in Preseason Opener: OL Depth Can Make or Break the Year
full_text:
Good news: the Vikings play a football game this weekend .
Sure, the results don’t matter in the standings, but the lessons learned will help to formulate what will ultimately become the 2026 Vikings roster. After two and a half weeks of training camp practices in the Minnesota humidity, players fighting to secure their spots on the 53-man roster will get their chance to prove their worth against opponents in a different jersey.
The team has put the quarterback competition to bed , allowing general manager Nolan Teasley, head coach Kevin O’Connell and their staffs to focus on the other question marks surrounding the team over their three preseason matchups.
From the trenches to the backfield to defensive utility players, here are three questions the Vikings need to answer at MetLife Stadium this weekend.
I feel confident saying this is my biggest concern for the Vikings in 2026. The Vikings experienced a rotational mess along the offensive line in 2025 as injuries impacted nearly every starter at one point or another. Ryan Kelly’s multiple concussions led to his retirement this past offseason, moving Blake Brandel into the spotlight as the projected starting center .
While O’Connell tends to avoid playing starters in preseason matchups, Brandel desperately needs the reps, especially since he had never snapped a ball in a competitive environment before last season. Backup center Michael Jurgens enters Year 3 with a significant task as well: proving the team can rely on him if and when he’s called upon.
Left tackle Christian Darrisaw seems to be back at 100%, but given his history of injuries, as well as that of right tackle Brian O’Neill, the team’s backup tackles will have a lot to prove as well. Third-round pick Caleb Tiernan and free agent addition Ryan Van Demark will be two names to keep an eye on.
Fan favorite Walter Rouse will need a great game to keep himself in consideration for the final roster
Demond Claiborne has been one of the more fascinating names to follow through Vikings camp so far. The 198th overall pick out of Wake Forest has his work cut out for him, but may have the raw physical tools to hit the ground running. At 5’10”, 188 lbs, Claiborne does not have the natural build of a traditional every-down back. What he does have is explosive, game-changing speed.
Claiborne’s camp has been inconsistent, with some early struggles with ball security and pass catching and an unspecified injury. In recent days, though, he’s come alive. Claiborne has showcased his home-run ability running (h/t VikingsFanPage) with burst around the edge and, importantly, as a pass catcher.
Demond Claiborne’s speed is something else. (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/qi7ZWSAEWW
Saturday could be the exact spotlight Claiborne needs to show what he can do in game action. I’d expect him to get more than enough opportunities to prove what he can do with the ball in his hands.
I’ll start with this disclaimer: defensive coordinator Brian Flores will not show his full defensive hand in this, or any other preseason game. The man loves surprising his opponents mid-season and won’t want to spoil the fun by putting it on tape ahead of time. But he does have some decisions to make, especially with two new additions who could make impacts in multiple spots.
Jake Golday has already surpassed expectations for many.
While it seemed that he would spend his first year largely with the MLB group, he’s already taking snaps outside with the first-team unit in camp. Maybe the early comps to Andrew Van Ginkel weren’t too far off. Flores will need to find a delicate balance this preseason of figuring out just how good Golday is as a utility player , while also making sure he gets the needed reps at the spot he sees him playing most in 2026.
Jamal Adams is another interesting rotational piece to keep an eye on. Adams changed jersey numbers shortly after joining the team to allow him to rotate in at safety and linebacker. Most of his practice snaps have been at safety over the last week, possibly due to Ivan Pace’s solid start to camp and fellow safety Jay Ward entering concussion protocol.
What will his workload and use look like on Saturday? We’ll have to see what Flores has planned for the 30-year-old former All-Pro.

title: Under-the-Radar Pass-Catcher Is Poised to Make Some Noise in Week 1 of Vikings' Preseason
full_text:
It's safe to say that Vikings tight end Gavin Bartholomew didn't have an ideal start to his NFL career. After being a sixth-round pick of the Vikings during the 2025 NFL Draft, the Pitt standout suffered a back injury that held him out of action for his entire rookie season, leaving him under the radar when the current offseason began.
Fast forward to this summer, when Bartholomew is thriving during the Vikings' training camp . The 6-foot-5, 249-pound Pennsylvania native is making a great case for earning the third tight end spot on the 53-man roster for the upcoming season.
Ben Yurosek, Bryson Nesbit, and Marshall Lang are all fighting for a tight end spot this season as well, but a solid performance during the preseason opener against the Giants could go a long way for Bartholomew.
At only 23 years old, Bartholomew has a bright future ahead of him with the Vikings. If training camp is any indication of his potential, watching him high-point passes and haul in difficult catches could help him earn a role for head coach Kevin O'Connell this season.
On Saturday, Vikings fans will want to keep an eye on Bartholomew against the Giants during the Purple and Gold's Week 1 exhibition game . He is in line to see the field as part of the offense and special teams, where he will have an opportunity to cement a role with the squad.
With his excellent training camp performance so far, Bartholomew doesn't need to have an amazing preseason performance to impress the coaching staff. He is already showing that he is ready to contribute; the only question is where he will be used and how often.
During his 50 games at Pitt, Bartholomew caught 105 passes for 1,257 yards and 11 touchdowns. That production, combined with his size and determination, should have everyone excited to watch him take the field this weekend. Still, the Giants were solid against TEs last season, allowing the 10th-fewest receiving yards and seventh-fewest yards to the position.
In his draft prospect profile on NFL.com, Bartholomew's blocking was praised for being "aggressive," and the site noted that he will likely be an in-line blocker at the NFL level despite having soft hands and a solid catch radius. It wasn't an eye-popping performance; however, the 52.7 run block grade he earned on Pro Football Focus in his final collegiate season was a career-high mark.
After not seeing Bartholomew take the field as a rookie, it is exciting to see what he will be capable of during Week 1 of the preseason. Hopefully, he can continue to build on an excellent training camp and force the Vikings to find a role for him this season.

title: Jake Golday's Outlook Could Be Limited by One Vikings Veteran's Strong Camp Performance
full_text:
The Vikings drafted linebacker Jake Golday out of Cincinnati in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft. The intriguing prospect is a unique fit for the team because of his ability to play as an interior linebacker or play on the edge, making him one of Minnesota's rookies to watch during training camp.
Golday's versatility makes him an extremely valuable piece in defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit. However, being able to play two positions makes it more difficult to establish him as a starter who will fill a particular role in the upcoming season.
On the edge and the inside, the Purple and Gold have several veterans—Andrew Van Ginkel, Dallas Turner and Eric Wilson—already occupying key roles, as well as another linebacker whose strong offseason performance could limit Golday's workload when the Vikings take the field against the Packers in Week 1.
Golday will eventually be a major contributor for the Vikings, but he may have to assume a backup or rotational role for the upcoming season. Taking a starting job (or even a 53-man roster spot) from one of the other linebackers is an uphill climb, and standing in his way is none other than Blake Cashman.
On the surface, Cashman should be the most threatened by the possible emergence of Golday, but a strong training camp and familiarity with the defense will make it hard for the rookie to unseat the veteran defender.
Cashman has been dealing with a finger injury that put his availability into question since the start of training camp, but that issue has been put to rest after he looked great at practice and made an astounding number of plays. He's been practicing with the first team, capitalizing on those opportunities with his interception against J.J. McCarthy on Aug. 1 being one example.
After Sunday night's practice, Bring Me The News ' Will Ragatz even lauded Cashman's success against Kyler Murray in practice.
The good news for Golday is that Cashman is in the final season of his three-year, $22.5 million contract .  Minnesota has had no problem moving on from higher-priced veterans in favor of youth and potential recently, so it might not be too long before the 23-year-old defender earns a starting role.
Until then, the Vikings will likely lean on Cashman to hold down the starting interior linebacker job next to Wilson in Flores's defense. Doing so allows Golday to move around the defense and play more situational football at multiple positions.
That versatility is a huge bonus for the team since it also allows the rookie time to develop and acclimate to the NFL level before being thrust into a starting role. And there is nothing wrong with having talent on the depth chart past the players who are named starters.

title: 3 Winners From Vikings' 8/11 Training Camp: Offense Humming With Kyler Murray at the Helm
full_text:
EAGAN, MN — There was a different energy in the air Tuesday at TCO Performance Center. Maybe it was the announcement that Kyler Murray was officially the starting QB for the Vikings, or maybe it was the fact that it was wide receiver autograph day. We may truly never know. Jokes aside, wideout day is typically the busiest non-night practice of training camp, bringing in an appropriately large crowd for the team’s first day with an established QB depth chart.
Conversations in the crowd indicated excitement from some and hesitation from others. Several J.J. McCarthy jerseys stood out in the purple-and-white crowd. Once practice kicked off, it seemed Kevin O’Connell had made the right call. The offense flowed with a consistency and purpose we had yet to see while reps were still being split. For the first time, we saw what the 2026 Vikings offense could look like, and it was promising.
Here's one player and two position groups that won the day with a more settled offense.
I mean, this one was obvious, right? Murray won the day before he even stepped on the field after O’Connell announced the team was moving forward with him as their starting QB. All he did after was put together one of his better practices of the summer.
Head Coach Kevin O'Connell on naming Kyler Murray the starting QB pic.twitter.com/YSUhnuem7J
Murray was incredibly accurate today, having only one incompletion by my count. He had several significant gains, with impressive plays to Justin Jefferson, Tai Frelton, and Jordan Addison. It was a thing of beauty.
Compared to Murray’s high-flying performance last Wednesday, this seemed more sustainable, calmer, and more like what you’d see in a real NFL game. Decisiveness and timing were key themes throughout the now-extinct QB competition, and Murray spent Tuesday proving why these assets allowed him to secure the starting gig. While the fanbase works through their feelings on the final QB decision, I hope they find the following to be an encouraging endorsement: If Murray plays like he practiced today, this season will be very fun for the purple and gold.
Kyler Murray and Jordan Addison have built a nice connection so far. Here’s another one from today. (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/RT4bvN1cNC
This one may be cheating, but a day where your QB is on fire tends to make your wideouts look pretty good. Of particular interest is Murray’s connection with Jefferson. The two connected on another big play today, and it's already ripe for debate online. Similar to their big connection last week, Murray seems to have a bit of a “frick it, Jefferson’s down there somewhere” mentality. He just seems willing to throw it up while trusting his top wideout to make a play. So far, it seems to work well.
Addison has seemingly ramped fully back into the offense after missing time last week with a thumb injury. Felton continues to stack impressive plays, this time snagging a throw from Murray for about 30 yards. Jauan Jennings had a quieter day but made his presence felt as a blocker in the run game, emphasizing the value he brings to the offense in totality. Myles Price also had a nice catch from McCarthy down the right sideline.
Dontae Fleming, Jeshaun Jones, and Dillon Bell didn’t make as much noise, but are in line for significant playing time this weekend against the Giants .
Kyler Murray calls playing with the Vikings WR group “a blessing.” “Everyone knows what we have in that room from top to bottom.” pic.twitter.com/xdRy1rWm3p
KOC has often talked about marrying the run and the pass throughout his tenure in Minnesota. Today’s practice showed what that could look like in 2026. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason were running all over the field on Tuesday. The new-look Vikings run scheme is already showing its potential, and I think much of it is still being kept under wraps. Mason did have a fumble, but tight end Josh Oliver was able to recover it.
Rookie speedster Demond Claiborne also made his presence felt after taking a short pass for a long-distance touchdown. After having some ups and downs early in camp with ball security and drops, it's been good to see Claiborne make more impact on the offense.
Zavier Scott also had a few nice runs, lowering his shoulder and picking up multiple first downs on the ground. Both Scott and Claiborne are expected to get a significant amount of reps against the Giants on Saturday.

title: McCarthy vs. Wentz: Debating Who Vikings Should Name as Kyler Murray's Backup
full_text:
It's no longer news that Kyler Murray is the Vikings' starting quarterback for the 2026 NFL season, as there's been more than enough time to digest the new reality. Without much surprise, Murray becoming the QB1 has left Vikings fans wondering what to make of J.J. McCarthy's outlook with the franchise .
For now, head coach Kevin O'Connell has made it crystal clear that the 23-year-old QB is "ready to go" when it comes to taking on backup duties , per Bring Me The News ' Will Ragatz. Even though that's another vote of confidence from his head coach, it doesn't exactly sound like O'Connell confirmed that McCarthy would be the de facto QB2—which is especially curious with Carson Wentz lurking in the shadows.
That said, it's time to examine whether McCarthy or Wentz is the better backup option for the Vikings.
Although he started 10 times last season, it's fair to doubt whether McCarthy is the right man for the job given that the results were... less than stellar.
He completed 57.6% of passes for 1,632 passing yards, 11 touchdowns, 12 interceptions and a 72.6 passer rating. McCarthy's 61.8 overall grade ranked 35th among 43 qualified quarterbacks on Pro Football Focus , giving a clearer picture of where he ranked around the league.
Couple that performance with an underwhelming training camp for the most part , and no one would blame the Vikings for wanting McCarthy to further prove himself. In fact, that's exactly what he should be doing. He's given the doubters too much material—between last season and this summer—to doubt his capabilities, and it's time to use the upcoming preseason slate to silence them.
As for his case, McCarthy's 10 starts indicate he should slot in seamlessly should he need to step in for Murray at any point. He'll have had another training camp and preseason to work with O'Connell, so there's no excuse not to be better than what we've already seen. Especially if McCarthy is fighting for his future at that point.
The fact that there are two years plus a fifth-year option remaining on his contract only adds to why the Vikings might want to keep McCarthy rather than expose him to waivers.
Bringing in Murray wasn't the only QB-related move the Vikings made this offseason, as they also re-signed Carson Wentz back in March.
The former Pro Bowler competed with McCarthy for the QB1 job, and while he initially lost, he made five starts as his younger counterpart faltered early on. Unfortunately, injuries—including a season-ending shoulder issue—limited his availability. Wentz finished the 2025 campaign with 1,216 yards, six TDs to five INTs and an 85.8 passer rating with a 65.1% completion rate.
Despite the injury-plagued year, all signs point to Wentz having a strong training camp so far.
On Saturday, Vikings OnSI 's Jason Harmon mentioned how the former NFL MVP finalist stood out among the rest and " flashed what remained of his mobility at age 33 by taking off for a scramble ." The preseason will reveal if the throwback performances in practice are a sign of what he can still do against an actual opponent, but it's safe to say that the early signs are encouraging.
Of course, the fact that Wentz has 99 regular-season starts and a Super Bowl ring in his collection helps strengthen his QB2 case. On the flip side, his recent injury history gives reason for pause.
Yes, last season was a frustrating experience. Yes, he's made some mistakes in training camp and will likely mess up a few more times in the preseason. Still, McCarthy is who the Vikings should roll with behind Murray, rather than choose Wentz.
Experience and results are on Wentz's side, but McCarthy's age and contract can't be ignored. He also still has O'Connell's trust, and that, regardless of what you think about it, means something. Whether McCarthy repays that trust by taking that next step remains to be seen, though.
At the end of the day, the Vikings could end up looking foolish by letting McCarthy go (either via cut or trade) and watching him develop into a legitimate starter elsewhere. He might even be ready to overtake Murray next season. Meanwhile, veterans like Wentz—as solid as he's been—can be found throughout the season.
For now, No. 9 should be QB2.

title: J.J. McCarthy Could Still Start After Losing Vikings' QB Battle (and Here's When)
full_text:
The Vikings are still a few weeks away from finalizing their 53-man roster , meaning there's plenty of time for the ongoing position battles to develop. That said, the team's competition under center is officially over . Head coach Kevin O'Connell named Kyler Murray as the Vikings' QB1 on Tuesday, leaving no doubt who'll lead the offense into Week 1 of the regular season and beyond.
Although he had his fair share of believers, it's fair to say that the writing was on the wall for J.J. McCarthy for a while now. Although not every shortcoming so far is his fault, McCarthy rarely looked like a legitimate QB1 in the 10 starts he saw last season, and a drastically inaccurate start to training camp left O'Connell & Co. with no other option but to roll with Murray as their top arm.
But just because one battle was lost doesn't mean that all hope is gone, as the Vikings' coaching staff still believes in the former Michigan signal-caller's potential .
"(J.J. is) still a guy that's only played 10 games. He's shown improvement off of last year," O'Connell said on Tuesday. "Even in this training camp with the work he's put in and his comfort level, just growing a little bit day in and day out. Very excited to continue to get to work with him every single day, coach him."
#Vikings HC Kevin O’Connell on JJ McCarthy’s future in Minnesota: “He’s still a guy that’s only played 10 games. He’s shown improvement off of last year… as he knows, he’s holding the pen on his story. We’re going to support him and try to help him continue to improve as a… pic.twitter.com/GdKql9mGsh
With his head coach still standing firmly behind him, there's a chance that McCarthy could wind up starting for the Vikings at some point this fall.
Murray might be the best pick to lead the Vikings' offense starting in Week 1, but that doesn't mean that he can rest on his laurels. The former Cardinals QB is still playing on a one-year contract, meaning his future is far from secure. He'll need to leave no room for questions as soon as the regular-season action begins.
Otherwise, the door will be open for a change.
The Vikings will open the season with back-to-back NFC North clashes against the Packers and Bears at home and on the road, respectively. It will be important for Murray to prove himself in these matchups, showing that the Vikings can compete with the two teams that finished first and second in last year's divisional race.
After that, he'll head into a Week 3 matchup against the Buccaneers, looking to out-duel Baker Mayfield, who's been floated as a potential QB option for Minnesota in 2027.
Games against the lowly Dolphins (Week 4) and Saints (Week 5) should be layups for Murray and company; however, they also have the potential to be trap games. If he struggles against either or both of those foes leading into the Week 6 bye, that could be the perfect excuse for the Vikings to switch things up under center.
Bye weeks are the perfect opportunity for coaches to make major lineup adjustments, including a quarterback change. Considering how the Vikings will have 14 days between their road game against the Saints and a home meeting with the Colts, McCarthy is likely looking at Week 7 as his best chance to take the reins back from Murray.
Hosting the Colts will start a tough five-game stretch that also features the Lions, Bills, Packers and 49ers. In other words, the Vikings will want the best man under center for that. If Murray proves that he can't be that guy, there won't be much to lose by throwing McCarthy back into the mix. It might be a one-game experience or last much longer.
Either way, the week leading up to Sunday, Oct. 25 is worth keeping track of.
Assuming that's McCarthy's likeliest date to return to starting duties, the 23-year-old QB has about two months to keep O'Connell and the rest of the Vikings' staff believing in him. Otherwise, regardless of how Murray performs, No. 9's time with the franchise could end sooner rather than later .

title: Mike Vrabel Has Confidence in Patriots' Andy Borregales After Trio of Missed FGs
full_text:
FOXBORO --- While the New England Patriots tied with the Indianapolis Colts 13-13 in Thursday evening's preseason opener, the game was one swing-of-the-leg away from going in New England's favor.
In the waning moments of the matchup, the Patriots' offense -- led by rookie Behren Morton -- drove downfield to set up a 49-yard field goal attempt for second-year kicker Andy Borregales.
The 23-year-old pushed it wide left, his third miss of the day on five attempts.
Borregales' night began with a 40-yard make on New England's opening drive of the game. In the final minute of the first quarter, he pulled a 56-yarder left of the goal posts. He drilled his next attempt from 52-yards out, but followed it up with misses to the left on a 55-yarder and the 49-yard go-ahead attempt.
Head coach Mike Vrabel, who is no stranger to kicker mishaps, was asked about Borregales' following New England's draw with Indianapolis.
"We're going to have mistakes. In everything we do, we just need to be able to come back," he said. "We need to be able to bounce back, and we need to be able to answer. Guys are going to drop a pass. Guys are going to miss a block. We're going to miss a kick.
"But you just have to not let those things pile up, and Andy's been really good with that, and I would anticipate him getting back to work and really starting to focus, and maybe it was a footwork thing or trying to overswing."
Vrabel has a history of kicker difficulties dating back to his time with the Tennessee Titans. In his six seasons as the organization's head coach, he had a different kicker lead the team in field goal attempts in five of them.
"If we make kicks, we will have the same kicker," Vrabel said on July 27. "It is important that we make all our field goals ... But obviously, having Andy make the type of big kicks that he made last year, we felt very comfortable having him back."
Last season, Borregales connected on 27 of his 32 field goal attempts and finished the year by connecting on 59-consecutive extra point attempts (including playoffs). Thursday was a stark change of pace from the kicker's impressive rookie year.
"I don't have a message (for Borregales)," Vrabel said postgame. "I mean, we're expecting to make them. It's pro football. (The Colts are) banging them in from 60 yards. They've got two kickers on the roster. So, you know, Andy knows we have to make those field goals."
Vrabel mentioned the team will discuss potentially bringing in competition for Borregales, who is currently the sole kicker on the roster. But for now, New England's head coach remains assured in his kicker.
"I have confidence in Andy," Vrabel said. "You want to be able to make those, and I think we got in a position to win the football game, and you want to be able to make them."

title: Patriots QB Report: How Did Tommy DeVito, Behren Morton Perform in Preseason Tie?
full_text:
FOXBORO --- The New England Patriots fans have gotten used to seeing Drake Maye trot out onto the field as the starting quarterback. In the team's 13-13 tie with the Indianapolis Colts in the preseason opener, fans in attendance watched his backups.
Both Tommy DeVito and Behren Morton got significant reps in their first game action of the year. Both of them got a half each, with DeVito bowing out as the third quarter began to give way for the Texas Tech rookie.
"It's good work," head coach Mike Vrabel said postgame on what he took away from Tuesday's joint practice and the preseason result. "Hopefully everybody came out as clean as possible. ... I felt like it was good to work with them and try to have a productive game."
It's clear that DeVito and Morton won't be a threat to Maye's job security any time soon. Each of the quarterbacks wish they had some plays back, but ultimately it wasn't the end of the world for the Patriots as they work through their backup options under center.
DeVito, who had been slinging it in training camp practices all summer, earned the starting nod. He started the game slow, opening up with three incompletions in his first five pass attempts. But he eventually settled in, hitting Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III and Eli Raridon on some chunk plays.
The big throw -- a 12-yard touchdown strike to Williams in the second quarter -- gave the Patriots their only touchdown of the night. It was a perfectly-placed back shoulder throw at the front pylon of the south end zone.
"I think just stuff is going to click," DeVito said postgame, admitting that the juices were flowing to open up the night. "Once you get into that flow and then start feeling it and the guys around you are playing, it just becomes easy at that point."
"I thought there may be a couple balls that he'd like to have back, but I thought that there was good operation. I thought there was good placement," Vrabel said. "I thought for the most part, he was fairly accurate and the ball came out on time."
DeVito's night ended with a final drive to close the first half , one that looked like it was going to end with points. He hit Williams outside the numbers for 25 yards, but a low throw to Tejhaun Palmer eventually ended that drive.
"The ball was moving down the field. But like I said, just did not start off hot enough," DeVito said. "And I think that a lot of the penalties and little mistakes here and there, they just need to get nipped in the bud early because it just kills drives."
Unlike DeVito, this was the first time Morton played on an NFL field . It was a big moment for the Patriots' seventh-string rookie, who didn't get the start, but came on to close out the night.
"You’re playing at such a legendary place, and so it was really cool to be there in that atmosphere," Morton said.
His performance wasn't the greatest by any stretch. There were a couple throws that sailed on him and the offense mustered just thre points once he entered the game. Still, it was a night of learning for Morton that his head coach appreciated.
"I think a lot of this is composure," Vrabel said. "It's the, you know, making sure that everybody's on the same page in a huddle, right? ... There's a big responsibility."
There was a chance for Morton to lead the Patriots to victory in the final seconds. Tied at 13 with more than a minute to go, the offense got some momentum following a pair of Kobe Prentice receptions and a 15-yard personal foul that pushed the Patriots into Colts territory.
It didn't happen, as the Patriots ran the ball twice before kicker Andy Borregales missed a 49-yard field goal (his third miss of the night) and ended the game with a tie score.
"We should’ve pushed the ball further down the field for Andy," Morton said. "But proud of the way that we responded. We got pretty sluggish in the third, sluggish in the fourth and finished off the fourth better."

title: 11 Takeaways From Patriots' Tough Preseason Tie over Colts
full_text:
FOXBORO --- The score won't truly dictate much about how the New England Patriots ' 2026 season will go, and the result certainly won't be remembered by many.
The Patriots nearly pulled out a win over the Indianapolis Colts, but had to settle for a 13-13 tie in what wasn't a pretty game by any stretch of the imagination. Four combined turnovers, nine combined punts and 11 combined penalties gave us a perfect example of the preseason vibes at Gillette Stadium.
It's the preseason, so of course not all of the Patriots' biggest names played. But a select group of players weren't spotted during pre-game warmups.
Wide receiver Kyle Dixon, defensive tackle Christian Barmore, linebacker Christian Elliss, cornerback Christian Gonzalez, cornerback Charles Woods and long snapper Julian Ashby weren't in pads as the team warmed up. Edge rusher Harold Landry (PUP) and safety Brenden Schooler (NFI) have yet to make their debuts this summer, and that didn't change Thursday.
This year's preseason home opener didn't have as many fireworks as last year's 48-18 win over the Washington Commanders, but Mike Vrabel and the Patriots did have some positives to take away.
Here's how it happened, and what it means moving forward:
Without Drake Maye in the starting lineup for obvious reasons, the Patriots turned to backup Tommy DeVito to start the game . He's been putting together a strong camp as the team's QB2, so it only made sense that he got a larger opportunity in a game situation.
DeVito game out and really tossed the ball well. He played just the first half, but had the Patriots up 10-7 by the time he was pulled for rookie Behren Morton to start the third quarter. He ended his day going 13-for-22 with 138 yards and a touchdown, and really looked comfortable in the huddle.
His day ended on a two-minute drill to close the first half. He took a hard hit in the pocket and delivered a 25-yard strike outside the numbers to Kyle Williams, before the drive stalled after a low throw to Tejhaun Palmer.
After the Patriots' opening drive stalled inside 30-yard line and were forced to kick a 40-yard field goal, the defense wasted no time getting the ball right back.
The Colts, set up by a big kick return from Coleman Owen and a 17-yard throw and catch between Anthony Richardson and Drew Olgetree, were starting to put together a nice drive. Instead, it was the free agent Vildor making the first big play of the preseason.
Richardson tried to hit Owen in the flat, but the wide receiver couldn't corral it. It felt right into Vildor's hands, and although he was ruled down by contact, the cornerback ran down the left sideline to the tune of cheers. It was a nice play by Vildor, who has spent most of camp working as either the fourth or fifth cornerback .
The Patriots have cycled through a lot of reserve running backs this week, eventually putting Myles Montgomery and Terrell Jennings on season-ending IR . That let rookie Jam Miller take control as the starter tonight. Although he did split some time with Lan Larison, it was clear that the Alabama rookie was the workhorse.
He finished the day with 14 carries for 55 yards, both team highs. He was also targeted one time in the passing game, but a high throw from DeVito left it uncatchable. Even deep into the fourth quarter, Miller ran with juice and burst, a good showing for a player now looking at a much larger role in the upcoming weeks.
New England's third offensive drive could have had some major highlights on the timeline. Instead, they kept getting pushed back. First round rookie Caleb Lomu , handling the starting right tackle duties, had several duds on that drive.
First, DeVito connected with rookie tight end Eli Raridon on a nice catch-and-run, but it was called back because Lomu was too far downfield. Later on the drive, Colts rookie edge rusher George Gumbs Jr. beat Lomu in a collapsing pocket for the game's only sack.
Lomu did end up having a few nice plays to close the first half, including picking up a blitzer on a 20-yard catch by Efton Chism III, but it was still a work in progress for the rookie tackle.
The offense wasn't able to get anything cooking, but the defense started to swing the game in New England's direction. With the Colts driving, what loked like a sure-bet rushing touchdown from Seth McGowan led to the football being on the ground. Jeremiah Pharms Jr. punched the ball out, and safety Dell Pettus recovered it at the 1-yard line .
Video assistance gives the ball to New England. They've got three takeaways already, and two in the last three plays. https://t.co/hARMMQRqAw
On the next defensive possesion, the Colts turned it over again. Anthony Richardson ran to his left trying to pick up some extra yardage. Linebacker K.J. Britt, who had clogged the running lanes one play prior, came flying in to knock it out of Richardson's hands. It was initially ruled down by contact, but a quick challenge from Vrabel led to it being overturned.
Late in the first half, the Colts would ultimately break through. Richardson bulldozed his way into the end zone on a one-yard quarterback keeper to give the Colts their first points of the night.
The Patriots entered the day with an already-thin group in the interior of their offensive line. They ended the night down one of their starters.
Ben Brown, who's consistently repped with the second-team offense at both center and guard, opened the game as the starting center. In the first quarter, DeVito scrambled out of the pocket. In the pile that later formed, it appeared that the Patriots quarterback was tackled into Brown's leg.
He would stay down for a brief period of time before eventually being helped up and led into the blue medical tent. After spending some time with members of the medical staff, Brown was taken to the locker room for further examination. Rookie Jacob Rizy came in to replace him at center.
It woukd get worse, as starting left guard Andrew Rupcich would grab his knee after a run in the fourth quarter. He would walk off the field under his own power, but wouldn't return to the game after a trip in the blue medical tent (though he did remain on the sideline). Mehki Butler came in to replace him.
The lone Patriots touchdown of the day capped off a really well-executived drive from DeVito and the offense. The quarterback connected with Cameron Dorner on a 17-yard catch before hitting Chism across the middle. A 15-yard outside run from Miller set the Patriots up inside Indianapolis' red zone.
That's when DeVito found Kyle Williams on a beautiful back-shoulder throw down the Patriots' sideline. He looked down Williams the whole way, and the second-year receiver easily beat Colts cornerback Johnathan Edwards for the 12-yard score.
Those type of plays are the ones that Williams -- who's stuck in a crowded receiver room -- needs to make this summer. He ended the night with two grabs on three targets and 37 yards (the most on the team).
The Colts replaced Richardson with Riley Leonard to open up the third quarter, and that move immediately came back to bite them. On their first drive of the half, Leonard lofted a prayer down the middle of the field intended for wide receiver Eli Pancol.
Instead, it fell right into the arms of second-year safety John Saunders Jr, who immediately scampered to pick up 26 yards on the return. Saunders closed Tuesday's joint practice with an interception and also had one earlier in training camp. He's starting to come on as one of the biggest ball hawks on this roster.
Despite getting a few runs early in the game, nothing really amounted to much on the ground for Larison (seven attempts, one yard). Where he made the most impact was in the passing game.
The running back was targeted seven times for six receptions, the most by any Patriot in the win. He tallied a team-high 39 receiving yards, most of them coming in the quick game out of the backfield. His first four catches were from DeVito in the first half, but Morton settled in to hit him on a…

title: Turnovers Lead The Way As Patriots Lead Colts at Halftime
full_text:
FOXBORO --- The first 30 minutes of New England Patriots preseason football in 2026 has come and gone, with the team taking a 10-7 lead over the Indianapolis Colts.
Here's everything you need to know from the first half of action.
New England capped off its first drive of the night with a 40-yard field goal by Andy Borregales. With Tommy DeVito under center, the Patriots' offense got down to Indianapolis' 21-yard line thanks in part to four Jam Miller rushes and a pair of defensive pass interference calls.
Skill position starters included Kayshon Boutte and Mack Hollins at wide receiver, Eli Raridon and Tanner Arkin at tight end, plus Miller at running back.
While the Colts drove down to the Patriots' 33-yard line after four plays of their opening drive, cornerback Kindle Vildor caught a bobbled pass from wide receiver Coleman Owen to regain possession for New England.
Each offense sputtered on the following three drives. While New England had big gains to Eli Raridon and Lan Larison on its third series of the game, the plays were brought back by respective penalties on Caleb Lomu and Efton Chism III. That drive was capped off by a 56-yard field goal attempt wide left by Borregales.
While the Colts drove to the Patriots' one-yard line on the opening drive of the second quarter, the tides quickly changed. Indianapolis running back Seth McGowan took a goal line carry and had the ball stripped by safety John Saunders Jr. Safety Dell Pettus recovered the loose ball.
Although the Patriots' offense followed the fumble recovery up with a three-and-out, the defense had its back. Linebacker K.J. Britt knocked the ball loose from a scrambling Anthony Richardson and defensive tackle Isaiah Iton fell on top of it.
After the forced turnover, New England's offense drove downfield despite playing some sloppy football, including a James Hudson III illegal man downfield penalty wiping out a 48-yard gain to Cameron Dorner.
Even still, chunk plays by Dorner, Chism and Miller got the Patriots into the redzone. DeVito then hit Kyle Williams from 12-yards out for a touchdown to put New England ahead 10-0.
The Colts, however, bounced back in swift fashion. Indianapolis drove downfield in under three minutes, capping off a seven-play 69-yard drive with a goal line keeper by Richardson.
Unsuccessful two-minute drills by both teams capped off the half.
Eight players did not suit up for the Patriots. LS Julian Ashby, DT Christian Barmore, WR Kyle Dixon, LB Christian Elliss, CB Christian Gonzalez, OLB Harold Landry III (physically unable to perform list), S Brenden Schooler (non-football injury list) and CB Charles Woods.
Elliss is the sole unexpected absence, as he is yet to miss a training camp practice. Most notably, despite being in the midst of contract negotiations with New England , Gonzalez missing time is not associated with a potential dispute, per Mike Vrabel.
"Everybody that was healthy practiced (on Tuesday)," Vrabel said pregame on 98.5 The Sports Hub when asked about the cornerback absences. "We didn't deem them healthy enough to go out there and participate. When they're ready, they'll be back out there."
Carlton Davis III, who Vrabel said last Friday was not expected to be healthy enough to play this week, is in full uniform.
Ben Brown, a top backup on the interior offensive line, had to be helped off the field by trainers toward the end of the first quarter. After a quick visit in the blue medical tent, he headed to the locker room.
Tommy DeVito: 13/22 passing, 138 yards, touchdown.
Kyle Williams: Two receptions, 37 yards, touchdown.
Jam Miller: 12 carries, 47 yards.
Lan Larison: Four carries, zero rushing yards, four receptions, 31 receiving yards.
Mack Hollins: Two receptions, 31 yards.
Efton Chism III: Three receptions, 21 yards.
Cameron Dorner: One reception, 17 yards.
Isaiah Iton: Fumble recovery.
K.J. Britt: Three tackles, forced fumble.
Kindle Vildor: One tackle, interception.
Channing Canada: Five tackles.
John Saunders Jr.: Two tackles, forced fumble.
Dell Pettus: Four tackles, fumble recovery.
Andy Borregales: 1/2 field goal attempts (40-yard kick made, 56-yard kick missed).

title: Patriots Place RB Terrell Jennings on Injured Reserve Ahead of Preseason Opener
full_text:
FOXBORO --- Prior to Thursday evening's preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, the New England Patriots announced running back Terrell Jennings has been placed on injured reserve with an undisclosed injury. In a corresponding move, the team signed running back JaMycal Hasty.
Jennings, who started training camp on the non-football injury list, was the clear favorite to win the Patriots' third running back job behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson.
"It was just something small," Jennings said on Monday when asked about the injury which held him out of the beginning of camp.
Now, the 25-year-old will be out for the 2026 season, barring a release via injury settlement. With Jennings out, what does this mean for the rest of the running back room?
Within the past day, New England has had to replace two running backs in an already competitive room. Prior to Thursday's roster moves, the team waived-injured undrafted free agent Myles Montgomery and signed Hassan Haskins.
With Jennings no longer in the picture for the team's running back competition, it now turns into an open trial between four players. Haskins, Hasty, sophomore Lan Larison and rookie Jam Miller.
Haskins, a 2022 fourth-round draft selection, spent the first two years of his career playing for Mike Vrabel with the Tennessee Titans. He has since spent two years with the Los Angeles Chargers, where he appeared in 29 games, primarily as a specialist.
Another veteran familiar with Vrabel, Hasty's signing marks his third stint with the Patriots. In fact, he has worked with each of the team's past three head coaches. Hasty was claimed off waivers in the middle of the 2023 season during Bill Belichick's regime, appeared in 15 games in 2024 under Jerod Mayo, and was signed during Vrabel's first season midway through training camp before being released during roster cutdowns.
At the beginning of training camp, while Jennings was on the NFI list, Larison worked as the Patriots' third running back. Now, with Jennings out, he catapults as the new favorite for the spot. Larison was a camp standout early last year before suffering a season-ending injury.
Miller, a seventh-round rookie from Alabama, has had flashes in training camp. Although he is in a log jam of running backs who have more familiarity with the coaching staff, if the 22-year-old can string together impressive preseason performances, he has a real shot at making the 53-man roster.
While the Patriots' depth took a hit with Jennings' injury, the team has a combination of veterans and younger talents who could earn a spot on the final roster as New England's third running back.

title: Patriots Preseason Opener vs. Colts: Which Storylines You Need to Watch
full_text:
Football is back in New England. After months of waiting, the New England Patriots will strap the pads on and take on the Indianapolis Colts in their preseason opener.
We won't see most of the starters, including quarterback Drake Maye, as the Patriots gave their top players most reps during Tuesday's joint practice. For the preseason game, it should be a healthy dose of the second- and third-string players in navy blue.
It was a productive joint practice for both sides, with the offenses having the upper hand for most of the day. We'll see if that carries into the game action, the first game back in Foxboro since the Patriots' thrilling AFC Divisional win over the Houston Texans in January.
"I know they are a physical football team," head coach Mike Vrabel said about Indianapolis last week. "They are well-coached. We didn't have a lot of crossover games with them (last year). We didn't see them a ton. We saw them a little bit. They are multiple on defense. Offensively, it's a good run football team that will run from the good tight ends, multiple tight ends, packages, an elite runner."
But that doesn't mean that there isn't exciting things to watch out for at Gillette Stadium. Here are some things to check out as the Patriots begin their summer slate.
We know that Maye won't play. But when we spoke to backup Tommy DeVito on Tuesday, he wasn't sure about the starting situation at that point in time. So it's a safe bet that it will be a healthy dose of both DeVito and rookie Behren Morton.
Both of them have looked good during the summer in varying degrees. DeVito shined in the joint practice , launching the ball deep (and often). Morton didn't get any snaps in the practice, signaling that he might be in for a larger workload in his NFL debut. Ultimately, these will be the two guys under center for the majority of August.
Ethan's Pre-Game Prediction: DeVito plays the first half, Morton plays the second. Morton will also have a touchdown that fans will drool over, either rushing or passing. Dealer's choice.
If we're going by the same logic given to Maye, it's safe to assume that A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs and  Kayshon Boutte would be relegated to the sideline. But some of the other receivers, including DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III, Mack Hollins and Kyle Williams, have all repped with the second-string offense at times.
Yes, we'll see plenty of the true backups in the preseason. The Patriots, however, have a crowded wide receiver room and need to weed it out somehow. These reps will be interesting to watch, especially because some of the undrafted receivers could also make some noise and compete for a spot on the 53-man roster.
Ethan's Pre-Game Prediction: Kyle Williams, after a slow start to the summer, will be a focal point to open up the game. His game-breaking speed will be on display early and often because he doesn't feel like a player penciled into a roster spot just yet.
Christian Gonzalez, Carlton Davis and Marcus Jones are locked in as New England's top three cornerbacks. Their top backup -- Charles Woods -- didn't participate in Tuesday's joint practice. So the secondary, one that struggled earlier in the week , is going to need a bounce-back performance.
Maybe they'll be able to get it from Kindle Vildor or Karon Prunty, two players who have worked into the starting defense at times. Other players have started to climb the depth chart though, including Kobee Minor and Channing Canada. If a player is on the field deep into the fourth quarter, that might not be the best of signs for their futures. Monitor which cornerbacks have limited snaps against the Colts.
Ethan's Pre-Game Prediction: Prunty was the team's fifth round pick this year and has shown flashes of being a physical corner at the line of scrimmage. If he gets the opportunity to meet the ball carrier in the open field, he could lay the boom.
It's hard to truly remember preseason games. They all blend together and half the time, the players aren't that recognizable. But the plays that sometimes come out of these games, especially the ones at home for the Patriots , can have a lasting impact.
What will Thursday's lasting moment be? Will be it be as iconic as Rhamondre Stevenson's 91-yard rushing touchdown against the Washington Football Team in 2021, or TreVeyon Henderson's opening kickoff return last year? You may forget the scores, but once a major play gets made, it's hard to forget the names like Danny Etling, Austin Carr and Ralph Webb. Don't fall asleep.
Ethan's Pre-Game Prediction: I wrote earlier in the week that undrafted wideout Cameron Dorner would become a fan favorite at some point this summer. He's been making plays in practice, and I think he'll make some more on the turf. Watch out for him.

title: Patriots Sign Pair of Veteran RBs: What That Means For Preseason
full_text:
The New England Patriots have their first preseason game of the year Thursday night, but that didn't stop them from making a few roster moves the night before.
After a closed walkthrough, the Patriots announced that they signed veteran running back Hassan Haskins and waived rookie running back Myles Montgomery with an injury designation. But that's not all. A few hours later, USA Today's Arye Pulli reported that the team also signed running back JaMycal Hasty to a one-year deal.
Both Hasty and Haskins were in the facility for workouts, along with free agents Shane Watts (who was with the Patriots last summer) and Leshon Williams. Ultimately, New England went with the two veterans that have plenty of experience with a Mike Vrabel-led team.
Here's what these moves for the Patriots , both for the preseason game later tonight as well as the rest of training camp this summer.
Haskins has the talent to stick around this team for longer than just the preseason. A former fourth round pick by the Tennessee Titans, the former Michigan Wolverine spent one season under Vrabel. He racked up 150 total yards of offense in 2022 before spending the last two seasons with the Los Angeles Chargers.
It was clear that Haskins would end up signing with the Patriots, even before the signing was announced. Media members on a tour of the Patriots' new practice facility got a look inside the team's virtual room, where Haskins was working on installing plays with running backs coach Tony Dews.
Behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson, Haskins could become the RB3 - if he's able to fend off the surging Terrell Jennings. The 26-year-old Haskins has been a valuable threat as both a receiving back and as a kick returner, two areas where Jennings could help the team. It will be interesting to see how many snaps he gets against the Colts less than a day after signing his contract.
Hasty is back the Patriots' backfield for what will be part of four years in a row. In 2023, he was claimed off of waivers and played in two games as a backup. He remained with the team the following year, totaling 20 rush attempts, 69 rushing yards, 10 receptions, 59 receiving yards and one receiving touchdown in 15 games. He wasn't re-signed after that year, but would pop right back up at training camp one year later.
He didn't make much noise in 2025, as was on the team for all three preseason games before being let go. But now he's back. There isn't much that Hasty can offer you in terms of game-breaking talent. He's shifty with the ball in his hands and can break tackles, but the Patriots won't be asking him to be a downfield runner.
Right now, it feels like Hasty is more of a camp body rather than anything else. He's a safe veteran option that can operate within the offense that Vrabel and offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels want to run . However, all things considered, it still feels like the third running back spot belongs to Jennings.
Montgomery signed with the Patriots out of UCF on a record-breaking contract . His $272,500 in total guarantees was the most ever given to an undrafted free agent by the Patriots. Despite that, Montgomery got the least amount of reps of any running back during camp.
The 5-foot-10 Montgomery ran the ball hard, but awasn't able to make any headway on the depth chart. He was stashed behind Stevenson, Henderson, Jennings, Lan Larison and fellow rookie Jam Miller in the running back room. Earlier in the summer, Montgomery had gotten some more reps, but once Jennings returned off of the non-football injury list, those snaps quickly evaporated.
Montgomery's tenure in New England could be over, as the team did technically release him with an injury designation. However, it's very uncommon for teams to claim injured players off of waivers. If Montgomery goes unclaimed, he'll revert to the Patriots' season-ending injured reserve , joining wide receivers Jimmy Kibble and Jeremiah Webb, and tight end Julian Hill.
That also doesn't mean that his three-year contract is done. Barring another roster move, Montgomery will be back in the fold for 2027 with a chance to get healthy and make his preseason debut.

title: Five Players to Watch in Patriots Preseason Opener vs. Colts
full_text:
New England Patriots football is back ... kind of.
On Thursday evening, the Patriots host the Indianapolis Colts for their preseason opener. With New England's starters not expected to receive extended playing time, all eyes will be on depth pieces fighting for roster spots.
Here are five names who'll likely get playing time that you should watch during the matchup.
Whether you want to or not, you'll be watching Morton if you tune into Thursday's game.
With Drake Maye not expected to play , Tommy DeVito will likely split time with Morton as the Patriots' signal callers. The Texas Tech alumni has looked surprisingly comfortable through the spring and summer as a seventh-round rookie working in Josh McDaniels' offense.
"I think that preparation's a big thing," Morton said when asked about that comfortability on Aug. 1. "I think coach Ashton Grant does a great job. Coach McDaniels is a tremendous coach. And so, I really got to give hats off to their coaching abilities, that in the meetings, installs, I can understand it. And so, when I do get a live rep at it, your pulse is low and you can operate and make a good play."
Morton's preseason play could be the deciding factor in keeping him around on the 53-man roster come September, or risking him clearing waivers to return on the practice squad.
An undrafted free agent, Jacobs has skyrocketed up the depth chart since signing in New England. The Missouri alumni has worked primarily as the Patriots' fourth linebacker, behind veterans Robert Spillane, Christian Eliss and Chad Muma.
"He stays late," Mike Vrabel said about Jacobs on Friday. "I see him here all the time. He loves just kind of when you put the ball down and play it, when you get to the team periods, you kind of notice his play speed, and I think that's a great thing to say."
A gameday is the epitome of "put the ball down and play it." Will Jacobs continue to step up to the plate and prove to be yet another undrafted gem for the Patriots?
In Morton's limited reps in team drills, he has looked most comfortable targeting Dorner. Listed at 6'1", 188 pounds, the North Texas product has had an impressive camp which would have likely earned him 53-man roster buzz in any other year.
However, in a crowded receiver room, Dorner's best opportunity may actually come on another team's roster. But for now, he is in New England and should be on the receiving end of multiple passes from Morton on Thursday.
If Dorner continues his training camp momentum into the preseason, he could be picked up elsewhere once teams across the NFL cut down their rosters.
Farmer makes an appearance as the only non-rookie on the list. While the trenches can be difficult to evaluate in training camp due to only limited contact being allowed, the 2025 fourth round pick has turned heads regardless.
Last season, the 23-year-old appeared in 13 games for New England and started in three. While the Patriots' top defensive lineman spots are near-locks to go to Milton Williams, Christian Barmore and Cory Durden, Farmer has looked to be the de facto fourth option.
If he can plug up run plays and get a handful of pressures on the quarterback on Thursday, Farmer's status will solidify even further.
Although the Patriots added Hassan Haskins and reportedly JaMycal Hasty on Wednesday, I would still expect Miller to get a high volume of reps from the Patriots' backfield.
Although he has had some explosive runs in camp, the Alabama product is currently a long shot to make the final roster as he sits behind Terrell Jennings and Lan Larison in a battle for the third running back spot.
However, jobs in the backfield can easily be won and lost in preseason games, as training camp team drills are not full contact. If Miller can shed through a few would-be tacklers on a handful of runs, he could gain some momentum in the fight for a roster spot.

title: Inside Mitch Van Vooren's 'Tremendous' Journey From D1 Track Star to Patriots
full_text:
Mitch Van Vooren told his roommates. Most of his other teammates weren't aware, at least not to his knowledge.
But the senior had plans after Marquette. The 6-foot-5 track star, one who had been named an All-Big East outdoor hurdler, was transferring. He recalled being asked about what he wanted to do in the workforce after his time at Marquette. Van Vooren had other ideas.
Thanks to an extra year of eligibility granted during the COVID-19 pandemic, Van Vooren decided to pursue a dream that most people thought was crazy.
He wanted to play professional football.
"My family and friends, they always believed in me," the New England Patriots tight end told Patriots On SI last week at training camp. "I believed in my athletic ability, so it got me here to where I'm today."
Before his time in college, Van Vooren was a star for the Peshtigo High School football program in Wisconsin. But track, especially at a Big East program like Marquette, was hard to pass up. Bert Rogers, the director of track & field and cross country, remembers recruiting Van Vooren, a player who earned a scholarship after lettering four times.
As a freshman, Van Vooren finished first at the UW-Parkside Classic in the 55m hurdles (7.96 seconds), good for a personal best. In the three years that followed, Van Vooren blossomed into one of the best hurdlers in the entire Big East -- "Mitch really learned how to tactically race," Rogers told Patriots On SI.
"Over his time at Marquette, he did fine-tune his hurdling form, which certainly helped," Rogers said. "Mitch had a strong aerobic engine for a sprinter, which made him so good at the longer sprints like the 400 meters and the 400 hurdles."
By the time Van Vooren graduated from Marquette, he was a three-time Big East All-Academic and broke the university record in the 400m hurdles (51.38) in the NCAA Tournament in 2023.
But he had an itch he couldn't scratch. He wanted to play in the NFL.
A hurdler at a university where the football team folded in 1960 wants to go to the NFL?
"I know there was routes to like get there," Van Vooren said. "If COVID never happened, I was gonna try out somehow and somehow get there. But with COVID, that extra year gave me the opportunity to play football. ... Everything happens for a reason, so it worked out a good way."
So Van Vooren, now in the transfer portal, looked for a new home. Sure, he had offers from Wisconsin and Miami to run track. But he wanted to stay close to home and play football. That's how he landed at St. Norbert, a Division III school in De Pere, Wisconsin -- a town with a population of about 25,000.
That doesn't scream NFL all that much. Still, Van Vooren knew what he wanted to do.
"That whole summer before I went to St. Norbert, I had a lot of good help and a lot of people around me (who) helped me make that transition," said Van Vooren, who admitted it took a lot of hard work behind the scenes.
The first year at St. Norbert was a grind, according to head coach Dan McCarty. Van Vooren came in wanting to play receiver. His body type might have screamed more of a tight end, but the transfer knew where he wanted to line up. Plus, his track background could translate to the route running needed.
"I think the whole first year was a learning curve, going from a track athlete, track mentality to a football player mentality," McCarty told Patriots On SI. "He'd been out of football for so long ... It was a lot of adjustment."
While he was at St. Norbert, Van Vooren didn't completely give up track. He ran for the Green Knights' track program, setting a program record in the 400m outdoor hurdles (52.02 seconds). He would qualify for the NCAA Division III Outdoor National Championship in the category and was named a First Team All-American.
"It was a chance for him to be able to continue doing track, but also play football," McCarty said.
In his first season with St. Norbert, he caught 32 passes for 535 yards and three touchdowns. "Decent," as Van Vooren put in.
In 2024, his final year of college eligibility is when he came into his own. He caught 33 passes for 510 yards and 10 touchdowns. He was named to the All-NACC First Team and started to look like he belonged on the field. After the season, he had earned an invite to the College Gridiron Showcase in front of scouts.
He was getting onto the radars of a few NFL teams.
"He's just got that tremendous work ethic," McCarty said. "I can't say enough good things about just the character of Mitch and the type of person he is."
Van Vooren went undrafted, later signing a free agent contract with the Seattle Seahawks. His time in the Pacific Northwest was short lived, as he was released just nine days later. He'd land on his feet and join the Cleveland Browns -- only to be released after 20 days. Van Vooren remained a free agent since.
"This last year, I took a lot of effort just to make sure that I was in the correct shape," Van Vooren said, "so when I did get another shot, I'd have a chance to make that more of an opportunity than last time."
The 25-year-old arrived in New England on July 22, thrown into the training camp fire without getting reps in OTAs or mandatory minicamp. Still, he's held his own and has made several plays with the third-string offense .
The Patriots offense is historically tough for tight ends to learn , especially for those who are still trying to play catch up with their peers who didn't take a four-year hiatus to run track. So other than making the 53-man roster, what does a successful summer look like for Van Vooren?
"You never know when's the last snap," Van Vooren said. "When I get in there, just showcase my ability and I know what I can do. So hopefully I can show the team and the general public what I believe myself."
"He obviously had the physical gift, but a lot of people do," Rogers said. "What separated Mitch was that attention to detail and the drive to become better."
Not many people expect to see St. Norbert next to an NFL player's name. Even less would expect to see Marquette. And yet, Van Vooren has cleared both those hurdles with ease.
"I like to say I'm keeping that football tradition alive," Van Vooren laughed. "It kind of gives me some some pride when people ask me where I went to my undergrad. It's like, 'Oh, I went to Marquette.' They're like, 'I didn't know they had a football team.'
"They don't," he said with a smile.
