title: Everything Inside Patriots' New Multi-Million Dollar Practice Facility
full_text:
FOXBORO — Even though they’ve been working out of the building for the last six months, the New England Patriots officially cut the ribbon for their New Balance Athletics Center Wednesday afternoon.
The 160,000 square foot facility, overlooking the team’s trio of practice fields, dwarfs the size of the operations that had been used inside Gillette Stadium. According to Sports Business Journal , the cost of the project was $95 million dollars.
Executives from New Balance and Suffolk Construction, along with Patriots owner Robert Kraft , head coach Mike Vrabel and executive vice president of player personnel Eliot Wolf were in attendance.
"When our family purchased the Patriots in ‘94, we made a commitment to all our fans to do everything we could to build a first-class organization and give the team the right resources to compete at the highest level," Kraft said. "This building is the latest example of that commitment."
🎗️✂️ pic.twitter.com/CMzzMZ689S
"You built such a wonderful building and practice facility and athletic performance facility that if we were to ever lose, I don't think we're going to be able to use facilities as a reason for our loss," Vrabel said to Kraft. "We spend more time here than we do at our own families, at our own homes, and we’re proud to call this home."
Patriots On SI beat reporters Ethan Hurwitz and Zac Ventola were part of the guided tour throughout the facility. From a new-look locker room to plenty of decorations lining the walls, here’s a rundown of what stood out.
The Patriots' new cafeteria, which combined with the kitchen totals 11,000 square feet, is formatted more similarly to a restaurant’s dining room than a traditional cafeteria. It provides players and staff with food made to order, a salad and fruit bar, and buffet-style proteins.
Wednesday afternoon’s buffet included t-bone steak, mac and cheese, waffle fries, miso mirin sea bass, barbecue chicken thighs and grilled chicken breast.
A quick look at the Patriots cafeteria, where several players (Behren Morton, Nick DeGennaro, Will Campbell, Morgan Moses) were spotted eating during our tour. pic.twitter.com/LNcsO7jJkH
Right by the room’s main doorway sits a coffee station, along with to-go bars equipped with five refrigerators of drinks and shelves full of snacks. The cafeteria is on the building’s second of three levels, right at the top of the primary staircase. Vice president of football operations and strategy John Streicher called it the first and last place in the building players visit on a daily basis.
The weight room has two levels, with the bottom floor housing the majority of equipment. The primary area houses numerous machines, a Patriots -branded turf strip for sled workouts, monitors for workouts to be displayed and a large Pat Patriot emblem squatting a barbell in front of word art in the shape of New England.
The top floor contains cardio machines such as treadmills, ellipticals and stationary bikes, plus an area which Streicher referred to as “the violence room.”
That room, which includes different types of punching bags, was championed by Vrabel and his staff as a necessity. Streicher said players often end their workouts in the area, at times finishing by hitting the spring-loaded blocking pads.
The Patriots’ weight room. Not pictured: What John Streicher referred to as the “violence room,” where players can work on hand placement with punching bags. pic.twitter.com/mLlMaN6OxJ
The team’s new locker room contains 92 permanent “Longhorn Lockers,” with state-of-the-art airflow for players’ equipment to stay dry.
The top of each locker has a screen with the player’s name, number, college and position. Lifting the screen reveals shelving where helmets, pads and shells can be placed to dry off. At the bottom of the shelf, which can be pulled down to hang from the top of the locker, has Kraft’s “We Are All Patriots” mantra.
Underneath that is an open shelf and an additional closed compartment for personal items. The largest portion of the locker is dedicated to player uniforms and other clothing, next to another area for personal items.
The bottom has a cushioned seat, which has a pull-out drawer for shoes. Below the left armrest is another compartment with air-flow for gloves, towels and other gear.
Connected to the locker room is a player’s lounge complete with sofas, massage chairs, four televisions, a ping-pong table and a two-seat barber setup.
The Patriots also installed a new aquatics recovery and training room. The hydrotherapy space alone is 3,700 square feet.
The pool room contains two cold tubs, two hot tubs, five ice water plunge tubs, a rehab pool and an underwater treadmill. The area dedicated to underwater recovery has four times as much pool space as the team had in its previous facilities.
Although the media was not shown the trainer’s room on Wednesday, we did see “The Best Ability Is Availability” above several tables.
Streicher calls it the virtual room. Vrabel calls it the remote classroom. Regardless of name, it’s 10,500 square feet of turf spanning the width of an entire football field. There’s a divider in the middle, allowing it to be split into two separate rooms.
Ultimately, it’s used for players to be able to get meaningful reps “on the field” without having to step on the field. Lined with hash marks and yard markers, players can easily see their splits and work on formations in a smaller environment.
A look at the virtual classroom, where players can get reps before even coming out to the practice field. pic.twitter.com/oqqO4bCuzT
Several positional rooms connect directly to the virtual room, and massive screens are also available to let players visually see what’s being taught by the coaching staff.
Each position group has their own meeting room all along one long hallway. Some, like the safeties and cornerbacks room, have a connecting door to create one larger defensive back room. In each of the rooms, the desks work as dry-erase boards, allowing players and coaches to draw and erase information right in front of them. Each room had its own personality, as the quarterback room had Drake Maye’s now-famous orange juicer while the defensive line room had a Trojan horse in the front.
The main team meeting room seats 160 people. At the front of the room was a larger-than-life video board. Streicher explained that the center part of the board would show film, while the outer screens on either side would show additional information like coaching points or formations.
Both walls also had the team’s identity on it, which read: “Effort & Finish”, “Ball Security & Ball Disruption”, “Details, Technique & Fundamentals,” and “Make Great Decisions.”
During April’s soft-launch tour, media members weren’t able to get a look inside the war room. They were today, as they were met with a massive video board on the left-hand side. That’s the board the team used for their completed draft board , as well as a screen to FaceTime drafted prospects. On the left side of the room, the Patriots keep tallies on the rest of the NFL’s draft picks with another screen.
When it’s not draft season, the room is used for other purposes. Streicher shared that a meeting with the team’s analytics staff was recently held, as was a meeting with the scouting department to watch recent film.
Inside the walls of the Patriots’ new facility: pic.twitter.com/Le5Zw3tcHX
There were not many blank spaces along the hallway walls throughout the building. When you first enter, right above the doorway is each of the Patriots ’ six Super Bowl championships (and space for more). Go up the front stairs and on your right, you’re greeted by a wall honoring all of the team’s captains since 2000.
Through the cafeteria hallway, plaques honoring the Patriots Hall of Fame and Pro Football Hall of Fame inductees lined the walls. Go up a flight of stairs and a mural with each of the Patriots’ Ron Burton Community Service Award winners was on the left.
Some of the biggest moments…

title: Saints Give Fans 3 Huge Reasons for Optimism after Dominating Jaguars Joint Practice
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints hosted the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday for a joint practice session.
With Saints fans in attendance, the Black and Gold put on a show and showed a lot of promise. The Jaguars were 13-4 last season, with a solid offense and one of the best defenses in the league, and the Saints outperformed them.
With many of the Saints’ starters not participating in the preseason game against Jacksonville on Saturday, this was a good opportunity to see how the Saints’ starters would fare against one of the league’s better teams.
Here are three key observations that should excite Who Dat Nation.
One of the biggest positives of the day was the run game.
Travis Etienne Jr handled a lot of the first-team work. Alvin Kamara worked with the first and second groups, and Audric Estime was the third back.
Etienne set the tone with two productive runs from the shotgun. One of the things I wanted to see was how well the offensive line would play against the top run defense in the league last season, and they did more than meet the task at hand.
“Credit to the O-line, those big guys up front,” Tyler Shough said. “I mean, it was unbelievable, especially back-to-back periods multiple times. There's not much rest time for those guys, and they're not getting subbed out like the D-line either.” Our extensive story with Shough can be found here .
The long ball stood out today.
The first long ball came from Zach Wilson to Bub Means for a touchdown.
The second long touchdown came on a wide-open bomb off a perfectly run wheel route for a 55-yard touchdown pass thrown by Shough. Chris Olave caught it, which was one of several big-time catches he had.
Shough said he did not enter practice determined to force the deep ball. He saw what Jacksonville gave him, and he took them.
“Whatever they were presenting, I was going to take advantage of it,” Shough said.
The third came from Spencer Rattler, who threw a deep touchdown to Bryce Lance in tight coverage in the end zone.
The Saints' defense has dominated the first-team offense throughout training camp, and they did the same thing against the Jaguars’ first-team offense.
Julian Blackmon picked off Trevor Lawrence with an interception on his very first pass attempt of the day as he undercut receiver Jakobi Meyers on a throw to the right sideline. Jonas Sanker , Quincy Riley and Kool-Aid McKinstry also had pass breakups.
Riley also made a great tackle on a running back in the flats, but it was late, leading to a traditional joint practice scuffle where both teams had to break it up.
The defensive line had six definite sacks and three more pressures that could have been sacks in a real-game situation, but officials allowed the plays to continue. Chase Young was involved in at least four of those sacks.
Nathan Shepherd had two solo sacks and shared a third sack with Young. Vernon Broughton and Carl Granderson were each in on three of the sacks or potential sacks. Khristian Boyd was in on another.
Here's the practice schedule for the rest of the week: - Friday, TBD, Walk-Thru (Closed) - Saturday, Saints vs. Jaguars, 3:00 p.m., Superdome

title: Saints Make Final Preparations Before Jaguars Joint Practice
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints had their final light day of practice before the Jacksonville Jaguars duke it out with the Saints on Airline Drive Thursday in a joint practice ahead of Saturday’s session.
The Saints had a light practice, as they were just in helmets. It was not a walkthrough, as there were two 11-on-11 periods and a goal-line period as well, but there was hardly any physicality. It was essentially two-hand touch and the play was over.
That is in part because of the joint practice happening tomorrow with the Jaguars. A lot of the starters will be participating in those collaborative sessions. Due to that, head coach Kellen Moore said to expect mostly the twos and threes to play on Saturday.
Here are some notes from everything I observed.
Nothing has changed since yesterday, but Devaughn Vele was the most notable absentee. However, Moore stated that Vele was healthy and was only taking a rest day. Vele was a starter in the slot for the Saints in the first unofficial depth chart they released next season.
Davon Godchaux (ankle) and Rejzohn Wright (hip) remained out after leaving practice early with trainers Tuesday. Kendre Miller (back), Devin Neal (hamstring), Cam Jordan (hamstring), defensive lineman John Ridgeway (back) and linebacker Chris Rumph (ankle) also were not seen.
These are in addition to defensive end Bryan Breese and offensive lineman Dillon Radunz being placed on the Injured/Reserved (IR) list. Both are out for the year .
The Saints added free agent defensive lineman Kahlil Saunders in the wake of placing Radunz on IR.
Saints sign DT Kahlil Saunders #Saints | @Shift4 https://t.co/hQ4ViGFrCz
In Vele’s absence, Kevin Austin Jr. took reps with the first team and Barion Brown rotated in as well.
William Sherman and rookie Jeremiah Wright played left guard and right guard for one team series with the first-team offense.
On defense, defensive tackle Khristian Boyd took reps with the first team while Godchaux took a break.
Linebacker Pete Werner was back as the starter alongside Kaden Elliss after missing yesterday. Werner was suited up, but he was on the sideline resting a groin injury. How much he will participate in the joint practice with the Jaguars is to be determined.
If Werner is a no-go, Danny Stutsman will take his place. Stutsman has been one of the breakout stars of training camp and has been pushing Werner for the starting position.
Jaylan Ford also took a few reps with the first team linebackers as well.
Despite a shorter practice than usual, there were still some highlights.
Cornerback I saac Yiadom made a great play in the first 11-on-11 session. Spencer Rattler threw a deep ball to Bryce Lance , and it looked like he was about to make the catch of the day, but Yiadom forced the ball out for an incomplete pass.
However, Lance made up for it when he hauled in a deep touchdown pass from Rattler in double coverage in the end zone. Lance has been better than expected throughout training camp and should be a lock on the 53-man roster.

title: 4 Major Takeaways from the Saints Unofficial Depth Chart
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints dropped its unofficial depth chart for the 2026 season, giving Saints fans a look of how the roster is taking part.
There were few notable surprises given that most of the starters returned from last season and the fact that most anticipated what the depth chart looks like right now. However, depth charts change all the time, and some players currently listed may not even be on the team by the end of the month, given that NFL teams are mandated to select 53 players on their final roster by 6 p.m. ET Aug. 30.
Without further ado, here are four notable things from the Saints’ unofficial depth chart for the 2026 preseason.
With Chris Olave and Jordyn Tyson locking up the starting spots on the outside, there were a lot of questions surrounding who was going to be the third receiver in the starting rotation. With the depth chart being released, that question has been answered as Devaughn Vele was listed as the No. 3 wide receiver in the rotation.
Vele had modest numbers last season with 25 catches for 293 yards and two touchdowns. However, he was a reliable target for Shough in the second half of the season, catching 26 passes for 238 yards and a touchdown in his final four games before missing the last three due to injury.
While Barion Brown did not make the starting rotation, he will definitely be a factor in the offense as well as special teams.
His performance in training camp so far likely has him as the fourth wide receiver in the rotation after Olave, Tyson and Vele. An All-American return specialist at both Kentucky and LSU, Brown is the No. 1 returner for both kickoffs and punts.
As expected, Travis Etienne and Alvin Kamara are listed as the first team backs. While it does have an “OR” in between the two tailbacks, expect Etienne to get a few more carries than Kamara. While the latter still has some of the things that made him a five-time Pro Bowler, Etienne is a little bit younger and is still in his prime as he is coming off his third 1,00 -yard season in four years.
Another interesting development from the depth chart in the running back room is Kendre Miller and Devin Neal being above Audric Estime.
Estime took first team reps alongside Etienne and Kamara while Miller (back) and Neal (hamstring) were out with day-to-day injuries. Estime took a majority of the snaps in the final two games rushing 35 times for 157 yards (4.5 yards per carry) for 157 yards and a touchdown.
While it was a given, everyone knows that Cam Jordan’s time is coming to an end and everyone who is part of Who Dat Nation wants to enjoy it while it lasts. But it is surprising that there is an “OR” next to his name in the same way that Chase Young, who is coming off a 10-sack season. So did Jordan, but Young is significantly younger than he and is on a longer and heftier contract.
Jordan is limping through a hamstring injury right now that will sideline him. For how long? Read our story here .
Vernon Broughton , Davon Godchaux and Nathan Shepherd are the starters on the inside. Broughton has shot up the depth chart after playing only one game last season.
One of the more noteworthy position battles has been for the starting kicker job between Charlie Smyth and Tanner Brown. Both kicked during Tuesday’s practice.
Smyth finished 5 of 6, with his one miss wide as he pushed it left from 55 yards on his last attempt. Meanwhile, Brown made all seven of his attempts, including the 55-yard attempt Smyth failed to convert.
According to NewOrleans.Football , Smyth is 27 of 35 (77.1%) throughout training camp, while Brown is 28 of 32 (87.5%).

title: Could the Saints be without Cam Jordan to Start the Season?
full_text:
New Orleans Saints defensive end Cameron Jordan may not suit up for the beginning of the season due to a lingering hamstring issue.
Jordan's injury occurred during Thursday's practice, and he has missed the past three practice sessions. He did not attend Saturday's practice because he attended Drew Brees' Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement .
Head coach Kellen Moore said "he's going to miss a little bit of time," noting that regular assessments will dictate the recovery process. Moore did not say when the eight-time Pro Bowler would return, but the injury was serious enough to have Moore admit that Jordan could remain sidelined beyond the preseason slate.
"It could possibly get into the season, but you never know," Moore said. "[You need] to have some patience with it, let it take its course and we'll collect more information as we go."
Jordan, who has been in the league since 2011, has played in all but two games oin his career. In 2022, he sat out for a Week 11 matchup following an orbital fracture, and previously, he was sidelined for a single game in 2021 after testing positive for COVID-19.
The 37-year-old edge rusher signed a one-year contract to return to New Orleans for a 16th season on June 16th.  Jordan's deal has a base value of $7.5 million ($6.15 million signing bonus, $1.35 million base) and is worth up to $11 million with sack incentives.
Replacing a veteran like Jordan is difficult; he is the roster's most tenured player and led the team with 10.5 sacks last season. However, they do have options on the edge, and great ones at that.
The Saints feature veteran pass rushers in Chase Young (10 sacks) and Carl Granderson (6 sacks) on the defensive line. New Orleans also bolstered its roster by trading for Tyree Wilson during the draft and signing former New England Patriots defensive end Anfernee Jennings in April.
"We certainly feel good about our depth in that position. We got some really talented players on the edge. We view it as a strength of our football team," Moore said. "We're going to need multiple guys to play throughout the season no matter what. ... So we'll take time to kind of evaluate while Cam's out and see where it looks here through training camp and then these other guys will be ready to go."

title: Saints Defense Dominates Again as Offensive Mistakes Pile Up Before Preseason Opener
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints were back on Airline Drive on Tuesday as they continued preparing for their first preseason game of the season against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Saturday.
The defense continued to dominate the offense, which is commonplace at any level during the preseason. However, the situational mistakes have continued and, to make matters worse, most of the day focused on late-game situations.
Here are some of the takeaways from today’s practice.
On the first team offense, nothing necessarily changed.
Tyler Shough was the starter at quarterback, a position he had held since the second half of last season. Spencer Rattler took reps with the second team while Zach Wilson took snaps with the third.
At running back, Trevor Etienne and Alvin Kamara both took reps with the first team. Audric Estime also took reps with the first team as Moore wanted him take reps there as well.
In the receiving corps, Chris Olave and Jordyn Tyson were the starters on the outside while Devaughn Vele was the starter in the slot. The second team consisted of the rookie duo of Barrion Brown and Bryce Lance , along with veteran Kevin Austin Jr.
At tight end, both Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant both rotated with the first team. Rookie Oscar Delp took reps with the second.
On the offensive line, it was the usual with Kelvin Banks and Taliese Fuaga starting at left and right tackle, David Edwards and Cesar Ruiz at left and right guard with Erik McCoy at center.
On the defensive line, Carl Granderson and Chase Young were the starters on the edge while Vernon Broughton and Nathan Shepherd were the No. 1 guys on the interior.
At linebacker, veteran Kaden Elliss was starting alongside Danny Stutsman . The latter has been slowly but surely locking up the starting role over longtime mainstay Peter Werner.
In the defensive backfield, nothing changed. Just like in the past couple of practices, Quincy Riley and Kool-Aid McKinstry were on the outside while Justin Reid and Jonas Sanker manned the safety positions.
Defensive tackle Davon Godchaux was off to the side after rolling an ankle, and Rezjohn Wright hurt his hip during Tuesday's practice.
Other than that , defensive end Cam Jordan was not available again at practice today because of a hamstring injury.
Defensive lineman John Ridgeway III i s dealing with a back issue and remains day to day.
Second-year running back Devin Neal was still off to the side doing rehab work for a hamstring issue and is day to day as well.
Pete Werner (groin) was back in uniform but did not appear to participate in any full-team drills.
The Saints’ strongest position group may be the defensive backfield with the amount of depth it has.
We saw that today with Martin Emerson Jr. The fifth-year cornerback out of Mississippi State had three pass breakups and an interception on the day. He should have had two if he had hauled one in during the second 11-on-11 session.
Carl Granderson made several big plays as he gave right tackle Taliese Fuaga all he could handle off the edge. Granderson was constantly forced pressure off the edge. He also had a presence in the passing game as he had an interception and nearly had another as well on the play right before it.
There were several plays stood out throughout the day.
Austin made several catches throughout the day, including a 25-yard touchdown catch on a nice ball from Rattler.
While it might of been a mixed day for him, Shough made some nice throws as well.
One that stood out was when he spiraled a touchdown throw on 4th down in the red zone to Johnson on a fade route in the back of the end zone over tight coverage from McKinstry to end the second session of 11-on-11 in a quasi two-minute drill.
He also made a nice play later in practice where he used his feet to escape pressure and found Tyson in the middle for a first down.
Riley snagged an interception from Shough to end the main practice session.
Shough was 15-for-27 and threw two interceptions on the day. Despite a rough start to practice, Rattler was 7-for-9, but he also threw an interception. Wilson was 9-for-15 (60%) and did not turn the ball over, but also did not necessarily do anything to separate himself from Rattler.
However, the most concerning thing about the offensive struggles is the lack of situational awareness, something that has been a recurring issue.
The most egregious one came when the offense faced third-and-2 with 14 seconds remaining during a full-field hurry-up drive and committed a costly false start. Shough bailed his offensive line out by converting a fourth-and-1 with a touchdown to Johnson.
However, Johnson committed another false start on the first play with just under 45 seconds on the clock in another 11-on-11 session.
The good thing for the Saints is that its just the preseason and these things can be ironed out before the season starts.

title: Saints Preseason Schedule 2026: Dates, Times, TV, Opponents
full_text:
After two weeks of the players in the franchise going up against each, the New Orleans Saints will finally play another team when it begins their three-week preseason slate starting on Saturday.
New Orleans opens up the preseason slate with a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Saturday at the Caesars Superdome before traveking to play the Los Angeles Rams (Aug. 22). Both games are set for a 3:00 p.m. kickoff. The Saints wrap up the preseason against rival Dallas Cowboys (Aug. 28) in Arlington for a 7:00 p.m. start.
Here is some info about all three teams along with the dates, times, locations and how you can watch all three games.
The Jaguars are coming off their first playoff appearance since 2022 and the most wins in a single season in franchise history after a 13-4 season under Liam Coen , who is entering his second year on the job.
The biggest question for the Jaguars throughout training camp is the running back spot. Travis Etienne has departed for the Saints. The battle is between Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr . Those are tough shoes to fill, considering Etienne rushed for 1,000 yards or more in three of the last four seasons.
The Los Angeles Rams are coming off a 12-5 season and an appearance in the NFC Championship Game, where they lost to eventual Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks .
The Rams made the biggest offseason move of the summer when they received All-Pro defensive end Myles Garrett from the Browns in exchange for a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick and a 2029 third-round pick. Garrett is the reigning Defensive Player of the Year after breaking the single-season sack record with 23 sacks. It was the second time he won the award.
There’s a chance we might see first-round draft pick Ty Simpson , who was shockingly drafted by the Ram with the 13th overall pick. He’s currently battling with Stetson Bennett for the backup role and could be the heir to the keys to the offense when reigning MVP Matthew Stafford retires.
Unlike the previous two franchises mentioned, the Dallas Cowboys have been a massive disappointment. Dallas has missed the playoffs for two consecutive seasons, finishing 7-10 in both. This came after three straight 12-win seasons.
While quarterback Dak Prescott and the Cowboys lit it up offensively by finishing second in the league in total offense, they also finished 30th in yards allowed and had the league's worst passing and scoring defense.
That resulted in the Cowboys drafting five defensive players with seven picks, with their first two picks being safety Caleb Downs of Alabama and Malachi Lawrence of UCF in the first round.

title: Saints’ Kelvin Banks Jr. Reveals Key Focus After Impressive Rookie Season
full_text:
New Orleans Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. is entering his second NFL season after an impressive rookie campaign.
Drafted ninth overall by the Saints, the 6-foot-5, 315-pound lineman became just the third Saints left tackle since 1978 to start every game at the position, earning consensus All-Rookie honors and a spot on the 2025 PFWA All-Rookie Team.
Banks allowed only five sacks and three accepted penalties across 681 pass-blocking snaps while ranking second among all rookie linemen in run blocking, according to Pro Football Focus.
Banks knows exactly where he wants to improve entering his second NFL season: consistency.
“Honestly, for me, it was more consistency because it'll be multitude of reps,” Banks said. "I'm looking flawless, taking the great set, doing this and that, and— and looking good. And it'll be that one or two reps where it's like, 'Oh, dang.' You know what I'm saying? Just making sure I clean the small mistakes up that I may be making throughout the game, whether it's getting fatigued or just not fully thinking throughout the play and just going out there and playing. So just small stuff like that is what I kind of took away from last year.”
Now, Banks is looking to clean up those small mistakes, build on his strong debut and help lead the Saints to an NFC South title and their first playoff berth since 2020.
Banks’ development is also tied to the growth of fellow offensive tackle Taliese Fuaga . With a full season together under their belts, the two young tackles are pushing each other to take another step, and Banks believes their shared work ethic could help them develop into one of the NFL’s top tackle duos.
“I mean, we literally just got done on the field after practice,” Banks said after the session on Aug. 6. “We were out there for an extra 30 minutes doing extra different sets and working different stuff that we may have slipped up on in practice. So I'll say that's the thing that excites me the most because I know how bad we want to be one of the best tackle duos in the league. So (it's) that eagerness to understand that we both have that same mindset.”
Fuaga, who played left tackle in 2024, started 13 games at right tackle for New Orleans in 2025.
While Banks and Fuaga give the Saints a young foundation at tackle, veteran David Edwards has brought another element to the offensive line room at guard.
Edwards, who is entering his eighth season in the league, has started 77 of the 103 games he played for the Los Angeles Rams (2019-2022) and Buffalo Bills (2022-2025), two of the league’s best teams. He was a starter for the Rams when they won Super Bowl LVI.
Banks believes Edwards’ experience, intelligence and personality have allowed him to quickly fit in with the group.
“He's brought a lot. Savviness, smarts, laughter,” Banks said. He's bringing everything to the room. I mean, he's definitely a guy who fits in well with our scheme and let alone not just our scheme, but our OLI room as a whole. So he's been a great piece to our puzzle, for sure.

title: Saints have an Intriguing New Weapon in Athletic Rookie Tight End Oscar Delp
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints drafted tight end Oscar Delp with the 73rd overall pick in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and they had good reason: his athleticism and speed are stuff you cannot teach.
Delp, a 6-foot-5, 245-pound Georgia product, had an impressive pro day as he registered a 4.49-second 40-yard dash and a 38-inch vertical. In four seasons with UGA, Delp totaled 70 receptions for 854 yards and nine touchdowns in his career.
It will be interesting to see how the Saints use Delp with veterans Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant . Regardless, the Saints have been delving into multiple tight end packages and Delp’s versatility could be used there.
Delp is in a loaded tight end room led by Johnson and Fant, so he may not get the most playing time as of right now. However, his versatility could get him on the field and Delp wants to do whatever he can to get on the field and help his team win games regardless of the role.
“Right now, I'm just trying to find a way to get on the field. I know that he's been very successful with tight ends in his past, and I feel like I can bring something to the table. And we got a lot of very talented guys in our room and just different ways to get us on the field. Anything they need me to do,  I'm willing to get out there and just help us be successful.”
Delp has had a chance  to learn from the Saints’ veteran players on how to approach everything as a professional from the film room to being on the pratice field.
“It's been great. A lot of learning, a lot of growing. I’m very fortunate and blessed to be in the tight end room with some vets and some guys. I've got some games under their belt to just learn a lot from everyone, just taking everything in.”
Delp said that Georgia helped him transition to the NFL. That makes sense because the Bulldogs have been one of the NFL’s talent factories since Kirby Smart took over in 2016, especially at the tight end position. Since 2017, Georgia has produced seven tight ends that ended up being draft picks, including Pro Bowl tight end Brock Bowers .
“I think Georgia did a tremendous job preparing me and other players for the transition from college football to the NFL. I've talked to guys for years while I was in college, figuring out what's different and what happens in that transition. It's just like everyone said about Kirby — he's very big on developing players and practicing hard, and here it's a lot more mental.”
“It's not going to be as bang-bang every day as it is in college, where you're practicing six days in a row, basically scrimmaging for two hours a day. And I think they've done a really good job preparing me to be a receiving tight end, a blocking tight end, wherever they need me. I've done it in college, and I feel comfortable doing whatever they want me to do in this offense.”
A lot of Saints fans are excited about this year’s offense. That’s because they have Tyler Shough coming back after a strong rookie season, a reenergized running back room with Travis Etienne joining the franchise and a deep receiving room led by Chris Olave .
Delp has liked what he’s seen from the Saints’ offense, and he has a first-person view of what it will ultimately look like.
“I mean, I think it's just very explosive. I mean, I think it'd be a really explosive offense. You know, we got the guys to run the ball when we need to run the ball, and then we got the dudes who can go out on field and make big plays. I really think that, you know, the sky's the limit for this offense. And, you know, with the guys like Tyler and Spencer (Rattler) back there, I mean, you know, I think we have a really, really special team.”

title: Drew Brees' Hall of Fame Speech was the Ultimate Love Letter to New Orleans
full_text:
Few athletes have ever become as synonymous with a city as Drew Brees has with New Orleans
Nearly 20 years after arriving in a city that was processing the destruction that Hurricane Katrina brought to the city, Brees was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame , adding the sport’s highest individual honor to what was already a loaded resume.
After all, Brees brought the city of New Orleans a Super Bowl championship, broke many of the NFL’s passing records while active, and of course, one of the most meaningful player-city relationships that we have seen in professional sports.
During his induction speech in Canton, Ohio, Brees made sure New Orleans – the city that embraced him when a torn rotator cuff nearly derailed his career – remained the center of his story.
The circumstances that brought Brees and New Orleans together made their eventual success even more remarkable.
Hurricane Katrina devastated New Orleans and the Gulf Coast on Aug. 30, 2005, killing nearly 1,400 people, displacing hundreds of thousands and would end up being the costliest natural disaster in U.S. history. The Saints were forced to spend the 2005 season away from the Superdome and finished 3-13, leaving the franchise facing an uncertain future of its own.
Brees was at a crossroads as well.
He suffered a 360-degree labrum and rotator cuff tear in the regular season finale in 2005 while a member of the San Diego Chargers, an injury serious enough where people thought his career would bever be the same at best.
Despite those concerns, the Saints took a chance and signed him to a six-year, $60 million contract with New Orleans on March 14, 2006.
This came after the only other team to go after him, the Miami Dolphins, backed away from Brees due to concerns around his throwing shoulder , giving a chance for not only Brees to resurrect his career but to give hope to a city that desperately needed it.
Brees did not just give a city hope, he gave it 15 years of jubilation, transforming the Saints into perennial contenders and leading the franchise to its first Super Bowl championship in a 31-17 win over New Orleans native Peyton Manning and the Indianapolis Colts. He also became one of the most prolific quarterbacks in NFL history and one of the most beloved athletes New Orleans has ever known.
"New Orleans ... You trusted me with the soul of the city, and I would’ve died to protect that calling." 📺 @ProFootballHOF Enshrinement on ESPN/NFLN pic.twitter.com/S0avpW9hDS
Nearly two decades after taking a chance on New Orleans — and New Orleans taking a chance on him — Brees stood in Canton surrounded by family, friends and members of the Who Dat Nation who made the trip to witness his induction.
When it came time to explain what New Orleans meant to him, Brees made it clear that New Orleans is a special city and the bond forged in 2006 never disappeared.
“New Orleans has been through a lot to the point where in some cases the feeling was we may have lost everything,” Brees said. “It may never come back the same. Storms teach us that our greatest treasures aren’t the things we own. They’re the people we love, and the way we show up for one another. It reminds us to hold our loved ones a little closer, to love a little harder, to laugh a little louder, and to never take a single day for granted. Sometimes it takes losing what can be replaced to truly appreciate the things that can’t.
"New Orleans, you accepted me; you embraced me; you believed in me but more importantly, you trusted me with the soul of the city and I would have died to protect that calling.”
As the saying goes, “If you love New Orleans, it will love you back.”

title: Pete Werner's Starting Job Suddenly in Jeopardy as Danny Stutsman Surges
full_text:
There are always offseason position battles in the NFL, and the New Orleans Saints are no exception.
Second-year linebacker Danny Stutsman has taken first-team reps ahead of veteran Pete Werner for the second straight practice, the clearest change in Wednesday’s rotation. This move also is the most seismic of them all as Werner has been a starter for the Saints since his rookie season, racking up 408 tackles with 256 of them being solo.
However, Werner did struggle a bit last season, as he had a 46.8 tackling grade and a 15.8 missed-tackle rate, according to Pro Football Focus. Combine that with Stutsman being drafted in the Kellen Moore era and a completely different defensive playcaller in Brandon Staley when they took over last season, and Werner may be in trouble.
Nonetheless, Moore said Monday that the changes were “no big deal,” adding that the Saints were going to rotate their players throughout training camp. Even so, that competition still matters to players like Stutsman and Werner, both of whom believe they belong in starting roles.
“There’s a respect between everyone in the room, but it’s the kind of job that you want to win. Every day you’re fighting out there and putting your best thing on tape.”
Stutsman was a fourth-round pick by the Saints in 2025 as a potential successor to DeMario Davis . While that may seem far-fetched because he was drafted in the middle of the draft, his production made you believe that he was a steal.
While in college, Stutsman recorded over 100 tackles in each of his final three seasons while at Oklahoma. He posted a career-high 125 tackles as a sophomore in 2022 and finished his time as a Sooner with 376 total stops — ninth in school history — along with 36 tackles for loss, eight sacks, three interceptions, four forced fumbles, and eight pass breakups.
Now, Stutsman has a shot to live up to his “draft steal” label and claim a starting role in the linebacking corps inside the same building where Rickey Jackson, Sam Mills and Jonathan Vilma once roamed.
“That’s a dream,” Stutsman said when asked about the possibility he wants to be a starter. “That’s kind of why you wake up. That’s motivation. At the end of the day, you want to contribute as much as you can for the defense to do as much as I can.

title: John Harbaugh Remains Tight-lipped About Whether Starters Will Play vs. Vikings
full_text:
A day after pleading the fifth regarding whether quarterback Jaxson Dart and the rest of the starters on both sides of the ball would see any snaps in the preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings on Saturday, New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh still wasn’t willing to reveal his exact plans.
“I plan on not talking about who's gonna play. That's what I plan on doing. I just decided to leave it out there,” Harbaugh said.
“We'll see when the game comes. That’ll make the speculation show so much more fun.”
Also undoubtedly frustrating for the Giants fans who are anxious to get their first look at how the team, and in particular the offense as led by Dart, the second-year quarterback look in the new offense implemented by offensive coordinator Matt Nagy.
There is sort of a precedent for what Harbaugh might do. When he was head coach of the Ravens, he only had quarterback Lamar Jackson take part in 123 preseason snaps dating back to Jackson’s rookie season in 2018.
But an argument can be made that the Ravens were in a little better place than the Giants, who are coming off a four-win season and are starting mostly from scratch under Harbaugh.
While Harbaugh insisted that he values preseason reps, he added that there is a balance to be struck, and that the balance consists of getting a look at other guys, getting the starters quality work against other opponents, and keeping everyone as healthy as possible.
“You have to make that decision,” he said. “In the past three or four years, we hardly played any starters. Before that, we would play them a series or two, and sometimes we even went in on all three games.
“People used a lot of different formulas. Our formula was pretty much to spread the reps out evenly through the three games for the guys that needed to play. And we have a plan for that right now.”
While no one is suggesting that Dart and the starters play an entire game, let alone an entire quarter, a couple of series for them to get their feet wet against live competition wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing to gauge where everything stands.
“That’s a big part of it – executing a new offense – but also a young quarterback,” Harbaugh acknowledged.
“We've got a young quarterback who's just in his second year, who didn't play a whole season even last year. So, he's just getting started. And we're going to be playing two of the best teams in our conference right out of the gates. And so, we'd like to be ready for that.”
The only way to be ready for that is to play the starters, even if it’s a little bit here and there.
It’s been a summer of inconsistency for Jaxson Dart as he acclimates to the new offense, but the second-year quarterback believes he’s light years ahead of where he was at this point last year.
“Yeah, I definitely feel like I'm way ahead of where I was last year from just an experience standpoint,” he said.
“Being able to learn conceptual NFL systems, being able to have the leadership, being able to see things through different lenses of different positions, just from obviously my experience.
“So, that's what makes me really excited about this year. I feel like it's just another opportunity for big growth, and I wouldn't want it with any other coaches than we have right now, as well as any other players in the group that we have.”
He’s especially excited by the offensive system that’s been implemented by offensive coordinator Matt Nagy.
“Yeah, he's definitely aggressive. He's definitely wanting to create explosive plays. But I think the big thing is he wants to always stay ahead of the sticks. He wants to be moving forward,” he said.
“That's the big point of emphasis that we have on any negative plays, whether it may be penalties, whether it may be loss of yardage on a run or sacks; he's really big on minimizing those things.
“I think that as an offensive coordinator, when you're able to get your players to do that, it definitely helps him feel like he's in control of the game, helps our offense get into a flow.”
In yet another positive step forward for wide receiver Malik Nabers, he donned the red “no-contact” jersey for the first time since beginning his rehab from a torn ACL.
That naturally generated some buzz, as Nabers, in participating in drills at a walkthrough pace, continues to ramp up toward possibly increasing his workload as soon as next week, at a faster pace.
“It's great to have him back out there,” Dart said. “I've said this before, he has a certain presence about him anytime he touches the field, and I think the big thing today was also you just saw how excited he was himself to be out there.
“Can't wait for him to be full go.”
Harbaugh said wide receiver Jalin Hyatt (leg) would not play Saturday against the Vikings, joining Nabers, who is also out.
Cornerback Paulson Adebo (hamstring) is among those players who will be a game-time decision.
And although Harbaugh didn’t mention center John Michael Schmitz (concussion) as being among those who won’t play Saturday, the fourth-year center’s availability would appear to be in doubt, which would give Bryan Hudson a chance to see extended playing time.

title: Giants Sign Two Cornerbacks, Cut Ties With Two Others Ahead of Preseason Opener
full_text:
Ahead of their preseason opener against Minnesota on Saturday, the New York Giants , who are currently thin at cornerback, have signed Ugo Amadi and Sam Webb and released David Long and waived/injured D.J. James, the latter two being players they had signed last week.
Amadi is a 2019 fourth-round draft pick by the Seattle Seahawks out of Oregon. He developed into a starter for the Seahawks in 2020. Still, after peaking, the Seahawks traded him to the Philadelphia Eagles in August 2022, who in turn traded him to the Tennessee Titans a week and a half later.
He spent the 2022 season with the Kansas City Chiefs, and from 2023 until last year, the 29-year-old Amadi was with the New Orleans Saints, where he contributed at nickel and on special teams.
The 5-foot-9, 201-pound Amadi has appeared in 85 regular season games with 17 starts over his career. He has one interception, 22 pass breakups, two forced fumbles, 208 total tackles, 12 tackles for loss and 2.0 sacks.
Amadi played just one snap on defense last season (in Week 3 against Seattle) after playing in 527 the year prior for the Saints. Amadi played in 96 special teams snaps in 2025, up from the 42 he logged for the Saints in 2024.
Webb, 28, signed as an undrafted free agent with the Las Vegas Raiders out of Missouri following the 2022 draft. He also made stops with the Carolina Panthers in 2023 before returning to the Raiders in 2024.
He was most recently with the Cleveland Browns, for whom he played 137 defensive snaps last season, all of those as a perimeter cornerback.
Webb, 6-foot and 194 pounds, has appeared in 28 regular-season games with three starts. He has four pass breakups and 37 tackles over his career.
The Giants' cornerback room has been hit hard by injuries. Currently, Dru Phillips (knee), Paulson Adebo (undisclosed), and Greg Newsome II (knee) are all dealing with injuries that, per head coach John Harbaugh, are not believed to be long-term concerns.
Still, those injuries will apparently leave the Giants short-staffed at the position when they hit the gridiron on Saturday to host the Minnesota Vikings.
The Gians hosted a visit with former Lions first-round pick Terrion Arnold on Wednesday, but  it's unknown if the talks progressed to the point of a potential contract.

title: Giants Camp Live Updates: Cornerback Injuries Piling Up Ahead of Preseason Opener
full_text:
The New York Giants are back on the practice field for practice No. 14 of the summer, a session scheduled to last 2.5 hours, the maximum allowed. It will also be the last full practice of this week before the team hits the MetLife Stadium field for Saturday’s preseason game against the Minnesota Vikings.
Head coach John Harbaugh has put the team to the test with the long, drawn-out practices that have packed a lot of reps into the allotted time. The sessions held each day at 1:30 p.m. aim to help the players get into optimal condition so they can come out of the gate quickly.
But the injuries are starting to pile up. While nothing is considered long-term, at least according to Harbaugh, the Giants' cornerbacks have been hit by the injury bug.
The team has been missing slot cornerback Dru Phillips (knee), Greg Newsome II (knee), newcomer D.J. James (undisclosed), and Paulson Adebo (undisclosed). With those guys banged up, the Giants are potentially looking at a starting cornerback group of Deonte Banks and rookie Colton Hood, with Nic Jones, Art Green, David Long, and Korie Black as the depth.
That’s not necessarily a good development for a position that was already in a potential state of flux. Again, none of the injuries are thought to be long-term, but with the preseason games starting up this weekend, every missed game doesn’t help settle what the final picture will be.
Also worth noting for today’s camp day, the assistant coaches will be speaking to the media for the first time this summer, so there are sure to be some interesting nuggets to come from those sessions. So be sure to follow our live blog, which will capture it all.
(Note: The Giants do not allow live tweeting during practice, but video clips and such taken before the team drills begin have been allowed, though they won’t be posted until after practice ends.)
This live blog will remain open until 6:00 p.m. The page should update automatically.

title: Giants' Presumed Starter at Safety Is Suddenly Fighting for His Job
full_text:
Summer training camp is a time of intense competition across the entire landscape of an NFL roster. But if we’re being real, some positions end up more competitive than others, and then there are some where, just when you think things are set, along comes a surprise.
Such is the case for the New York Giants , who have themselves a competition brewing for a starting job at safety between Tyler Nubin, Jason Pinnock and Ar’Darius Washington.
Nubin, the incumbent, was the team’s second-round pick in 2024 out of Minnesota and came into the NFL with a reputation as a ballhawk after recording 13 interceptions during his college career.
But after a promising rookie season that was cut short by four games because of an ankle injury, Nubin took a noticeable step backward last season.
His missed-tackle percentage rose sharply from 4.9% as a rookie to 9.3%, a result of taking bad angles and overcommitting to filling inside gaps while leaving the edges exposed.
His coverage rating also deteriorated , jumping from 95.7 in his rookie campaign to 119.5 last season. Nubin has recorded only two pass breakups in two seasons and has yet to record an interception in the NFL.
This summer, Nubin has been moving around the formation, working closer to the box where it’s thought his skill set is a better fit.
“Tyler Nubin is getting better,” defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said on Tuesday.
“His biggest challenge right now is just looking at the right things. When he looks at the right things on a consistent level, he makes plays. So, that's been his focus, but he's flashed.”
Apparently not enough. The coaches are exploring their options with Washington, who was with Wilson (when he was the Ravens' defensive backs coach in 2023) and Harbaugh in Baltimore, and Pinnock, who is back with the Giants after a one-year stop in San Francisco.
Washington and Pinnock were both signed this past offseason in free agency after the Giants lost Dane Belton to the Jets.
Washington is a Swiss Army knife who can play safety or in the slot. He’s been limited to just 29 games in his career, mainly due to injuries, and yes, he’s undersized at just 5-foot-8 and 180 pounds.
But when he has played, there has been much to like, including the fact that he plays fearlessly and plays with the physicality of a much bigger safety.
His elite football instincts allow him to play faster because he can process what’s unfolding before him rapidly. This has helped him anticipate where a ball is going to be thrown so that, if he’s in the vicinity, he can get a jump on the route.
In 2024, the lone season in which he played in 17 games, he recorded his two career interceptions to date. He also posted a career-best 78.1 coverage rating that year and allowed just 62.7% of the passes against him to be completed.
Pinnock, whose bread and butter has been in run support given his downhill style, has been better in coverage at the third level, showing efficiency as the defender on vertical passes and in getting into position on deep passes.
He also kept up with tight ends coming up the seam, and not only has he been a sound tackler, but he’s also a good blitzer, having blitzed 91 times in his career, generating 6.5 sacks, seven hurries and four knockdowns.
There is still time before the Giants have to decide who they’ll be rolling with and in what situations, but Harbaugh admitted that he’s been pleased with the level of competition shown thus far at the position.
“I think it's a credit to how well those guys are playing. They have played like starters for quite a number of reps. So, let's take a look at them with that group,” he said this week.
While the players’ histories offer a glimpse into what they’re capable of delivering, Pinnock said it’s all about what is done today.
“Day by day. Opportunity arises, I rise to the occasion. Every time you throw me in there, I'm gonna ball. This is a new regime, so ‘22 to ‘24 [doesn’t matter]. It's about ‘26,” he said.

title: Giants QB Brandon Allen Is Quietly an NFL Preseason Legend Over Last Decade
full_text:
NFL preseason games offer players at the end of the depth chart a chance to make an on-field impact, showcasing themselves to their coaching staff in a final push for a roster spot.
New York Giants backup quarterback Brandon Allen is more than familiar with the process. Allen isn't just experienced in the preseason. He's the most productive quarterback in the last decade of NFL preseason games, according to Pro Football Focus , with 2,579 preseason passing yards.
Allen has spent time on various NFL rosters across his nine seasons in the league. He has played in the preseason for the Jacksonville Jaguars, Los Angeles Rams, Cincinnati Bengals, San Francisco 49ers, and Tennessee Titans.
Across those nine preseason campaigns, he has thrown 385 passes, completing 242 of them for 2,579 yards, nine touchdowns, and 16 interceptions.
He has an average NFL passer rating of 72.9 in the preseason. Those numbers would line up with a discouraging single-season campaign for a starting quarterback.
The Giants signed Allen this offseason on a one-year, $1.45 million contract. He is currently the team's third quarterback, behind Jaxson Dart and Jameis Winston. Allen is a long shot to make New York's final 53-man roster.
Still, he should get plenty of opportunities throughout the preseason to increase his counting stats. Giants head coach John Harbaugh has not made it clear how much he will play his starters in the preseason, but Dart likely won't see much work.
Allen should command most of the late-game snaps in each of New York's three preseason matchups, especially considering that the Giants don't have a young backup QB to develop. Playing with a deep group of receivers, he should continue his high preseason production.
As far as a roster spot though, he is once again looking fromt he outside in unless the Giants plan to keep three quarterbacks on the roster.
Preseason stats aren't necessarily a sign of quality. Typically, NFL teams only play their starters for a series or two in preseason games before letting backups take over for the rest of the way. The best quarterbacks in the league are never going to have the highest totals in passing yards or passing touchdowns.
Still, the 33-year-old quarterback can hang his hat on being one of the most productive preseason players over the last ten years.

title: Does Giants' Offensive "Gumbo" Recipe Have Too Many Cooks in the Kitchen?
full_text:
Making a gumbo might seem as easy as throwing together a bunch of high-quality ingredients in a pot and letting the flavors blend, sort of like what the New York Giants are doing on offense.
But in reality, a good gumbo takes time and a degree of discipline to find the right blend.
The Giants’ attempt to create their own “gumbo” by using bits and pieces of the recipes of multiple assistant coaches who have prior coordinator experience with other NFL teams has proven to be a challenge as the offense looks to smooth out the inconsistencies it has encountered and get into a rhythm.
The Giants offense, headed by coordinator Matt Nagy, has been inconsistent this summer, with quarterback Jaxson Dart trying to find a comfort level working under center, getting used to new receivers, and operating on a whole new level that barely matches what he did in college or his rookie season.
This is not to say that Dart is the sole reason for the offense’s inconsistency–credit has to be given to the defense, which has thrown a lot at their teammate in an effort to help him become the best version of himself–but it’s fair to wonder if less is more in this instance.
Backup quarterback Jameis Winston believes the intention behind the offense is “exciting” given the creativity of those coaches with prior coordinator experience contributing to the build: Nagy, senior offensive assistant Greg Roman, quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan, and tight ends coach Tim Kelly.
“I think that's a great example of the leadership that (Head) Coach (John) Harbaugh has, that he's letting his coaches build a system that is very unique to all of them.
“I can compare it to gumbo,” Winston said. “There's just so many good mixes in there. You’ve got the old school, you’ve got the new school, and you’ve got just this melting pot of greatness. So, it's really fun.”
It’s also somewhat concerning after Nagy revealed that the team was about halfway through all its installs with a little more than a month to go before the start of the regular season. But Harbaugh tried to downplay the notion of the offense being behind the curve.
“That's normal,” he said when told of Nagy’s comment. “He says halfway through. I would say probably the truth of it is he's probably like five percent through because throughout the course of the season, a lot of the things that you do–how do you define the install? Is it the plays, or is it all the ways you can run the plays, and all the personnel groups you can run, and all the formations you can run them out and hide them in?
“You've watched Matt Nagy, and you've watched the offenses he's been a part of. They hide their plays all the time, but they have core principles in the offense. So, I would say most of our core principles are in, but some of our methodology is going to be basic methodology to get the plays in; it's not in yet.”
While one can appreciate the team’s desire to find the right blend for their “gumbo,” it's also fair to wonder — given that the Giants need a fast start to the season — whether the offense will eventually need to scale back and simplify things if the inconsistency continues.

title: Giants Notebook: Beckham Set to Play, Dart's Status a Mystery, Zvada Booms a 62-Yarder
full_text:
John Harbaugh’s New York Giants will get their first taste of live action against an opponent donning another colored jersey on Saturday when the Giants host the Minnesota Vikings at MetLife Stadium in a 1 p.m. kickoff.
Harbaugh didn’t go into his plans regarding who is going to play and who won’t–the Giants still have another couple of days before needing to make that decision. But one player who will definitely be part of the action is receiver Odell Beckham Jr.
“I think he's ramped up, honestly,” Harbaugh said after Wednesday’s practice. “You saw him on the sideline over there. I mean, he almost got his feet down on that really tough catch. He's looked good. He's in shape. He's taking every rep he's supposed to take in practice.
“I feel like he's getting stronger every day. He's in a good place. He will play, and I'm looking forward to seeing him play.”
Giants fans have long awaited the chance to see Beckham back in a Big Blue uniform. While Beckham is not the same player he was the first time around with the Giants, Harbaugh apparently feels that the 33-year-old receiver is in good enough shape to give the team quality snaps.
Beckham, who last played in 2024 as a member of the Miami Dolphins, only appeared in nine games and looked far from healthy. But in 2023, when he was with Harbaugh in Baltimore, Beckham, in 14 games with six starts, gave the Ravens 35 receptions for 565 yards and three scores.
Beckham has been diligent in his training to ensure that he finishes his NFL career on his terms. When he was first signed in the spring, he seemed sluggish all around, but since camp has begun, Beckham is showing signs of having something left in the tank as far as getting open and being able to separate.
“I probably want to see him play enough, but you got to play other guys too,” Harbaugh said when asked how much time Beckham would see on Saturday.
“I think he could play the whole game and he'd be fine. He's in shape to do it, but we're not going to play anybody really the whole game just because we've got 90 guys.”
While Beckham will be among those playing on offense on Saturday, Harbaugh was a lot less forthcoming when it came to the question of who will be throwing him the ball.
“That’s a good question,” Harbaugh said when asked if quarterback Jaxson Dart would be playing in the preseason opener. “I’m gonna have to dodge. I'm going to have to bob and weave. I'll let you know later.”
Dart has been having an up-and-down camp so far as he gets acclimated to the new offense, which requires him to work under center. He did have a pair of on-target passes during Wednesday’s padded session, hitting running back Devin Singletary on a wheel route and also connecting with rookie Malachi Fields in a 7-on-7 drill.
Receiver Malik Nabers, who has been steady as far as getting some on-field work every day, worked out with a trainer for a short bit before heading inside for the rest of the practice.
But the good news is that Nabers could be ramping up further very soon, according to Harbaugh.
“Yeah, he's kind of exactly where he's been,” Harbaugh said. “And we're looking towards soon ramping him up into some group periods and perhaps some team periods. Maybe next week; we'll see.”
To date, Nabers hasn’t done anything with 7-on-7s or team drills at full speed, though he did partake in team drills during a walkthrough pace when the team was in West Virginia.
But despite that, the receiver also hasn’t had any known setbacks that have forced the team to dial back on his reps, which is a positive sign in his quest to be ready for Week 1 of the regular season.
“He's doing great. He's working hard. Spirits are high. And yeah, we'll see where we're at next week,” Harbaugh said.
The following Giants did not take part in Wednesday’s practice:
Harbaugh said that Hyatt, whose hold on a roster spot is slipping with each passing day, “should be back in a reasonable period.”
He also said that Adebo is day-to-day, but did not specify what the cornerback is dealing with.
Others who were limited included cornerbacks Greg Newsome II (knee) and Dru Phillips (knee), both of whom took part in individual drills only.
Rookie guard Francis Mauigoa (neck) took his full practice workload after being limited in Tuesday’s session.
Undrafted rookie free agent kicker Dominic Zvada ended practice with a 62-yard field goal that had plenty of distance with 11 seconds to go in a simulated end-of-game situation.
“I thought he was going to make it,” Harbaugh said of Zvada’s attempt. “(Assistant Head Coach/Special Teams Coordinator) Chris Horton told me the 42 is the line, so I had to give him a hard time after that. So, it was actually a little further back, and it was a great kick, great snap, nice to see.”
Zvada, who hit all six of his attempts (Ben Sauls went 4-of-5 on his), appears to have a slight edge in the kicking competition, but Harbaugh gave an indication that the competition with Sauls is far from being over.
“The bottom line is you got to kick it straight consistently,” he said. “So, having a big leg is a big deal. Kicking it straight consistently is a bigger deal.
“I think both those guys have done that very well, and Ben has a very good leg, too. I don't want to imply that he doesn't. Ben's a very strong leg guy, as well, but they're both having really good camps.”

title: John Harbaugh Breaks Down Giants' Risk-Reward Calculus on Terrion Arnold
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is on a mission to hit the ground running in his first season at the team’s helm, and to accomplish that, he’s all about bringing in good players whose skill sets can help out.
That’s the reason behind the Giants’ interest in former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold, who is currently facing felony charges that led to the Lions parting ways with their former first-round draft pick.
“We want to be aggressive in every way, whatever we can do, find everything out we can about any player that can help us be better,” Harbaugh said when asked about Arnold.
“The margins are tight in the National Football League. You try to win a game. You come up with a good play. You can find a play on the internet that somebody puts out there that one of your opponents is running in practice, man. You look for those too. So, we're looking for players that can help us all the time. And he's a player that can help us.”
The Giants hosted a visit by Arnold on Wednesday, presumably to get to know him and to gain additional clarity about Arnold’s situation. Harbaugh said that the organization has already performed a deep dive into Arnold’s circumstances and has presented the head coach with an overview.
“If there is a decision to be made on any player that you don't want to go there with a player, then this organization, they won't go there,” Harbaugh said. “And so, that decision would also have to be made.
“It's more than just what you read in the papers, though. I mean, you got to find out exactly where everything stands. And I think, I do know that our people do a great job of that.”
Arnold, who has denied any wrongdoing , could be looking at a lengthy legal process while he fights to clear his name, according to Harbaugh. And that is something the Giants have also weighed when deciding whether to make an offer.
“I think you have to decide, where does the legal process stand? What are we really talking about here? What does it look like? And you have to make a judgment along those lines,” he said, also acknowledging that the league could put the cornerback on the exempt list while he sorts out his situation," Harbaugh said.
Therein lies another consideration for the Giants. “You try to do the best you can to anticipate what that might be and see if it's worth it,” Harbaugh said.
“There's risk-reward. There are things to be gained and things to be lost. And you just got to balance it out and try to make a two-fold decision.”

title: Why the Giants Kicking Battle Isn't Nearly as Close as Fans Think
full_text:
For those who think that the New York Giants kicker battle has already been decided in favor of undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada over Ben Sauls, assistant head coach/special teams coordinator Chris Horton said no such decision has been made.
“ It's two young guys that are doing very well,” Horton said of Zvada and incumbent Ben Sauls, both of whom are listed as being dead even on the team’s newly released unofficial depth chart .
“Both guys, where they are right now from where they were during this spring, I mean, it's been tremendous growth just watching these guys go out and compete against each other. They know that they compete, and they come out every day, and they work hard.”
The Giants have had the kickers alternate during team periods, with field goal attempts from varying distances. Back in the spring, Zvada, who struggled in his final year at Michigan, was perfect during OTAs while Sauls struggled with his conversions.
So far this summer, it’s fair to say that the battle has been even as the coaches try to figure out which of the two they can trust the most.
“Trust is a big thing, right? Trust comes with a lot of responsibility,” Horton said. “It's not because they're young that you have to find a way to trust them. It's what they do when they're out there. You build trust through your work. You build trust through your preparation, and the preparation that both these guys are bringing every day—we're trusting them, right?
“We're trusting them, but we're going to have to trust them in the big moments, and we try to put them in those situations so when they go out there, we feel pretty good about it.”
The Giants obviously have enough trust in both young legs, and that was made evident when they did not bring in a veteran kicker to compete with the duo after cutting Jason Sanders earlier in the year.
But whereas past Giants staffs have preferred battle-tested kickers, this staff seems willing to take a leap of faith, realizing that even the best kickers in the game had to start somewhere.
“That's 100% correct. We think about how we all started, right?” Horton said. “When I got up to be a coordinator for the very first time, there were things that I needed to learn on the job, and so it's just like any other position, just like any other thing, that we all got to start somewhere, right?
“Somebody's just got to be willing to give you an opportunity, but that opportunity, as I said, comes with the process. Once you go through the process, you follow that process, and you believe in yourself, everything else takes care of itself because it comes with discipline and consistency.
“For the kickers, consistency is making kicks.”
And for the coaches, it’s about being patient, particularly if a kicker hits a rough spot.
“They're judged on makes and misses, right?” Horton said. “Sometimes you've got to go through a couple things to get yourself out of those things. And it's a lot easier to say, ‘Well, let's find the next guy,’ but then you're starting all over with the next guy.
“The next guy's on the street because he had the same issues that probably one of these young guys had. So, you try to go through the process. You weed out all that stuff, and you say, ‘Okay, what's the standard? What's going to be our standard?’ And as long as we uphold that standard and we're consistent in what we do, we're going to be fine.”
They’ll find out starting this weekend if Horton’s belief comes to fruition.

title: Giants Unofficial Depth Chart Takeaways: Rookies Rising, Battles Still Unsettled
full_text:
The New York Giants have released their first unofficial depth chart of the summer— unofficial because the depth chart does not come from the coaches but is instead compiled by the staff based on interpretations of where guys have taken the majority of their practice reps.
Still, the depth chart is always fun to dissect for clues as to how the team is taking shape, so let’s look at some of the key takeaways.
As anticipated, first-rounders Francis Mauigoa and Arvell Reese are listed as starters at their respective positions (right guard and inside linebacker).
Second-round pick Colton Hood is currently listed as the third cornerback behind projected starter Paulson Adebo and veteran Deonte Banks.
But with Adebo and Greg Newsome II both dealing with injuries that make them question marks for Saturday’s preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings, Hood could very well find himself with an opportunity to start.
Receiver Malachi Fields, the third-round pick, is listed as the third receiver, behind Malik Nabers and Calvin Austin III.
Defensive lineman Bobby Jamison-Travis currently is third on the chart at nose tackle, behind D.J. Reader and Leki Fotu.
Meanwhile, offensive tackle J.C. Davis, the second of the three sixth-round draft picks, is listed as the third-string left tackle, behind starter Andrew Thomas and backup Marcus Mbow.
Jack Kelly, the last of the three sixth-round picks, is listed as the backup weakside linebacker behind Reese. Kelly has been having a solid camp and projects not only to nail down a spot as the fourth inside linebacker but also a core special teams role.
No surprise here, as Darius Alexander is listed as the first-team defensive end next to Shelby Harris at defensive tackle and D.J. Reader at nose tackle.
Alexander has been pushing for a job on the first-team defense as far back as the end of last season, having continued his quest over the spring and summer.
The Giants list Aaron Stinnie OR Evan Neal as the backup right guard behind Mauigoa. There are actually several instances where two players are listed, an indication that the competition is either close or there is no clear-cut guy at that spot.
But what’s most interesting about this one is that Neal has been “glued” to the third-team offense, something that might not necessarily be the case given the depth chart listing.
What’s also interesting is that Stinnie has mainly been a career left guard and has played just 15 regular-season snaps on the right side , all coming in 2019, his rookie year.
Despite there being a rotation at cornerback on the first-team defense, Paulson Adebo is still listed among the starters.
Again, though, with Adebo nursing some injury, it remains to be seen whether he plays in Saturday's preseason opener.
Even when Adebo does return to play, it’s clear that he’s still in competition to hold onto his starting job.
In another somewhat surprising move, the unofficial depth chart lists Abdul Carter OR Kayvon Thibodeaux as the starting SAM linebacker.
Entering camp, it was thought that perhaps Carter, who finished the 2025 season in place of the injured Thibodeaux on a strong note, would lead to Thibodeaux working mostly with the second-team defense in camp.
Head coach John Harbaugh, however, didn’t see it that way when asked about Thibodeaux’s handling of being with the second-team defense.
“I don't think he's worried about it. He knows he's going to play a bunch. These guys know. We have three starters at outside linebacker. Those are all starting football players. So, slice it how you want. Do a depth chart any way you want. Those guys are all going to play a ton of football,” he said.
Finally, we get to the position group that everyone wants to know about: receivers.
The first thing that jumps out is that this depth chart doesn’t list a slot receiver. That doesn’t mean the Giants won’t have one, but it's likely a sign they will be leaning more into 12- and 13-personnel, or they could be planning to deploy tight end Isaiah Likely into more of that role.
As for how the receivers stack up, it looks like it will be a mix-and-match. As already noted, the top three receivers at one spot are Nabers, Austin, and Fields.
At the other receiver spot, Darius Slayton, Darnell Mooney, and Odell Beckham Jr. are the top three, followed by veteran JuJu Smith-Schuster, Jalin Hyatt, Dalen Cambre, and Xavier Gipson.
Nabers isn’t expected to play in any of the preseason games as he continues his ramp-up from ACL surgery.
Fields has been having a solid camp thus far, to the point where he could be in line for a bigger role on offense than maybe initially thought as his NFL career gets underway.
The Giants have the same situation at running back where they list “Cam Skattebo OR Tyrone Tracy, Jr” as the first-team running back.
New York is expected to deploy a committee approach at running back rather than name one specific guy as the bellcow, so this development really doesn’t come as a surprise, nor does it necessarily indicate which running back is going to see the bulk of the carries any given week, as the specific opponent and matchups will instead dictate that.
Braxton Berrios, who has had himself a solid camp, is listed as the main punt returner, followed by Calvin Austin III and then Xavier Gipson.
Berrios is also second on the unofficial depth chart at kickoff returner, behind cornerback Deonte Banks. Dante Miller and Eric Gray are third and fourth guys at kickoff returner.
Despite undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada having jumped out in terms of consistency this summer, he is not listed as being equal to Ben Sauls for the kicking job.
